# Eight-video mining: one coherent Jet, complete useful jobs

**Research captured 2026-09-11, with individually dated revisions. DOCS ONLY.** Earlier source captures and executable observations retain their original identities and limits.

**Research and preparation closed 2026-09-12.** All eight analyses, 124 independent ballots and 329 work homes are reconciled and read back. Tower holds 105 ready owner-review surfaces and 19 complete performance-gated drafts. Every work home has an existing epoch, a meaningful same-epoch milestone, priority and work order. No new choice is ratified; no implementation, current-tree runtime parity or competitive win is claimed.

<a id="result"></a>

## The recommendation: make one correct meaning carry the whole job

Jet's strongest direction is not a larger collection of clever spellings. It is a language in which the same checked meaning survives every step of useful work: choosing a value, reading data, stopping a loop, closing a resource, serving a request, changing a program, and running on a real target.

That is an **analyst recommendation**, not a demonstrated competitive victory. The captured material contains strong ideas and concrete failures. It does not establish that current Jet is the best default in all eight areas. The right response is neither to copy every peer feature nor to dismiss the failures as unfinished polish. Complete the shared mechanisms, repair the broken promises, and add a public surface only when its benefit survives a fair whole-job comparison.

The low-regret direction has four parts:

1. **Make existing promises true.** A diagnostic must name the right file. Cleanup must happen at the right scope boundary. A stopped iterator must not consume work it was required to leave alone. A typed operation must preserve its selected data and numeric meaning.
2. **Reuse the owner of each rule.** One checked program should supply editor facts. One coding model should supply data validation. One ownership model should govern views, streams and resources. Related clients should not each invent their own version of those rules.
3. **Finish ordinary jobs.** A useful script or service includes input, errors, cancellation, cleanup, packaging and an understandable result—not only an attractive happy-path function.
4. **Earn specialized surfaces.** If a new public operation is justified by less work, less memory or faster execution, its complete candidate program must beat an equivalent ordinary program before that option is ratified—the owner approves that public contract. Source-level arithmetic counts are not that proof.

The aim is to remove avoidable drawbacks, not to write flattering ballots. A second validator, scheduler or semantic index is often an avoidable cost. A borrowed result's dependence on its source storage is a real contract. A GPU collective's participation rules are real obligations. Keep those distinctions visible; do not bury genuine costs or pad every option with “more code” and “implementation effort.”

### A reading path, not a data dump

- Start with [the eight programmer questions](#eight-questions) for the direction and evidence limits.
- Read the choices that need explanation (source-cited record; not a new campaign choice) before considering individual ballots.
- Use [the dependency hierarchy](#execution-hierarchy) to understand the recorded ordering constraints. The verified epoch, milestone and work-order homes are in [Appendix G](#final-dispositions); Tower owns the queue.
- Use [the evidence contrasts](#exercised-contrasts) to see what actually happened on the recorded snapshots.
- Open [the complete topic analyses](#complete-analyses) for every worked comparison, micro-surface sweep and proposal.
- Use the [finding catalogue](#finding-catalogue), [finite inventories](#finite-inventories), [scope contracts](#scope-contracts) and [exact witnesses](#exact-witnesses) for exhaustive detail. The appendices preserve the accounting; they are not the argument.

## Eight videos, eight programmer questions, one direction

| Lens | The programmer's question | Recommended direction | What the evidence does not let us claim |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Enums](#topic-enums) | “Which kind of value is this, and what can I do with it?” | Preserve the existing closed-choice model, with honest case identity, metadata and checked external input. | A few successful cases do not establish recursive layout, arbitrary callback binary compatibility, allocation cost or every target. |
| [Iterators](#topic-iterators) | “What comes next, and who owns what I have already read?” | Make consumption, borrowing, failure, waiting and stopping explicit; then complete the useful adapter families. | A short chain is not proof of laziness, no copying, full stable-library parity or correct custom cursors. |
| [CoreLib](#topic-corelib) | “Can I do ordinary work without rebuilding the plumbing?” | Complete useful libraries around one coding, validation, ownership and error model; separate adoption, API profile and placement. | Exported names and peer documentation do not prove executable parity or equivalent format coverage. |
| [NestJS](#topic-nestjs) | “Will my form, server and client agree about the same request?” | Project checked application and data facts into a complete service; use explicit adapters rather than a parallel framework of hidden rules. | The frozen form failed before application work. It did not exercise HTTP validation, dependency-injection scope or a transport integration. |
| [Readability](#topic-readability) | “Can I understand what this code will do, here?” | Explain accurate local consequences and repair choices through existing tools; preserve canonical text composition and cleanup. | A tidy example or fewer lines does not establish comprehension, correct scope timing or faster human work. |
| [GPU](#topic-gpu) | “Do I need ordinary array operations, or explicit device cooperation?” | Start with truthful storage, placement and completion; reuse existing operations; admit expert surfaces only after exact legality and matched proof. | A CPU answer, a CUDA excerpt or a tiny matrix example does not establish Jet GPU execution or a speed win. |
| [Scripting](#topic-scripting) | “Can I finish this small job from first input to final cleanup?” | Keep one language from script to package to embedded component; make ordinary libraries and capability boundaries usable. | Narrow entry successes do not prove every process, HTTP, SQL, package, host or component lifecycle. |
| [Big codebases](#topic-bigcode) | “Can I make a safe change without reading the whole project?” | Make checked identities, versions and source ranges trustworthy; then project them into focused editor and review actions. | Existing compiler machinery is not evidence that every consumer preserves its meaning or that the resulting workflow improves productivity. |

These are not eight unrelated expansion programmes. They meet at a few mechanisms. A codec is the rule for turning values into an external representation and back. A view is access to someone else's storage under an ownership contract. A checked fact is something the compiler has established about a particular program version. A projection is another useful presentation of that same fact—not a second source of truth.

### Unity does not mean erasing useful distinctions

Consider two business cases that both contain an integer: an amount charged and an amount refunded. The payload type alone cannot tell them apart. A named case preserves that meaning. In contrast, a structural choice of the same member type twice does not manufacture two business roles. The shared sum mechanism should support both forms without pretending that their identities or conversions are identical.

The same rule applies elsewhere. A value arriving later is not an ended stream. A malformed tag is not necessarily a valid but unfamiliar tag. A host-owned buffer is not proof that a device kernel accesses it safely. Native in-process extension and an isolated component do not have the same boundary. Reuse the mechanism when the contracts match; preserve the distinction when it changes the caller's job.

<a id="decision-reader-guide"></a>

## Owner choices should teach the difference they ask the owner to accept

The canonical closure contains 124 independent choices: 8 Enum, 45 Iterator, 34 CoreLib, 17 NestJS, 3 Readability, 10 GPU, 2 Scripting and 5 BigCode. Their independence matters. An approval to maintain a codec is not approval for every wire category, its package placement, or a vendor dependency. An approval for a protocol adapter is not approval for its public cancellation and failure contract.

A reader should not need to decode a metadata container to understand a ballot. Lead with the job, show the same input under each option, and show the resulting value, error, ownership state or interaction. Then explain the precise contract and prerequisite evidence. Put historical source payloads and technical provenance outside the effective option text. When a retained old contract differs from the current option, label it as history; do not make the reader decide which nested paragraph wins.

The examples below are **teaching explanations**, not new Jet spellings or execution receipts. The exact authored code, recorded input bytes and observed outputs remain distinct in the topic and witness sections.

### 1. Continue, replay and restore are different iterator jobs

Imagine a cursor that has already read the first two rows of a file.

- **Continue** means read the next row from that cursor's current position.
- **Replay** means obtain the sequence again under an explicit source contract. A list can remain available; a live channel cannot be silently reopened.
- **Restore or copy a cursor state** means recover the same progress and associated state when that capability actually exists. Constructing a new cursor at the beginning is not restoration.

This difference controls the meaning of resume, replay, copy, Cartesian reuse and recovery proposals. It is not solved by giving all of them a convenient method name. The choices must state what happens to already-read items, external effects, buffered values and ownership. The recorded valid-prefix example demonstrates a stopping boundary; it is not a general checkpoint proof.

Some statements belong in the contract rather than the “downsides” column. `flat_map` visits each child sequence in order. It cannot reach a later child while it is still traversing an endless earlier child. A Cartesian product pairs every left item with every right item. It must make the reused dimension available under either a library adapter or ordinary nested loops. Those are not special defects invented by one alternative. A fair ballot explains them once, then identifies what actually differs.

### 2. Borrowing can save copies while making the caller keep storage available

Suppose a program selects two short strings from a much larger input. An owned copy can survive after the original input is released. A borrowed result still needs the original storage to remain available. That difference is meaningful even when both displays show the same two strings.

`D-ITER-VIEWCOLLECT1` therefore needs a lifetime example, not only matching `[1,2,3]` output. Its appeal is explicit borrowed materialization under existing provenance checks. Its genuine boundary is the caller's continuing obligation to the source owner. Do not claim that ordinary collection becomes silently no-copy, and do not benchmark a caller that needs independent ownership against one that does not.

Likewise, a scoped keyed run can expose values without first retaining the complete group, but advancing its parent may drain an unfinished group. That can perform reads or work the caller has not explicitly consumed. Explain that observable behaviour in `D-ITER-KEYRUNS1`; it is more useful than a generic warning that the API is complicated.

### 3. Binary interoperability has more than one independent decision

For BSON and MessagePack, the wire format is the bytes another program receives; the API is the operations a Jet caller uses. Separate three questions:

1. **Maintenance:** should Jet maintain this codec at all?
2. **Wire/API profile:** which values are preserved, and which produce an explicit error?
3. **Placement:** is the admitted codec stock or an optional first-party package?

The added adoption/profile choices make those questions independently answerable. Neither adoption nor placement silently selects Glaze or a MongoDB driver. MessagePack admission does not reopen the selected first binary format.

The native-profile examples must make the consequence visible:

| Input meaning | Native-preserving profile | JSON-shaped rejecting profile |
|---|---|---|
| A record with `count = 2` | Decode the count as 2. | Decode the count as 2. |
| A BSON record also carrying the ObjectId bytes `00` through `0b` | Preserve the ObjectId through the selected format-specific typed value. | Report the located unsupported native value; do not turn it into a string or silently omit it. |
| A MessagePack extension with type 1 and payload `[2]` | Preserve both the signed extension type and the payload. | Report unsupported extension data rather than invent a JSON-shaped substitute. |

These are intended option results, not observed decoder output. The retained wire fixtures are analyst derivations until exact-input execution cross-checks them.

The native profile's real commitment is format-specific typed meaning and its validation boundaries. The rejecting profile's real limitation is that otherwise ordinary native-containing documents cannot pass through that interface. Calling both “BSON support” without showing this difference hides the decision. The existing closed `DataTree` remains closed; typed native support does not authorize a second generic value algebra.

### 4. A GPU teaching example must not make the ordinary path artificially worse

For the group sum-of-squares choice, both programs must square the same input values, accumulate under the same numeric rule, produce the same shape and complete the same work. The ordinary path can use the existing square operation followed by `sum_axis`. The captured source makes the rank-one reduction result shape `[1]`; a further reshape to `[1]` adds no semantic value. It must not inflate the plain side of a performance comparison.

For the tile choice, ordinary `matmul`, `add` and `maximum` already express the whole finite job. The expert alternative is about explicit collective reuse and arithmetic control—not the invention of matrix multiplication. A 2×2 example can teach the intended stages. It cannot establish the benefit of a public tile protocol.

The same caution applies to physical types. Small integer-valued answers such as `[5,7,9]` can look correct under several storage and arithmetic choices. They do not establish 32-bit floating-point (F32) storage, rounding, device layout or GPU completion. The current source's host representation is not permission to reinterpret an ordinary Atomic cell—a cell with indivisible updates— as a device atomic.

### 5. A source site is different from a useful event name

`D-READ-LOGSITE1` asks whether existing `core.log` calls should carry a compiler-bound emitting site. Option A keeps the call unchanged and illustrates an additional known site containing the source identity, file, line, column, function and source digest. Option B keeps explicit author-supplied event fields and existing source lookup.

A stable event key can group all `row.saved` events. A compiler-bound site can identify the exact statement that emitted one record. Those are useful but different jobs. Show the unchanged call and the added site beside the event-only alternative. Do not imply that one replaces the other, and do not claim source lookup is exact when the record is bound to the wrong or stale source version.

The other local-reading and big-code proposals follow the same rule: expose checked facts accurately, then explain them. A shorter summary that hides an obligation or an edit projected onto the wrong declaration is not a readability improvement.

### 6. Protocol behaviour and distribution must remain separate

A first-party gRPC adapter can still have a poor cancellation or output-admission contract. A clear API can still be placed in the wrong package for its users. `D-NEST-GRPC-API1` and `D-NEST-GRPC1` therefore constrain different decisions. The selected API must spell out admission, deadlines/cancellation, status, bounded demand and cleanup; the placement vote does not settle those rules or approve a linked dependency.

Apply the same separation to the other seven added NestJS API choices. They should read as complete user jobs, not transport-name checkboxes. The ordinary form/server/client path remains a prerequisite for claims that those layers share validation; a compiler-lowering failure does not count as an HTTP error response.

### What makes a worthwhile tradeoff

A real tradeoff changes something the caller must care about: accepted values, ownership, progress, retained storage, ordering, deployment compatibility or the available result. A missing experiment is a proof gap. An input precondition is part of the contract. “Needs implementation” is neither an informative loss nor an argument against an option.

Prefer a design that removes an avoidable loss while preserving the job. Do not create an awkward second API to give a ballot two visibly different sides. Do not make the plain example copy, allocate, sort or materialize more than a lawful ordinary solution needs. When an existing operation already completes the job, it remains the real alternative—not an impoverished strawman.

<a id="execution-hierarchy"></a>

## Execute through existing epochs, with real mechanism dependencies

This hierarchy is an **execution recommendation**, not a new Tower queue, invented epoch taxonomy or blanket serialization plan. Main has bound and read back all 329 concrete work homes in existing epochs—the board’s established delivery groupings—and meaningful same-epoch milestones. Research provenance does not make a card a sidequest. A milestone should say what a user can now rely on, not that a document or implementation file exists.

Within the existing epoch structure, give shared correctness blockers priority over consumers that depend on them. Then complete useful capability families. Admit specialized performance surfaces only after their own evidence. Independent consumer repairs and unrelated adapters can proceed in parallel when they do not need the same missing fact or mutation boundary.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F[Checked identities, source versions and ranges] --> T[Editor, CLI and review projections]
    F --> C[Canonical typed metadata and validation]
    E[Closed-choice identity and checked ingress] --> C
    O[Ownership, effects and scope cleanup] --> I[Iterator and stream contracts]
    O --> R[HTTP, process and Plugin lifetimes]
    C --> A[Forms, server functions and explicit adapters]
    R --> A
    I --> D[Capability-dependent adapters and sources]
    O --> G[Truthful tensor storage, placement and completion]
    G --> P[Equivalent complete candidate and plain jobs]
    P --> S[Performance-shaped public option admission]
```

The arrows mean “the consumer must use a trustworthy version of this fact or contract.” They do not mean that every producer card must finish before any consumer-only fix can proceed. Shared callable-fact conformance on#2986 is not a reason to bury independent hover/signature or duplicate-label repairs under that card, or to block them on unrelated producer work.

### Recommended dependency packets and meaningful milestone boundaries

| Mechanism owner and scope | Ordering constraint | Milestone that means something |
|---|---|---|
| Checked source identity and change safety: BIG-F01/F02/F08/F14; READ-F16 | Repair incorrect identities, versions and ranges before new projections rely on them. A consumer-only rendering repair can proceed independently when the producer is already correct. | An imported diagnostic points to its own file/range; a change uses the expected program version and either performs the intended edit or rejects the stale one. |
| Scope cleanup: READ-F05/F14; ITER-F030 | Establish the existing stop/exit contract before HTTP, process, Plugin or resource-producing iterator work claims lifecycle completeness. | Required cleanup occurs at the required scope boundary, in the selected order, once, including early stop and failure on the selected execution modes and targets. |
| Canonical data meaning: CORE-F004/F035; ENUM-F02 | Preserve typed metadata, validation and checked ingress before adapters project them. CORE-F005 is an independent duplicate-key admission choice; do not silently impose a new policy. | The same field has the selected meaning across coding and validation clients; malformed, unsupported and valid unfamiliar data remain distinguishable under the chosen contract. |
| Borrowed iteration: ITER-F006/F027/F066 | Fix element identity and trait/protocol routing before dependent borrowed grouping, remainder and view collection: F028/F065/F083. | The adapter preserves the promised item identity and owner lifetime, consumes only what its contract permits, and exposes no capability it cannot uphold. |
| Iterator source and stop boundaries: ITER-F030/F032/F064 | Keep waiting, failure, end and partial-input behaviour explicit before network/I/O iteration and capability-dependent adaptation. | A waiting source is not treated as ended; failure, early stop and unfinished input have the specified state and cleanup consequences. |
| HTTP typed-error projection: SCRIPT-F01 / D-SCRIPT-HTTP-DECODE1 | Reuse the existing typed JSON `FieldError` contract: the structured record of which fields failed and why. Core SELECT/EXCLUDE encoder optimizations are separate work and must not block this correction. | A data-validation failure keeps its structured field cause instead of being confused with transport framing or flattened into an unrelated decoder error. |
| Existing local and review tools: READ-F01/F10/F13/F17; BIG-F05/F20–F23 | Consume checked facts from the shared service selected by D-LSP1=C. Keep public projections independently decidable without building another semantic engine. | The reader can identify the relevant obligation, source site or change consequence, and the displayed identity remains tied to the checked version. |
| Accepted application protocols | Both the relevant API contract and its independently selected placement constrain a shipped integration; neither approves the other or an external dependency. | One complete valid/invalid/cancelled protocol job follows the chosen admission, data, status, demand and cleanup rules. |
| GPU foundations and cooperative work | Establish dtype, invocation/resource legality, bounds, layout and completion before cooperative proof. Ranked work includes non-contiguous layouts. | Every required result cell, error and completion condition matches the exact numeric and storage contract; unsupported execution remains explicit rather than becoming a hidden substitute. |
| Performance-motivated options | A registered equivalent pair and strict matched win precede ratification of each named option. Reader approval and old scheduler law are not substitutes. | The correct complete candidate beats the correct complete ordinary program on every required comparable cell and metric, with losses and missing evidence retained on the same work home. |

An import-only native closure failure such as CORE-F001 can block fresh native evidence for an affected path; it is not evidence that every exported library feature is absent. Likewise, the Core, form and iterator lowering failures should not be merged into one root cause merely because they all stop compilation. Close the exact boundary each card owns.

### Do not gate everything on everything

- A correct hover/signature rendering fix need not wait for an unrelated semantic producer repair.
- HTTP decoder error projection need not wait for a faster JSON selected-field encoder.
- A particular protocol integration needs its own API and placement choices, not every transport ballot.
- A borrowed adapter needs its actual ownership and source capabilities, not all 45 Iterator choices.
- Existing ordinary GPU operations remain useful alternatives while an expert surface lacks its strict-win evidence.
- A historical source-integrity gap must remain labelled; it does not automatically prevent all work supported by different, sufficient evidence.

This is how the later orchestrator can move quickly without losing correctness: keep hard dependencies precise, keep independent work parallel, reuse the right mechanism, and stop treating a shared topic as proof of a shared implementation boundary.

<a id="performance-admission"></a>

## Performance admission is an option-level gate, not a slogan

The released canonical checkpoint identifies 21 active performance-motivated options across 19 choices: the two Core selected/excluding writer options, seven GPU options, and 12 options in 10 Iterator choices. The other 82 Iterator options are not blanket-gated. Some choices have more than one gated alternative; both parallel alternatives need their own evidence. This is not a claim that any option has already won.

A candidate and its ordinary comparison must perform the same useful job. They must agree about input, output, errors, ownership requirements, ordering and completion before their costs are comparable. Include the work that matters to that job: setup, construction, allocation, retained memory, encoding, scheduling, transfer and readback. Do not hide those costs outside the measured region.

Several retained teaching examples deliberately do not yet meet that standard. The Cartesian illustration collects and prints a list on one side and prints separate tuples on the other. The nested-source illustration constructs a `Stream` on one side and lists on the other. A borrowed-result comparison must use a caller that does not require independent ownership. Those limitations are explicit proof work, not demonstrated wins.

The rule is strict: candidate/plain must be below 1 on every required comparable cell and metric. Equality, wrong output, unmatched work, stale identity, absent cells and inconclusive results do not pass. The separate Rust peer noise band does not establish a candidate/plain win. Keep a losing or missing cell on its actual work home; do not remove the motivation or choose an easier workload to evade the gate.

A performance-shaped proposal may be a promising research candidate while its public option remains blocked. Only appropriately authorized experimental work can produce the missing evidence. That is different from silently shipping the proposed API under the label of a benchmark.

### What “better” must eventually mean

The source videos are useful lenses, not a league table. Rust supplies real ownership and iterator capabilities; Python, Go, Java and .NET supply substantial ordinary libraries and tools; Nest and its peers supply integrated workflows; typed GPU launches and safe host wrappers already exist elsewhere. Compare those real capabilities and useful ecosystem additions, not a bare-language caricature.

A faster command is not automatically a faster programmer. The five agent-loop quantities and the local-readability questions remain separate measurements. Preserve source context, task correctness, failed attempts, repair choices and complete task time. Do not replace a comprehension or safe-change study with line counts, a pleasing diagram or a historical deployment percentage.

The competitive claim worth earning is concrete: a programmer finishes the same useful job, with fewer avoidable concepts and less repeated work, without losing correctness, control, evidence or the expert path. The rest of this report records exactly where that direction is supported, where it failed on the frozen snapshots, and what remains to be decided or proved.

## How the source themes fit together

### Multi-source reconciliation

The rows below compare themes; they do not merge source identities or manufacture independent corroboration of a technical guarantee.

| Theme | Relation | Independent sources and retained difference | Jet consequence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Remove caller-owned machinery | Repeated design theme | CoreLib clip names algorithms; Nest short names application wiring; Lua interview distinguishes host-supplied libraries from standalone batteries | Remove repeated work through the correct existing owner; do not call all three mechanisms one API |
| Make behavior understandable | Repeated design theme | Readability clip argues visible control flow; Lua interview stresses human review and learning cost; O'Hearn describes useful change-time feedback | Improve accurate local explanation and repair, then measure completed tasks; no line-count proxy |
| Small surface versus useful batteries | Different workload, not contradiction | Lua is intentionally hostable; the CoreLib and standalone-script jobs need ordinary batteries | Keep one language and permit explicit library placement decisions rather than one universal package-size target |
| Concise chains versus readable code | Apparent tension | Iterator clip demonstrates composition; readability clip warns about hidden work; neither runs a learnability trial | Show laziness, ownership, evaluation count, failure and cleanup; avoid style bans and syntax proliferation |
| Safety claims at boundaries | Shared question, different mechanisms | Enum ingress, typed JSON, Component calls and GPU resources each have distinct validity and lifetime conditions | Reuse common facts where their contracts match; preserve independent boundary checks and measurements |
| Prompt feedback versus deeper analysis | Qualified source claim | O'Hearn's historical deployment report favors relevant change-time feedback; Q&A does not say false positives are irrelevant | Preserve soundness and unknown labels; measure latency, cancellation, relevance and repair rather than copying a historical percentage |
| One model across execution paths | Jet contract, not peer consensus | I9 and existing Jet decisions are local authority; the videos do not prove them | Use the frozen contrasts to define proof work. Do not claim current-source tier or device parity |

The detailed micro sweeps and five agent-loop quantities remain in the topic sections. Their estimates are qualitative unless a receipt supplies a measured value. They are not a campaign-wide productivity score.

## What the exercised contrasts establish

These are readings of Main's original receipts. No program was run by this synthesis analyst. The complete inputs and outputs are retained below; the small table does not replace them.

| Topic | Actual bounded contrast | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enums | Same-payload named cases print `7` and `-7`; the missing case produces E0307; named/noncapturing/capturing call forms each print `7` in the recorded default, interpreter and AOT paths. | Recursive layout, callback ABI, equal allocation cost, wire evolution or web parity. |
| Iterators | Reusing the consumed source produces E0121. The repaired fallible prefix prints `visit=1` and `[1]` without visiting the bad tail; the longer recovery witness visits `oops` and yields `[1, 7]`. | Complete stable capability parity, absence of allocations, arbitrary custom-cursor correctness or a current-tree tier sweep. |
| CoreLib | The grouped-marker witness prints `valid:accepted:2`, `unknown:rejected`, `duplicate:accepted:3` in its recorded default, interpreter and AOT runs. | Unknown-field rejection is not duplicate-key rejection. This does not establish every canonical decoder policy or broad stock-library parity. The earlier witness reconstruction is a separate digest-matched input. |
| NestJS | The exact frozen form input stops before application work with internal lowering failure, exit101. | No HTTP request, validation response, DI scope, queue job, auth flow or framework performance was exercised by that failure. |
| Readability | The same `guard-order` input omits `close` output under default and prints both close messages after both body messages under AOT. The separate scope-guard interpreter receipt rejects opaque callback marshalling with E0956. | Exit0 and a native lambda trace do not prove cleanup execution or its required scope timing. The observations do not identify one proved root cause. |
| GPU | A marked scalar call prints `kernel:42` and `bounds:true`; a selected built-in Vulkan path reports F32 placement and result `[8.0]`, while other tested input/provider paths reject. | A scalar call is not an authored device dispatch. Placement strings are not physical-adapter identity, zero-copy proof, universal backend support or matched speed. |
| Scripting | Two exact entry forms print the same `first` and `script:42` output on three CLI paths. Mixed bare statements and `fn run` produce E0621. Separate dev logs show readiness/output. | Dev logs do not inherit missing full input/binary hashes from CLI runs. No hostile embedding, native containment, install/update or generic host API parity follows. |
| Big code | Exact multi-file checks and LSP streams expose the retained symbol/location/rename results; the corrected binding witness and original binding witness remain different hashed inputs. | A semantic record's presence is not a correct URI/span, safe edit, causal review report or low-latency incremental implementation. No rename or other edit was applied. |

The useful order is contract, exact input identity, observed outcome, then explanation. A failed compiler path remains a useful defect witness; it is not a failed end-to-end application benchmark. A successful tiny path remains useful evidence; it is not a whole-language claim.

<a id="evidence-rules"></a>

## Evidence rules and corrections

| Label | What it establishes | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source claim | What the named speaker, document, or audience record says | Correctness, general adoption, safety, or speed |
| Primary-source corroboration | A specific rule or implementation at the recorded release, commit, or retrieval date | A tested installation, every platform, or the newest release when the source is older |
| Inspected Jet source | A mechanism or mismatch in the captured files and ranges, including pre-existing owner changes | Equivalence to HEAD alone or to an earlier executable |
| Frozen observation | The exact recorded command, complete matching input where available, executable identity where recorded, exit, stdout, and stderr | Current-tree behavior, broad tier parity, peer performance, or unexercised branches |
| Ratified, not proved here | An existing owner decision or contract | Shipped or correctly exercised behavior |
| Hypothesis or proposed surface | A reasoned candidate and its explicit acceptance gate | Current syntax, API availability, approval, or performance |
| Explicit unknown | A bounded missing source, execution, comparison, or provenance fact | Feature absence or permission to discard useful investigation |

**The source tree changed during the campaign. Main's later build failed in `jet-jit` with 13 errors.** Earlier results remain evidence for their recorded executables only. There is no successful rebuild of the final changing tree in this report. An inspected source digest and an executable digest are different identities. Neither implies their equivalence.

The integrity appendices control exact quotations and program identity. A report's shortened example is not automatically the input that produced an output. Corrected, original, and grammar-rejected variants remain distinct. A missing input hash is not repaired by the current file at the same path. A later receipt cannot retroactively attest an earlier execution. Retrospective authored-input witnesses retain that narrower label.

The following corrections materially affect interpretation:

1. **Enum models:** representable integer, declared member, nominal case, structural union member, and finite set are different invariants. C can warn about missing enum cases. An explicit cast does not necessarily check membership. A physical tag need not be a separate integer. These corrections do not reopen Jet's ratified nominal-enum/structural-union boundary.
2. **Rust iteration:** method names and documentation counts are not parity. The stable denominator excludes unstable APIs and the Windows `Incoming` item mistakenly included by a raw index. Producer relations, concrete iterator types, inherent APIs, and trait capabilities are different counts. Stable, nightly, target-specific, and ecosystem contracts stay separate.
3. **CoreLib:** complete accounting of selected families is not complete capture of every public symbol, overload, default, allocation, or error. Glaze release navigation and mutable rendered page bodies do not share an automatic version pin. A source index cannot establish a best-in-history library or zero-cost operation.
4. **NestJS:** the source is a short about integrated TypeScript, construction, and route metadata, not an enterprise adoption study. Jet's focused form input failed before application execution. Source-derived OpenAPI, client, queue, and transport contracts are not end-to-end results.
5. **Readability:** the video narrator's rules, collective Linux guidance, and authenticated statements by Linus are different sources. Missing visual tokens cannot become exact runnable examples. The frozen cleanup-order contrasts establish only the recorded symptoms, not the cause in the changing source tree.
6. **GPU:** official hiring text signals intent, not a shipped compiler. `cuda-oxide`, `cutile-rs`, `rust-gpu`, Rust-CUDA, host wrappers, and tensor systems are distinct technologies. <a id="topic-enums"></a>
## Enums


**Independent research proposal — 2026-09-11. Campaign #3070. Implementation and owner decisions remain separate from this report.**

### 1. Verdict

Jet should keep its ratified model: **a named enum is a documented, nominal choice of labeled cases; `A | B` is a structural choice whose cases are identified by member types. Both use one closed-sum mechanism.** They are related, but naming is not their only semantic difference. Do not introduce automatic named-enum/union conversions. D-UNIONTYPE1=A already requires ordinary match conversion at that boundary. This report does not reopen it. [EN-C13–C15]

The strongest opportunities are not another enum keyword, a second flags family, or a parallel codec. They are complete validity checks, reliable case metadata, exhaustive diagnostics, explicit external representation, and proof that the existing behavior agrees across execution modes. Several of those surfaces have source evidence but not runtime evidence. A broad superiority or speed claim would be false.

The video is useful as a map of competing meanings. It is not a reliable performance comparison. It overstates C's inability to diagnose missing cases, Go's restriction to contiguous constants, and TypeScript's need for runtime enum objects. Its claim that Java must use expensive reflection is not supported by the captured primary language rules or by measurements. [EN-C05–C08, C19, C25, C27–C28]

#### Decisions by level

- **Strategic:** model program states, not integer abbreviations. Keep one valid closed choice by default. Treat a wire code and a set of choices as different values because they have different invariants.
- **Operational:** reuse the enum/union case facts for construction, matching, codecs, diagnostics and representation. Retain nominal boundaries and type-keyed structural normalization. Reuse `Set`, ordered maps, `Tally`, ordinary functions and `Codable` rather than adding parallel enum-specific families.
- **Tactical:** the focused repeated-payload, missing-case and callable contrasts have exact recorded results. Close the remaining conversion, generic, recursive, codec, tool and performance jobs against an identified source snapshot. Eight independent owner choices now have complete drafts; none is ratified or proved by source inspection.

### 2. Source thesis, corrections and audience

#### Identity and coverage

The assigned playlist title was **“Why can't we agree on what an enum is?”** The direct video ID is **JaOzpMQEUnI**; its captured current title is **“Why do we keep reinventing enums?”**, by rats159. Canonical source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JaOzpMQEUnI>. The publication date is 2026-09-11 and duration is 571 seconds. Preserve both titles; this is not a substitute video.

I read the full creator-caption English transcript, 108 timestamped lines from 00:00 through 09:27. The shared capture includes 144 comments: 48 roots and 96 replies. There are 58 orphan replies, so record count agreement does not prove complete threads. I read every supplied top-root, recent, and technical-correction stratum, including substantive disagreement and low-visibility serialization comments. These strata overlap; they are not independent samples or a popularity survey.

Exact on-screen demo spelling remains limited. Direct browser/video capture failed, but the shared collector later recovered storyboard JPEGs. I inspected contact sheets 02, 05, 09 and 11: each visibly contains a 3×3 grid of low-resolution frames. They corroborate the C/C++, Java-to-Rust, Go and TypeScript demonstrations; fine punctuation is not reliably readable. The audience allegation about a malformed Rust `OreVeinType` example remains unverified. No code in this report is represented as an exact transcription of an unreadable screen. The contact-sheet index preserves approximate times; it is not a full-frame video review.

#### What the source actually argues

| Time | Source argument | Evidence assessment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 00:00–01:54 | C integer constants and C++ scoped enums cover simple named choices and flags. | Useful numeric-domain contrast. C++ unscoped enums are not identical to C: integer-to-enum assignment is not implicit in C++. |
| 01:59–03:24 | Java attaches data and behavior to singleton constants; Rust attaches payloads to each value. | Important distinction. Case metadata and per-instance payload must not be conflated. |
| 03:30–04:52 | A closed list of Rust cases enables layout knowledge and exhaustive matching. | Supported in principle. A logical discriminant need not be a separately stored integer; recursion needs finite storage. |
| 04:52–05:10 | C cannot check exhaustiveness; Java must use expensive reflection. | GCC has named-case diagnostics. Java has specified type tests and patterns. Neither video nor comments provide matched performance evidence. |
| 05:34–06:52 | Go uses `iota`; gaps are difficult or impossible and type association is weak. | `iota` is optional convenience. Typed, negative and explicitly gapped constants are legal. The real loss is no closed relation between a type and all its constants. |
| 07:09–08:07 | TypeScript enums become runtime objects. | Correct for ordinary enums, incomplete for `const enum`; ambient const enums have version/build hazards. Structural discriminated unions are another relevant peer surface. |
| 08:12–09:21 | Odin combines explicit numeric casts with enums, type unions, bit sets and enum-indexed arrays. | Useful decomposition. Explicit cast syntax does not, by itself, prove membership checking. |

#### Audience signals, not votes

The most-liked captured root praises C++ enums and Rust exhaustive matching. Other roots praise Rust's data-carrying cases, recommend Zig, or dislike using the word `enum` for sums. One recent reply explicitly retracts an objective “best” ranking and frames it as preference. Those comments support a **learnability question**, not an etymological veto or universal ranking. Use a small rule and examples rather than asking beginners to settle terminology disputes.

A low-visibility thread identifies the more consequential omission: persisted enum data outlives a program version. That question belongs in the design even when the video spends little time on it. Relevant stable comment IDs are `UgzU4PcHFomhekqrTGt4AaABAg` and its reply `...AaceZGRpxNuAacmEIDm2kW`. [EN-C10–C11]

Corrections also need correction. Odin `#partial switch`, Rust `#[non_exhaustive]`, and Zig's trailing `_` are not interchangeable. One relaxes handling at a use site, one protects library evolution, and one admits unknown numeric tag values. A TypeScript type annotation disappearing does not mean a discriminator field or dispatch is free. Python `StrEnum.auto()` lowercases names; the sampled capitalized example is inaccurate. Likes establish none of these facts.

### 3. Finite peer capability inventory

The six-language campaign baseline is present: C++, Rust, Python, Go, Java and .NET. C, Odin, Swift, Zig and TypeScript are added because they expose the owner's exact questions. The finite corpus includes C++ `std::variant` and Glaze, Rust Serde, Java `EnumSet`, Python `enum`, and .NET `System.Text.Json`. These are ordinary-use comparators, not niche packages. No claim is made about every ecosystem library.

The mechanical inventories contain **15 dimensions for every selected entry**. Low-level entries include five current languages, the historical C11 contrast and Glaze as a library entry; high-level entries contain six languages. This is a coverage ledger, not a percentage of language superiority. An `unknown` cell means the chosen primary spans did not establish it, not that the language lacks it. The tables below retain the substantive inventory in a publication-readable form.

#### Identity, alternatives and behavior

| Peer and source version | Identity and cases | Payload, generic/recursive and empty cases | Matching, construction and behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C23 N3096; C11 N1570 historical | Tagged and anonymous declarations create distinct types. Enumerator names are integer constants; a C union overlaps members and does not track an active tag. | No enum payload grammar. Union members can carry data, but an external discriminator is an application invariant. Generic/recursive and empty/singleton rules beyond the captured grammar are not claimed. | Constants, `switch`, ordinary functions. GCC 15.2 `-Wswitch-enum` checks missing named cases even with `default`; it does not validate incoming integers. |
| C++23 N4950-era draft | Scoped/unscoped nominal enums. `std::variant<T...>` uses alternative index, not a user-written case name. | `variant<int,int>` retains two indices; `get<int>` requires uniqueness. `variant<>` is ill-formed. `monostate` supplies an empty payload. Recursive storage requires separate consideration; it is not established by the captured variant clauses. | `index`, `get<I>`, `get<T>`, `get_if`, `holds_alternative`, `visit`; a visitor must be valid for every alternative combination. `valueless_by_exception` is an extra state that must be accounted for. |
| Rust 1.98.1 stable identity; pinned Reference | Nominal labeled sums. Unit, tuple and named-field cases share one enum mechanism. | Repeated payload types retain labels. Generic parameters and bounds are in enum grammar. Zero-variant enum has no valid values; it is not freely coerced like `!`. A unit case is one value; a one-case enum with payload need not be a singleton. | Variant constructors and pattern matching. Ordinary implementations and traits belong to the same nominal type; callable constructor items also have function-item types. Exact match/evolution supplement is separately cited below. |
| Odin current overview; repository SHA in sources | Enum constants and distinct type-alternative tagged unions are separate surfaces. A union includes `nil` by default; `#no_nil` changes that contract. | Type-only alternatives cannot document two equal-type roles without distinct wrapper types. Generic/recursive and empty enum details are not established by the captured overview. | Explicit selectors, type assertions with comma-ok, type switches; default enum/union switch coverage and explicit `#partial`. Enum values can be iterated. |
| Zig 0.15.2 | Named fields in enums/unions; `union(enum)` can infer a tag enum. Bare, tagged, `extern` and `packed` unions have different representation/safety contracts. | Payload belongs to the selected named field. Repeated payload types are not collapsed by the field labels. Generic/recursive and empty enum details remain outside the selected spans. | `switch` with payload capture; namespaced methods; `@intFromEnum`, `@enumFromInt`, `@tagName`, `@typeInfo`. A tagged union may project to its tag enum, losing payload. |
| Swift pinned current guide; requested 6.2 mapping unresolved | Nominal named cases with raw values or per-instance associated values. Extensions add behavior, not a new set of cases. | `indirect` marks recursive storage. Repeated types can occupy separately labeled cases/fields. Generic and empty-layout details are not established by this capture. | `switch`, initializers, computed properties, methods, protocols, `RawRepresentable`, `CaseIterable`, `Codable`. Nonfrozen enums require a default; `@unknown default` still warns about unhandled known cases. |
| TypeScript pinned v2 handbook; requested 5.9 mapping unresolved | Ordinary enum types/runtime objects differ from structural unions. A discriminated union uses a literal field such as `kind`. | Payloads are ordinary object fields. Equal-shaped objects are structural; labels in literal fields distinguish roles. Generic/recursive and empty-enum details are not established by selected sections. | Property construction, control-flow narrowing, `switch`, a `never` assignment for exhaustive checks, `keyof typeof`; no automatic runtime input validation follows from the types. |
| Python 3.14 | Enum classes bind member names to values; aliases may share a member. `IntEnum` and `Flag` alter operations. | Member metadata may be any object; multiple assigned values feed `__init__`. This is not per-construction Rust-style variant payload. Generic/recursive/empty and static exhaustiveness are not established by these sources. | Name indexing, value lookup, canonical iteration, `__members__`, `_missing_`, `_generate_next_value_`, `unique`, `verify`; runtime rather than language-enforced exhaustive dispatch. |
| Go 1.26.0 | Defined types add identity; aliases do not. Constants may be typed or untyped. No enum declaration binds a type to a closed case set. | Basic interfaces hold implementing values. An interface containing a non-basic type union is a generic constraint, not a runtime sum variable. | `const`, optional `iota`, explicit values, ordinary methods/functions and switches. No enum-specific exhaustive/iteration/reflection API is established by this specification. |
| Java 25 | Enum classes have exactly their singleton constants; sealed classes/interfaces provide a different closed-alternative model. | Constructor data on an enum constant is shared metadata. Sealed records/classes carry per-instance payloads. Enum declarations are not generic sum declarations merely because `Enum<E>` is generic. | Constructors, fields, methods, interfaces; `values`, `valueOf`, `name`, `ordinal`; exhaustive enum/sealed pattern switches. `null` handling remains a separate Java concern. |
| .NET 10 / current C# sources with release caveats | Enum is a distinct integral value type with named constants; constants may share numbers. Delegates, separately, are nominal callable types. | No enum-associated payload syntax. Empty enum body still has representable numeric values, including default zero. A generic constraint on `Enum` is not a generic data-carrying enum declaration. | Extension members rather than in-enum methods; `GetName(s)`, `GetValues`, `IsDefined`, `Parse`, `TryParse`, `ToObject`, `HasFlag`. Exhaustive switch details were not captured. |

#### Numeric validity, representation, sets and data evolution

| Peer | Numeric and representation contract | Sets, metadata and serialization | Evolution limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C | Integer promotion/assignment rules permit unnamed representable values. C23 fixed underlying type controls conversion and representation; untagged unions can have an inconsistent application tag. | Bit masks use integer operations. The captured language clauses do not supply enum reflection or codecs. | Reordering automatically numbered constants is not a safe wire policy. No wire standard follows from an enum declaration. |
| C++ | Unscoped enum-to-int is implicit; int-to-enum is not. Scoped conversion is explicit. Fixed-underlying casts check no named membership; nonfixed out-of-range cast can be undefined. `variant` holds payload inline, but payloads themselves may allocate. | Glaze: numeric enums by default, named metadata for strings; variant `tag`, `content`, `ids`, internal/adjacent forms and catch-all tags. Untagged selection can be order/shape dependent. | A library variant and a numeric ABI enum do not promise the same wire contract. Glaze catch-all can retain the received tag. |
| Rust | A logical tag may use niches or another layout. `repr(C)`/integer repr does not legalize invalid cases. Explicit fieldful repr can suppress null-pointer optimization. | Serde external/default, internal, adjacent and untagged representations. Untagged selects the first successful alternative; some forms need allocation to decode. | Library non-exhaustiveness is not permission to create unknown numeric discriminants. Stable wire codes require a separate deliberate codec contract. |
| Odin | Explicit cast syntax; backing type defaults to `int` and can be fixed. A targeted pinned compiler-source lookup did not establish membership enforcement, so that point remains unknown rather than inferred from spelling. | Enum iteration, enumerated arrays, and `bit_set` mathematical set operations with bit-vector storage and optional backing type. | `#partial` permits an incomplete use site; it is not proof of an open-value domain. |
| Zig | Ordinary `@enumFromInt` on an absent value invokes safety-checked illegal behavior, not a recoverable optional result. Trailing `_` admits every representable integer tag. `enum(c_int)`/`extern union` expose C-compatible representation. | `@typeInfo` fields/tag type and `@tagName`; no serialization API or specialized set library was selected. | A non-exhaustive numeric enum and a closed tagged union have different valid-value sets. |
| Swift | `init?(rawValue:)` rejects absent raw codes. No ABI/niche conclusion from the language-guide capture. | `allCases` synthesizes for eligible payload-free enums. `OptionSet` is a bitfield with nonfailable raw construction. SE-0295 synthesizes associated-value Codable cases and keys. | Nonfrozen library evolution and Codable field evolution differ from language source/binary compatibility. |
| TypeScript | Ordinary numeric reverse map, string map without reverse lookup, or erased/inlined const enum. No memory-layout or runtime-validity guarantee from type erasure. | Literal-field discriminated objects work with ordinary data formats; runtime schema validation remains separate. | Ambient const enum inlining can disagree with a dependency's runtime version. |
| Python | `IntEnum` integer arithmetic loses enum status. `FlagBoundary.STRICT`, `CONFORM`, `EJECT`, `KEEP` differ; `Flag` and `IntFlag` have different defaults. | Rich member lookup/alias/iteration; `Flag`/`IntFlag` bit operations. Selected docs do not establish one wire format. | Alias and `_missing_` hooks are policy, not an automatic compatibility guarantee. |
| Go | Typed/untyped constant rules permit negative/gapped values and masks. No membership check arises from `iota`. | Ordinary code must define names and codecs; enum-specific tools were not selected or claimed absent ecosystem-wide. | Type identity does not close a list of declared constants. |
| Java | Objects and type tests are specified; their exact memory layout and relative dispatch cost are not measured here. `ordinal` is a declaration position, not a durable protocol code. | `EnumSet` uses bit vectors; `values` returns declaration order. Java serialization gives enums special, noncustomizable handling. | Sealed permitted subclasses and fixed enum constants are not arbitrary third-party extension registries. |
| .NET | `checked` controls numeric overflow, not named membership. Zero may be unnamed but still is the default. `IsDefined` checks a named value, not validity of every flag combination. | `[Flags]`, enum reflection APIs; `System.Text.Json` numeric default or string converter. Converter defaults can allow integer values. | A declared case list and all representable backing integers are different domains. |

#### Named function versus anonymous lambda: the second half of the owner's analogy

A name is a binding. A closure environment is data. A callable type controls invocation. None is the other.

- **Swift is the strongest positive example:** named nested functions and anonymous closure expressions can both capture. The same function-signature surface can describe them. This supports one callable model, not the proposition that only anonymous functions capture.
- **Rust is a decisive counterexample to name-only identity:** each function item has a distinct zero-sized type; each closure has a distinct anonymous type whose captures affect `Fn`/`FnMut`/`FnOnce`. Selected noncapturing closures and function items can coerce to a function pointer. Giving the closure a variable name does not erase its environment.
- **C++ also separates spelling from type:** a lambda creates a unique unnamed closure class, including for a noncapturing lambda. Selected lambdas convert to a function pointer. A named ordinary function is not simply that closure class with a name attached.
- **Go** shares captured variables in function literals. **Python** returns function objects from both forms, but lambda bodies are expression-only and cannot carry statements or annotations. **Java** targets a functional interface and restricts captures to effectively-final locals. **C#** converts lambdas/methods to compatible delegates, yet separately declared delegates remain nominal even with equal signatures.
- **Odin and Zig** expose procedure/function-pointer rules in the capture; their full closure and named/anonymous type-identity rules remain explicit unknowns here, not guessed capabilities.

**Answer:** Jet should have one callable invocation model and allow useful named/anonymous organization. It should not pretend capture, mutability, escape, calling convention or nominal callback identity disappear with a name. D-CALLVALUE1=B protects one function-value lowering and the `.call(...)` spelling for a function-valued result. Current `Type::Fn` source also preserves labels/zones as callable identity, treats effect bounds as call-site obligations, and carries view provenance. Lambda lowering consumes checked capture/escape facts. This is stronger than a naming analogy, but it does not prove equal allocation or storage. [EN-C16, C30, C36]
