### 3. The core application model: gains, costs and the Jet consequence

#### Composition is the benefit; runtime class lookup is one implementation

[Nest providers](https://docs.nestjs.com/providers) use constructor dependencies, `@Injectable()` metadata and module registration. Tokens plus `@Inject()` support values that are not runtime classes. Custom values and factories matter: Nest is not restricted to a class for every domain function. Its testing tools also support manual construction and provider overrides.

The costs are specific. TypeScript interfaces and aliases disappear at runtime, so they are not class lookup tokens. Request lifetime can spread through the dependent graph. Module imports, providers, exports and registration describe availability separately from ordinary source references. These facts can cause startup or request-time surprises. Do not turn the justified complaint into a blanket assertion that dependency injection or modules are bad.

For Jet, reuse ordinary functions, structs and explicit values at the existing App composition point. A shared database pool is application-owned. A principal, deadline and transaction are request-owned. A request-specific value must not silently become application state. The interface should expose that distinction without constructing a new service graph for every request. This is a design requirement, not a claim that the current compiler proves every lifetime.

#### Lifetimes are observable behavior

[Nest injection scopes](https://docs.nestjs.com/fundamentals/injection-scopes) distinguish `Scope.DEFAULT`, `Scope.REQUEST` and `Scope.TRANSIENT`. Request scope propagates to dependent consumers; transient scope does not change a singleton consumer's lifetime. Durable providers can group a graph by tenant, but the documented example warns against a large tenant population. A source contradiction matters: that page still warns against request-scoped gateways, while the [v12 gateway chapter](https://docs.nestjs.com/websockets/gateways#request-scoped-gateways) explicitly supports per-connection scope. Pinned [v12.0.1 dispatch code](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/blob/v12.0.1/packages/websockets/web-sockets-controller.ts#L368-L503) resolves the conflict in favor of the newer capability. I read that code and its fixture; I did not run the socket test. The old blanket restriction must not become a Jet beat claim.

The source's approximately 5% request-scope latency guidance is not a reproduced bound. The source also describes singleton use as safe in the Node model. That does not prove that shared mutable per-request data or operations spanning `await` are logically isolated. A transport thread model is not a transaction model.

[Lifecycle hooks](https://docs.nestjs.com/fundamentals/lifecycle-events) include `onModuleInit`, `onApplicationBootstrap`, `onModuleDestroy`, `beforeApplicationShutdown` and `onApplicationShutdown`. `enableShutdownHooks()` opts into system-signal listeners. Request-scoped classes do not receive these application hooks. `app.close()` does not automatically terminate background tasks or the process. Jet should make startup readiness, admission stop, request drain and resource cleanup visible as one application lifecycle, with explicit bounded shutdown rather than a promise inferred from garbage collection.

#### Ordered policy is more important than extension-name parity

[Nest's request lifecycle](https://docs.nestjs.com/faq/request-lifecycle) is middleware, guards, inbound interceptors, pipes, handler, then outbound interceptors. Inbound global/controller/route order reverses on the interceptor return path. Parameter pipes run from the last parameter toward the first. The nearest matching exception filter handles an uncaught error; filters are not an ordinary chain.

This is meaningful control, but the user must know more than the five nouns. Jet should preserve one ordered execution path with inspectable stage facts. Authentication must establish a principal before authorization reads it. Decode and validation must happen before a business operation can mutate state. A handler error must become a typed public failure while private diagnostics remain private. The expert path should change a stage's policy, not add a second dispatch engine.

The inspected `WebServerFn.rs:878-942` already has a concrete dispatch order. Its generated adapters and helpers must be traced together before calling that order complete. A middleware name or metadata field alone is not evidence that a security operation ran.

#### Best-tooling Nest already attacks schema duplication

The [Swagger CLI plugin](https://docs.nestjs.com/openapi/cli-plugin) derives `@ApiProperty` metadata from the TypeScript AST and can reuse class-validator constraints. On that class-based path, runtime validation still needs validators; filenames and builder/test setup matter. More importantly, current Nest also offers [StandardSchemaValidationPipe](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/validation), `StandardSchemaSerializerInterceptor` and [Swagger Standard Schema conversion](https://docs.nestjs.com/openapi/introduction#standard-schema-zod-valibot). Schema libraries can provide `~standard.jsonSchema`; otherwise `standardSchemaConverter` can supply input/output projections, including `zod-openapi`. Best-tooling Nest can already share a runtime schema, inferred TypeScript types and generated OpenAPI. Jet must improve the whole checked workflow, not claim this solved problem as an exclusive advantage.

The Jet opportunity is not “all records are the same schema.” A create command, persisted row and public response often need different fields and authority. The useful rule is: **declare each genuine contract once, then derive its compatible projections**. Never publish an ORM entity automatically. Reuse the existing Core codec/validation facts and App operation facts, not a web-only validator.

Nest also supplies [`PartialType`, `PickType`, `OmitType` and `IntersectionType`](https://docs.nestjs.com/openapi/mapped-types). These compose class-based contract variants, so create/update boilerplate is not an unsolved Nest problem. Jet should reuse ordinary type/codec capabilities where the semantics match. It must not equate “optional update field” with “publicly writable stored field,” or erase the distinction between omitted and explicitly empty values.

#### Adapter independence has a boundary

[Nest's Fastify guide](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/performance) documents `FastifyAdapter`, while Express remains the default. It explicitly warns that Express recipes may not work on Fastify. Middleware gets raw Node request/response objects, not Fastify wrappers. The guide's nearly-twice benchmark statement is not a matched Nest/Jet application result.

The primary current pin is **Nest core 12.0.1, Swagger 12.0.1 and CLI 12.0.0**, verified through official npm metadata and dist-tags on 2026-09-11. Core commit: `4c751c503bc753095f4b4f052e106f95218cc33f`. The earlier 11.1.6 source capture is historical evidence only. Current route conflict/specificity and per-connection gateway scope have focused v12 source witnesses; other live-document claims remain documentation evidence. This corrects the initial historical baseline rather than silently comparing Jet with an obsolete competitor.

#### Exact ordinary programs

**Peer: ordinary Nest endpoint and service.** This is a compact assembly of the documented provider/controller/module pattern, not a production persistence example and not an executed benchmark.

```typescript
import { Controller, Get, Injectable, Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';

@Injectable()
class GreetingService {
  greeting(): string { return 'hello'; }
}
@Controller('greeting')
class GreetingController {
  constructor(private readonly service: GreetingService) {}
  @Get() get(): string { return this.service.greeting(); }
}
@Module({ controllers: [GreetingController], providers: [GreetingService] })
class AppModule {}

const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
app.enableShutdownHooks();
await app.listen(3000);
```

**Current Jet HTTP spelling, source-derived and NOT RUN here.** It uses the existing function-first API. It does not invent a route decorator.

```jet
use core.http.server as server

fn greeting() String -> "hello"
fn run() {
    mux :: server.mux()
    mux.get("/greeting", () -> server.response(200, greeting()))
    server.serve("127.0.0.1:3000", mux) ?? panic("serve failed")
}
```

The file named `NEST-P001-aot.json` records `run --profile=debug`, not a successful standalone AOT build. No generated application reached execution. The four source-inspection hashes are recorded in [the Jet packet](#artifact-4a8f7ca80c4b); they identify inspected helpers, not the executable that produced these failures.

Main then repeated the three command routes on the frozen executable `coordination/jet-probe`. All again exited 101 with the same lowering error. The three `NEST-P001-*-frozen.json` receipts record binary SHA-256 `e841150f5a02f14a7b6b19003a7b8dd32d1fd95b4aa8d7bb4d34e30d376bee3e` and input SHA-256 `72facb9077dbb3168de2278f426ef4ae4df4b48dd19ee03931b829463984772e`. The integrity ledger matches that input hash to the complete 294-byte form file. Original receipts have neither input nor executable hashes; no later digest can attest their exact historical input or binary. [Frozen provenance](#frozen-binary-provenance) explicitly leaves current-source equivalence unestablished.

Further inspected evidence prevents three false gap claims. `state_surface.jet:301-303` already calls `web.openapi(http_router)`, so OpenAPI is not absent. `battery/run.jet:19-37,68-92,127-174` already combines an App action/form, database-backed order handlers, login, session cookies and an HTTP client. `Auth.rs:1-39` and `DbPool.rs:245-300,366-456,536-680` contain strict token-policy and bounded pool-lifecycle machinery. These are source witnesses, not proof that the battery ran. The captured battery's manual form parser and typed App form are separate paths whose semantic agreement remains unverified.

### 5. Whole-loop tooling lessons

[Nest testing](https://docs.nestjs.com/fundamentals/testing) supports `Test.createTestingModule(...).overrideProvider(...).useValue(...).compile()`, then `createNestApplication`, `app.init`, HTTP requests and `app.close`. Fastify has an `app.inject` path and requires readiness. The test lesson is replaceable dependencies and real endpoint behavior, not a mandate to test the container's field wiring.

[Nest Devtools](https://docs.nestjs.com/devtools/overview) exposes the application graph through `snapshot: true` and `@nestjs/devtools-integration`. A bootstrap failure can be exported with `PartialGraphHost.toString()` and `abortOnError: false`. This is a concrete response to dependency-resolution difficulty. The integration should not run in production. Jet should expose its existing checked App facts locally and machine-readably, with source-linked errors and no separate runtime graph reconstruction or public secret-bearing debug endpoint.

After independent drafts, BigCodeAstra identified `jet-semindex`, `jet-impact`, `QueryService`'s `ReverdictReceipt` and `reasoning_view_json` as the existing general facts path. This proposal uses that path for App/request-specific views; it does not create another graph store. CorelibAstra owns codec policy. Its recorded default-run JSON output reports acceptance of exact `9007199254740993`, rejection of quoted/fractional/missing integer fields, acceptance of unknown members, and last-duplicate-value behavior. Receipt: `CORE-json-boundaries-default.json`. That original receipt has no input or binary hash, and its exact historical input is unavailable. A later same-path AOT input hash cannot attest the default run. Retain the recorded output, not a hash-verified reproduction claim. Reuse `Codable`; do not infer a blanket strict-boundary policy or add a parallel web validator.

[Nest SWC](https://docs.nestjs.com/recipes/swc) offers `nest start -b swc -w`; type checking needs `--type-check`. Monorepo plugins require extra metadata-generation setup. Do not trade verdict fidelity for a fast “started” message. Jet's loop must report check readiness separately from server readiness and preserve the same contract across dev, build, tests and deployment.

[Nest workspaces](https://docs.nestjs.com/cli/monorepo) have standard and monorepo modes; `nest generate app` converts a canonical project layout. The source warns that conversion can fail or become unreliable for noncanonical layouts. This is a tooling/layout rule, not a different backend semantic model. Jet should keep one module/application model and make any project transformation explicit and inspectable, rather than introducing a second framework workspace language.

| Agent-loop quantity | Nest evidence | Jet's required result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Verdict fidelity | TypeScript checks code; erased metadata and runtime validation still matter. | Check graph and operation contracts before dispatch; do not count generated Rust rejection as a user verdict. |
| Verdict latency | SWC and watch improve the loop, with separately configured checks. | Measure edit-to-correct-verdict, not transpile time alone. |
| Verdict actionability | Devtools exports a partial dependency graph on bootstrap failure. | Source-linked causal facts and machine-readable repair targets. The observed 0..0 ICE is currently a weak result. |
| Context economy | Decorators and generators compress wiring but leave lifetime/order rules elsewhere. | A small App surface whose expanded facts are available on demand. |
| Repair determinism | Tokens, provider exports, scopes, adapters and plugin configuration offer several failure causes. | One checked contract and one pointed repair rather than competing metadata stores. |

No measured agent-success or token-efficiency claim is made. The weakest demonstrated Jet quantity is verdict fidelity/completion on the ordinary form path, followed by the actionability of its source span.

### 6. Capability inventory: compare the useful system, not the logo

`Documented` below means an official API/source witness was read. It does not mean this campaign ran the peer. `Jet source` does not mean shipped end-to-end. The detailed API locators and package pins live in the two [peer evidence packets](#source-provenance).

| Capability | Best-tooling Nest surface | Ownership and continuing cost | Stock Jet comparison and next requirement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Construction and application boundaries | `@Module`, imports/providers/controllers/exports; `@Injectable`, `@Inject`, `useValue`, `useClass`, `useFactory`; dynamic modules | Nest owns provider lookup and lifecycle. Application authors still own dependency direction and token identity. | Existing App plus functions/values is the right base. Do not copy a runtime class container. Prove shared resources and request values remain distinct. |
| Routing | `@Controller`, `@Get/Post/Put/Delete/Patch`, `@Param/Query/Body`, `@HttpCode`, versioning | Nest collects routes; Express/Fastify determine adapter behavior. v12 adds `routeConflictPolicy` and `routeResolutionStrategy`. | `mux` already detects duplicate route shapes. Check typed/static/dynamic overlap and same ordering across checked router, App and adapters before declaring a gap. |
| Request policy | middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes, exception filters | Core supplies stages, not domain authorization. Order and error mapping remain a contract. | Inspect one server-function dispatch order. Expose source-linked stage facts; test denial before mutation and cancellation before retry. |
| Decode, validate, serialize | `ValidationPipe`, `ParseIntPipe`, `ClassSerializerInterceptor`; Standard Schema pipes/interceptors | class-validator/class-transformer or schema libraries supply substantial behavior. `whitelist`, coercion and output policy are choices. | Reuse `Codable` and one validation policy. The measured JSON witness accepts unknown fields and last duplicate values; do not label every boundary strict. |
| OpenAPI | `SwaggerModule.createDocument/setup`; CLI metadata plugin; Standard Schema input/output conversion | `@nestjs/swagger` and schema converters are integrations. Generated descriptions still need meaningful errors, auth and version policy. | `web.openapi(http_router)` exists. The unresolved work is faithful projection from the existing App operation to external schema/client/UI, not inventing OpenAPI. |
| HTTP adapter | default Express; `FastifyAdapter` | Express/Fastify middleware, body handling and request objects are not interchangeable. | Preserve explicit transport capability and reject unsupported options. No adapter-conformance receipt is available. |
| Testing and diagnostics | `Test.createTestingModule`, provider overrides, Supertest, Fastify injection; Devtools graph and partial graph | Jest/Supertest/Fastify and Devtools integration are outside the core runtime. | Run a real endpoint with replaceable resources; expose existing checked graph facts through existing tooling. Avoid container-wiring tests and a second graph database. |
| GraphQL | `GraphQLModule.forRoot`, Apollo/Mercurius drivers, `autoSchemaFile` or `typePaths`, `GraphQLSchemaHost` | `@nestjs/graphql` plus driver/GraphQL packages; resolver authorization, N+1 loading and schema evolution still belong to the app. | No captured Jet GraphQL integration proof. Treat a broadly useful adapter as a separate integration, not a second operation model or automatic ORM publication. |
| WebSocket | `@WebSocketGateway`, `@SubscribeMessage`, `@MessageBody`, lifecycle hooks, v12 request-scoped gateways | Socket.IO/native WS semantics differ. Acknowledgements described for Socket.IO do not transfer to native WS. | No captured socket adapter runtime proof. Require per-connection context, cleanup, cancellation and bounded outgoing queues. A typed message is not a delivery guarantee. |
| TCP RPC | `createMicroservice`, `@MessagePattern`, `@EventPattern`, `ClientProxy.send/emit` | `send` is a cold Observable; `emit` is hot. Default TCP retries are zero. Request/response uses separate logical channels. | Model calls and events distinctly through the same operation facts. Specify timeout, remote failure and uncertain completion; never retry mutation merely because a response vanished. |
| gRPC | `.proto`, `protoPath`, `@GrpcMethod`, gRPC clients and streaming | `@grpc/grpc-js`, proto-loader and generated/schema tooling own protocol details. Status, deadlines and stream cancellation need mapping. | Candidate external schema adapter. Preserve wire compatibility and typed public failures. Do not claim automatic equivalence to Jet failure unions. |
| Kafka | `ClientsModule`, `Transport.KAFKA`, `KafkaContext`, reply-topic subscription, heartbeat and offset APIs | KafkaJS and broker configuration own partitions, consumer groups and delivery. Rebalance and commit behavior remain visible. | Candidate broker adapter, not generic RPC with a different URL. Make acknowledgement, retry and idempotency observable. No exactly-once claim. |
| RabbitMQ | `Transport.RMQ`, `RmqContext`, `noAck: false`, channel `ack` | amqplib, connection manager and broker own queues/requeue/durability. Missing acknowledgements can redeliver work. | Same typed operation can consume a message, but acknowledgement is a transport effect. Specify failure after commit and before acknowledgement. |
| Persistence and transactions | TypeORM integration or Prisma recipe | ORM/query library, driver, database and migrations remain dependencies. A module import does not make writes atomic. | Data/DB source and the web battery exist. Verify one transaction commits only after authorized valid input; exercise rollback, pool exhaustion and drain rather than add another repository layer. |
| Authentication and authorization | `JwtService.signAsync/verifyAsync`, guard examples, RBAC/claims policy | `@nestjs/jwt` wraps JWT tooling; application policy remains essential. Tutorial passwords/secrets are not production recommendations. | Strict standalone token code and session state exist. Prove route denial, claims policy and session behavior; do not copy a sample secret or equate valid token with allowed action. |
| Browser security | Helmet, CORS, CSRF, Throttler | Adapter plugins, proxy trust, cookie/session setup and ordering matter. Current Throttler's Nest12 compatibility is not established by its peer range. | Existing server-function CSRF/capability fields are only source evidence. Require real browser and proxy-boundary failure tests before claiming a safe default. |
| Configuration, jobs, cache, health and shutdown | Official integration packages, application hooks and deployment guidance | Redis/cache stores, cron, workers, exporters and process orchestrators retain distinct semantics. | Reuse App resource ownership and DB drain machinery. Require readiness, bounded drain and secret-safe diagnostics; package-specific work remains separately decidable. |
| UI-to-backend work | Nest serves a backend contract; a frontend consumes HTTP/GraphQL or sockets | Nest is not a frontend component framework. Frontend generators/frameworks can reduce contract duplication. | Jet's real chance is a typed App operation shared by native form, script client and UI state. Existing `.action/.form`, `web.form`, Query and portable UI are the base; NEST-P001 has not delivered a form. |

#### Transport semantics must survive abstraction

The [microservices overview](https://docs.nestjs.com/microservices/basics), [Kafka](https://docs.nestjs.com/microservices/kafka), [RabbitMQ](https://docs.nestjs.com/microservices/rabbitmq) and [gRPC](https://docs.nestjs.com/microservices/grpc) chapters do not describe interchangeable guarantees. A request/reply call has a result. An event has delivery and acknowledgement states. A stream has demand, cancellation and partial progress. The shared mechanism should carry typed input, output, failure and policy facts; adapters must retain these real distinctions.

For a create-order operation, consider a committed database transaction followed by a lost reply or missing broker acknowledgement. A blind retry can create a second order. An idempotency key plus stored outcome can prevent that only under its stated atomicity and retention policy. Jet's source already names retry/idempotency and uncertain-completion states. The next task is a failure-injection proof of those states, not an invented “exactly once” option.

#### Security is policy, not an annotation count

[Nest authentication](https://docs.nestjs.com/security/authentication) is a tutorial with explicit warnings about plaintext passwords and sample secrets. [Authorization](https://docs.nestjs.com/security/authorization) distinguishes simple role checks from business policy. [Helmet](https://docs.nestjs.com/security/helmet), [CSRF](https://docs.nestjs.com/security/csrf), [CORS](https://docs.nestjs.com/security/cors) and [rate limiting](https://docs.nestjs.com/security/rate-limiting) require adapter and deployment context.

Jet should make the safe beginner path concrete: malformed input cannot mutate state; authenticated identity is separate from permission; browser actions receive CSRF protection where applicable; credentials never appear in exported diagnostics; limits include bodies and queues. Experts may select documented alternatives without bypassing the same checks. This report does not establish current end-to-end enforcement of those requirements.

### 7. One mechanism, with a small beginner path and an honest expert path

#### Keep the existing typed operation

The current battery already writes this connection:

```jet
fn app_create_action(input: battery.NewOrder) String -> {
    inserted :: battery.insert_order("/tmp/jet-web-battery.sqlite", input.item, input.quantity) ?? return "database write failed"
    return "created={inserted}"
}

// Existing source, battery/run.jet:24-34; source reading, not a passing run.
fn app_graph() App -> {
    return core_web
        .app()
        .ssr()
        .route("/", app_home)
        .route("/orders", app_orders)
        .loader(app_orders, app_orders_loader, true)
        .route("/orders/:id", app_order_detail)
        .action("create-order", app_create_action)
        .form("order", app_create_action)
        .island()
}
```

The original continues with assets and hydration settings. This bounded excerpt preserves the existing action/form relationship. Its string result is not a model for typed public business failures; the ratified server-function boundary already requires checked input, success and failure contracts. Keep genuine domain types separate: `NewOrder` is not a database row and a public receipt is not an internal exception.

The recommended flow is:

```text
checked input + operation + public failure + policy
    -> the existing App operation facts
    -> HTTP/native-form/script-client projections
    -> UI field errors, pending/result state and cancellation
```

This is a proposed completion of the existing contract, not a new syntax. A field validation error, unauthorized request, business rejection and uncertain transport completion must remain distinguishable. The no-script form and scripted UI must invoke the same operation policy. Query revalidation happens only after a confirmed mutation outcome, under the already chosen Query mechanism. A lost reply must not silently become either success or a second mutation.

#### Do not hide expert obligations

| Beginner experience | Expert control | What must stay one mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Register a typed action and form. | Choose input/output visibility and public failure mapping. | One checked operation contract; no hand-copied DTO for every projection. |
| Use an application-owned database pool. | Supply a bounded transaction and deadline to the operation. | Explicit values and existing resource ownership, not an implicit DI scope that spreads. |
| Receive field errors and pending state. | Control cancellation, retry/idempotency and uncertain completion policy. | Existing server-function/Query state, not a second frontend RPC client. |
| Start the App with normal diagnostics. | Inspect expanded route/policy/resource facts locally. | Existing semantic index/reasoning facts, not reflection at a live public endpoint. |
| Use the normal HTTP path. | Select an adapter with explicit supported capabilities. | Same checked operation, with honest protocol-specific states rather than hidden emulation. |

No new lifetime type, effect spelling, annotation or keyword is proposed. If implementation reveals that existing effects/resources cannot express a required lifetime, that is a separate owner decision with a concrete counterexample. It is not permission to slip in a framework-specific lifetime language.

#### One App access API choice, not a second OpenAPI mechanism

Jet already exposes `web.openapi(http_router)`. Its inspected signature accepts `HTTPRouter`, not App. Completeness of action/form failure projection is unproved. The proposed choice is how to reach the same checked HTTP contract from the existing App:

**A — recommended; PROPOSED overload, not current API:**

```jet
app :: core_web.app().action("create-order", app_create_action)
contract :: core_web.openapi(app)
```


That API boundary is confirmed in inspected source: `fixed_sigs.rs:403,432` binds `openapi` to `HTTPRouter` and returns `String`; `OpenAPI.rs:1655-1669` takes `&JetHTTPRouter`. No App overload appears in that match. Main's complete 1,144-record decision index has no `D-WEBOPENAPI1`; the source header is not a ratification receipt. The exact law is **D-FOUND-COREAPI1=A**, ratified 2026-09-03: `web.openapi(router)` is an approved ordinary Core addition. Card **#2852** records source completion, with runtime proof retained in **#2919**. **D-ENDPOINT-SHAPE1=A** on **#2962** already requires one checked endpoint descriptor for dispatch, OpenAPI and generated clients. The new ballot must cover only App access to that existing model, not reopen export, codec metadata or client generation.
**B — alternative; PROPOSED projection method, not current API:**

```jet
app :: core_web.app().action("create-order", app_create_action)
http_router :: app.http_router()
contract :: core_web.openapi(http_router)
```

Both options must consume existing checked facts. Neither may reconstruct a second router or publish internal resources. A is the smaller beginner path. B makes the HTTP projection explicit for reuse by other tools, but introduces another public value and step for a simple export. Existing HTTP-router callers remain valid in either choice. The [short ballot draft](#ballots-nestjs) concerns this new API only; it does not reopen the ratified server-function or App decisions. No performance claim ranks these options.

#### Competing designs rejected

- **A Nest-like decorator/service container:** it adds runtime lookup, registration and scope rules where Jet already has checked functions and App composition. The peer demonstrates useful composition, not the necessity of that implementation.
- **A web-only schema language:** it duplicates Core codec/validation semantics. Nest's Standard Schema support shows that shared facts can cross library boundaries without a framework-owned duplicate.
- **Generate everything from a database entity:** authority and visibility differ between stored data, create input and public response. Fewer types would be a safety regression.
- **Erase all transport distinctions:** a call, event and stream have different completion states. One semantic model must represent the differences, not deny them.
- **Add a new graph service for AI tools:** existing semantic facts and reasoning views are the right source. More stores increase repair ambiguity.

### 8. Six-language comparison, with broadly useful libraries included

The corpus is deliberately finite. The pins below identify source witnesses, not a claim that each is the latest release in its ecosystem. Nest's current release was checked separately. No peer was compiled, run or benchmarked. Stock Jet is compared with these useful library-assisted paths, not six deliberately bare standard libraries.

| Peer and source pin | Exact useful surface | What Jet must match or improve | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

Jet needs a simpler checked boundary with reliable diagnostics, not a claim that C++ needs hand-written JSON. | Drogon's README lists async HTTP/DB, filters and WebSockets; no integrated Drogon+Glaze bridge was run. Glaze's network API is marked changing. The pin requires C++23 and little-endian systems; buffer termination is an explicit parsing option. |

Jet should make the same obligations visible without a parallel framework type system. | sqlx transaction drop rolls back according to the docs; no database operation was run. The corpus does not establish all Tower middleware or Rust ecosystem capabilities. |
| **Python: FastAPI 0.141.1 metadata/live docs; Pydantic 2.10.6/2.10 docs; SQLAlchemy 2.0.52 page metadata** | `FastAPI`, `@app.get/post`, Pydantic `BaseModel`, `model_validate/model_dump/model_json_schema`; `Session.begin()` | A small declaration already drives validation and schema. #### Two competitive counterexamples to easy victory claims

**ASP.NET Core 10 already uses a typed result union.** This is the captured MinimalSample's endpoint, not a Jet proposal:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/todo/{id}", Results<Ok<Todo>, NotFound, BadRequest> (int id) => id switch
    {
        <= 0 => TypedResults.BadRequest(),
        >= 1 and <= 10 => TypedResults.Ok(new Todo(id, "Walk the dog")),
        _ => TypedResults.NotFound()
    });
```

**Glaze already decodes a typed record without a handwritten field parser.** This assembly uses its documented API and is NOT RUN:

```cpp
struct NewOrder { std::string item; int quantity; };
auto order = glz::read_json<NewOrder>(buffer);
if (!order) {
    // Return the parse failure before calling the operation.
}
```

The comment is a stated obligation, not an implemented HTTP error response. Glaze's selected buffer options still apply. The point is that typed JSON and generated schema are not unique to Jet. Jet's opportunity is to preserve one contract through checking, dispatch, diagnostics and its own UI.

### 9. Operational lessons beyond endpoint syntax

#### Persistence and job ownership

[Nest TypeORM integration](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/database) supplies `TypeOrmModule.forRoot` and documents both `QueryRunner` and callback-style `DataSource.transaction`. The manual path must release the runner. Its `synchronize: true` example explicitly warns of production data loss. Connection retry defaults of 10 attempts and 3000 ms delay are integration behavior, not a guarantee that startup becomes ready promptly.

The [Nest Prisma recipe](https://docs.nestjs.com/recipes/prisma) uses generated `PrismaClient` and a database adapter. The separately captured [current Prisma transaction page](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/fundamentals/transactions) uses `db.transaction` and `tx.orm`. These are distinct documentation generations; this report does not present them as one installed API. Generated client regeneration, migrations and database compatibility remain real operating costs.

[BullMQ integration](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/queues) requires Redis and `@nestjs/bullmq` plus `bullmq`. `@Processor`/`WorkerHost.process` are the current example; the page warns that Bull's named `@Process` behavior does not carry over. [Scheduling](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/task-scheduling) registers cron jobs during application bootstrap. A recurring in-process callback is not a durable queue or a distributed singleton. Jet should expose those differences through existing task/resource concepts and package contracts, not one misleading “background” feature.

The exact current queue authority is now captured: **D-DX-QUEUE1=A/#2457** requires bundled SQLite by default, an explicit configured database-provider override, and one Prelude-owned enqueue/lease/acknowledge/retry/dead-letter/wait/status contract. At-least-once delivery can repeat work, so external effects need idempotency. Its source closure includes typed payloads, committed lifecycle facts and bounded payload-free status; runtime proof remains **#2919**. Jet therefore does not need another durable queue mechanism. `D-NEST-REMOTEQUEUE1` concerns only an **added broker-store adapter** that preserves this existing contract. Exact selected terms and card receipts are in [queue-law-exact.json](#artifact-83188fd69090).

#### Configuration, cache and readiness

[ConfigModule.forRoot](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/configuration) loads `.env`, with runtime environment values taking precedence. Current documentation accepts Standard Schema validation and custom validation. This is another place where shared schema facts already reduce repetition. Jet's typed configuration should fail before serving, report all relevant key paths, and redact secret values. Environment strings still require explicit parsing policy.

Existing authority must not be blurred here: **D-APP-ARGS1=A/#1450** and **D-CLI-FIELD-MARKERS1=A/#1277** establish the typed App/CLI input path and command-over-environment-over-default precedence. **D-CONFIG-ENV1** is an open spec-only import on **#1735**, not a ratified separate `.env` merge policy. The configuration finding first identifies which existing parser owns each input; it does not silently choose a new config rule.

[CacheModule](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/caching) defaults to an in-memory Keyv-backed store through cache-manager. TTL units are milliseconds. HTTP `CacheInterceptor` applies to GET, excludes native-response handlers, and is explicitly unsuitable as a generic GraphQL field cache. Do not replace absence with a falsy-value check; valid cached `0`, `false` or empty text must remain values. Query revalidation, HTTP response caching and a durable data store are different contracts even if they share a cache primitive.

[Terminus](https://docs.nestjs.com/recipes/terminus) composes health indicators and recommends enabled shutdown hooks. A positive database probe is not proof of request admission or complete application readiness. Jet's existing pool state should feed App readiness. Shutdown should first stop admission, then drain or cancel bounded work, then close resources. Failed drain must be reported, not silently relabeled clean.

#### Observability is part of best-tooling Nest

The current official [Observe overview](https://docs.nestjs.com/observability/overview) and [SDK](https://docs.nestjs.com/observability/sdk) document `createObserveModule`, the `instrument` hook, auto-instrumented controller/provider/job traces and agent-facing telemetry features. The [manual API](https://docs.nestjs.com/observability/manual-instrumentation) adds `TracerService.createSpan`, context attributes and handled-error capture. This corrects any comparison that treats Nest as having only a text logger.

These are documented service capabilities, not measured results. They also introduce operational cost: credentials, external telemetry disclosure, metered events, retention and sampling policy. Log forwarding defaults off; when enabled, redaction defaults on. The [distributed tracing guide](https://docs.nestjs.com/observability/distributed-tracing) still requires caller propagation across services. An auto-instrumented local trace is not automatically an end-to-end trace.

Jet should make operation identity, source location and failure state available to standard telemetry adapters and local tools. Use explicit context for authority-bearing data; ambient tracing context must never become an unchecked principal. No cloud account, telemetry disclosure or new dependency is authorized by this report.

The retained inventory attributes `core.log.set_sink`, `otlp_file`, spans, trace identity and structured-field names to `Log.rs:1-273`. Exact callable signatures, implementation bytes and hashes are not retained there. These names guide reconciliation; they do not provide a complete sink-binding fixture or runtime proof. **D-OBSERVE-LIVE1=A/#506** is ratified; **D-LOGFMT1** and **D-OBS3** are open imports. The optional exporter-placement ballot does not approve a duplicate tracing mechanism. Likewise, **D-AUTH1/AUTH2/AUTH-TOKENPOLICY1=A/#506** owns passwords, sessions, OAuth/magic links and token admission; its `password_login` source is not a password-security runtime receipt.

The original inventory also attributed `CoreLib/Top/Observe.rs:1-183`, `CoreLib/Top/DevtoolsTelemetryPanel.rs:1-170` and `CoreLib/Top/EnvConfig.rs:1-144`. These three locators are unavailable in the current tree, with no retained exact bytes or hash. They therefore provide no current implementation proof. Their unavailability does not establish that the features are absent. The [qualified inventory](#inventory-50cbc51b5208) preserves this attribution history separately from the ratified law and remaining source witnesses.

#### Version compatibility is a capability boundary

The captured pins include config 12.0.0, BullMQ integration 12.0.0, schedule 12.0.1, cache-manager integration 12.0.0, TypeORM integration 12.0.1, JWT integration 12.0.1, GraphQL/Apollo 14.0.0, Terminus 12.0.0 and Observe 0.1.8. These names do not imply one verified installation. For example, [Throttler 6.5.0 metadata](https://registry.npmjs.org/@nestjs/throttler/6.5.0) declares Nest core/common peers only through `^11.0.0`, while the selected current core is 12.0.1.

This is a declared compatibility gap, not proof that the package fails at runtime. Do not bypass it and then claim a supported stack. The [operations manifest](#artifact-d8176d231227) preserves exact Node and package peer ranges. The appropriate Jet lesson is compatible pins and supported capabilities in ordinary application evidence. CorelibAstra's **CORE-F020** owns current-version comparison and **CORE-F042** owns build/package/debug provenance; this report does not propose a new package or lockfile policy.

### 10. Delivery proposal: strategic, operational and tactical

**Strategic:** make Jet's existing App operation the checked boundary for backend, generated clients and Jet UI. Do not build a Nest clone. A new user should complete an authenticated, validated create-and-list workflow without maintaining multiple contracts. An expert should see lifetime, transaction, protocol and deployment obligations rather than discover them through hidden framework rules.

**Operational:** publish a reproducible capability receipt, not a feature list. It must identify compiler/source state, adapter/package versions, actual commands and the stages reached. Cover success and failure for input validation, authorization, transaction rollback, cancellation, lost replies and shutdown. Keep HTTP, WebSocket, GraphQL, TCP, gRPC, Kafka and RabbitMQ separately accountable. A missing adapter must remain missing rather than inherit a success mark from a different transport.

**Tactical order:**

1. Repair and prove the existing typed-form lowering path. The current recorded failure blocks the beginner promise before framework design matters.
2. Complete operation contract continuity: one authorized mutation, native form, scripted UI, typed public failure and checked OpenAPI projection. Reconcile the small API ballot with existing law.
3. Prove request isolation, ordered policy, route conflict behavior, transaction outcomes and application readiness/drain using existing mechanisms.
4. Expose actionable App facts through existing diagnostic tools. Compare the whole edit/check/repair/check loop with Nest's checked tooling.
5. Evaluate each external protocol/integration against its own failure semantics. A first-party package claim needs a compatible install and a real client/broker receipt.

Steps 1–4 repair or complete existing contracts. Step 5 first checks actual coverage and ownership; this research did not establish that every integration is absent. No dependency choice is silently approved.

### 11. Where Jet could win, and what it must avoid

#### Equal-maturity technical comparison

No categorical competitive win is established here. Nest's ecosystem, hiring pool or age is not used as an excuse. Conversely, Jet does not win by counting fewer source lines while omitting validation, schema, testing or deployment.

| Priority vector | Candidate Jet advantage | Why it is not yet a win |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Safety | Checked operation/effect/resource facts can reject invalid composition before an HTTP server starts. | Current form delivery fails. Rust already offers static ownership, and schema-assisted Nest reduces erased-type gaps. Exact accepted/rejected cases need proof. |
| Beginner experience | One typed operation can serve Jet UI, no-script forms and external clients without copy-maintained contracts. | Shared TypeScript/schema tooling already helps Nest frontends. Jet must deliver the complete workflow, not just a type declaration. |
| Runtime performance | Compiled, precomputed route/codec facts may remove runtime reflection and avoid request graph allocation. | Glaze, Rust and .NET are strong compiled baselines. No matched latency, throughput, memory or startup result exists. |
| One mechanism | App, server function, Query and Core codec facts can be reused across projections. | Existing names alone do not prove one semantic path; the manual and typed battery paths still need agreement proof. |
| Tooling and auditability | Source-linked checked graphs can explain policy/order/failure before deployment and feed agent tools directly. | Nest Devtools and Observe already supply useful runtime context. Jet's observed 0..0 error is not an actionable advantage. |

A compiler-enforced effect/resource contract is harder for a runtime decorator framework to copy without adopting a build-time checker. That is a plausible architectural distinction, not a universal advantage: peers can generate code and Rust already checks strong static properties. Judge Jet by the concrete errors prevented and the control retained.

#### Avoid list

| Mistake | Evidence | Jet exposure and response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treat a decorator as complete semantics. | Nest request order and provider scopes have rules beyond annotation text. | Expose one checked expansion; do not add hidden registration rules. |
| Confuse type metadata with input validation. | Nest class metadata is erased/limited; Standard Schema supplies runtime facts explicitly. | Use canonical codec/validation; test actual boundary policy. |
| Declare all shared mutable state safe because of the runtime model. | Request-scope docs discuss singleton reuse, not transaction isolation across awaits. | Keep request authority explicit and resource lifetimes separate. |
| Make a transport abstraction promise more than the protocol. | Kafka replies, RMQ acknowledgements, gRPC streams and native WS differ. | Represent those states; do not add a fake exactly-once option. |
| Copy a tutorial production default. | TypeORM warns against `synchronize: true`; auth examples warn about secrets/passwords. | Safe scaffolds and operational receipts, not unexamined example copying. |
| Count unavailable or incompatible integrations as shipped. | Current package peers and documentation generations differ. | Record compatible pins and actual install/run evidence. |
| Hide external disclosure in a debugging feature. | Observe log forwarding moves data to external infrastructure. | Explicit opt-in, redaction and local-first facts. |
| Add a second framework mechanism to solve a missing projection. | Jet already has App/server-function/HTTP/OpenAPI/Core codec machinery. | Finish the existing path. Jet is not yet structurally immune to duplication. |

#### Performance proof, if the owner wants a competitive verdict

Use the same authenticated create-order/list workload, input limits, schema checks, error mapping, database server, pool size, logging policy and response bytes. Pin Nest 12.0.1 with Fastify 5.12.1 through platform-fastify 12.0.1, plus its validation/schema packages. Pin the Jet compiler and inspected source separately. Do not disable security or validation on one side.

Measure cold startup separately from warmed steady state. Report throughput only at a stated latency/error budget, plus p50/p95/p99, CPU, memory and allocation evidence where supported. Run fixed-rate and overload/failure cases; include invalid input and database delay. Record client placement, hardware, repetitions and confidence intervals. A hello-world route, the Nest docs' Fastify ratio, or compiler elapsed seconds cannot establish this claim.

### 12. Micro-surface sweep

All ten categories apply to this backend/API/tooling subject.

| Category | Concrete signal | Jet disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Syntax | Nest decorators compress registration; Jet already has `.route/.action/.form`. | Keep current grammar. The App export API and independent integration-placement choices are balloted; no new syntax is proposed. |
| Ergonomics | Nest provider/module wiring and plugin setup add steps, while Standard Schema removes some duplication. | Count the whole typed form/client/server workflow, including failure handling, not decorators alone. |
| Surfaces | Nest groups core, adapters and official integrations visibly. | Clarify existing `core.web`, canonical HTTP router and visual WebRouter without merging unlike contracts. |
| APIs, types and methods | `Results<Ok<T>,NotFound,BadRequest>`, `Json<T>`, `glz::read_json<T>` and Nest schema APIs are serious peers. | Typed failure/codec/schema continuity is required; names alone do not beat them. |
| Defaults | Nest has explicit choices for validation/coercion, adapters, shutdown and cache. | Prove safe input, authority, bounds and secret handling on the default beginner path. |
| Naming | Audience Nest/Next confusion; call/event and request/connection “scope” differ. | Use task/protocol terms that predict behavior. Do not rename mature APIs merely for cosmetic symmetry. |
| Error text and diagnostics | Jet says the ICE is its bug, but reports 0..0 rather than the user's construct. | Retain honest blame; add the source and causal repair facts. |
| UX and DX | Nest testing/Devtools/SWC provide different feedback stages. | Check readiness is not server readiness; show the stage reached and a reliable repair loop. |
| Tooling and CLI shape | `nest start -b swc -w --type-check` and plugin setup are concrete costs. | Use existing Jet commands/fact views; no speculative standalone web CLI. |
| Ceremony versus control | Automatic DI and ambient context reduce arguments but hide lookup/lifetime; explicit values expose control. | Small typed defaults with explicit resource/protocol policy. Do not force a service class or a second configuration DSL. |

## Readability


### Verdict

Jet should not turn this video into four compiler-enforced style rules. Its strongest transferable lesson is narrower: **remove unnecessary reasoning work without hiding the program's real contract**. Keep the current formatter, safe collection operations, write-access markers, failure contracts and compiler-owned explanation facts. Improve how a reader reaches those facts. Do not add an eight-column rule, a maximum-function-length error, a ban on explanatory comments, or a second effect mechanism.

The first operational priority is an observed **frozen-binary cleanup gap**. Default execution omits guard callbacks; interpreter mode rejects the typed callback bridge; AOT executes callbacks after the body but in declaration order rather than the required reverse order. A body-marker contrast distinguishes that ordering error from immediate-at-registration execution. The inspector still reports IO effects and explicit failure contracts. Current captured source retains `scope.guard` and its binding-lifetime contract; resource-only `defer` did not retire it. These observations do not identify a source-matched compiler root cause, but they prevent claiming that readable cleanup syntax or exit 0 is enough.

Three presentation/diagnostic proposals follow:

1. Offer an **opt-in local callable summary** through the existing editor reasoning surface. Show the selected function's checked failure, write-access and effect consequences before expandable derivation metadata. This is a new presentation choice, not new Jet syntax. It needs an owner ballot.
2. Make the **collection-mutation diagnostic's repair contract honest**. Frozen E0507 confirms the generic index-loop recipe. Explain whether the programmer must build a new result, mutate a fixed set of original elements, or change a work queue. Do not imply that arbitrary index traversal preserves behavior.
3. Make the **text-plus repair source-specific**. The exercised E0109 suggests `"{a}{b}"` for operands named `first` and `last`. Show the actual operands, or an explicitly labeled schematic example, rather than an apparent paste-ready fix with unrelated names.

The exhaustive value-closure pass retains **17 findings: 12 card-required scopes, three independently owner-gated choices, and two genuine no-new-feature dispositions**. It also maps peer-owned work rather than opening duplicate queues. The additional public choices are bounded local-obligation facts in the existing compiler facade and compiler-bound emitting-site metadata in existing `core.log`. Neither adds a new library or dependency. The complete 41-row ledger is [value-coverage.json](#coverage-readability); useful uncertainty is scoped work, not a reason to discard value.

The strongest evidenced correction is to the video, not Jet: preserving a single runtime log line and preserving a whole message for source search are different requirements. The video's concatenation workaround addresses the former but does not preserve the latter. A second correction concerns the displayed C refactor: it copies the terminating zero, but does not leave the pointers at the same positions as the compact form.

**Evidence status.** This is DOCS ONLY. Source excerpts came from a dirty working tree. No analyst build, test suite, formatter gate or implementation ran. Main owns focused executable receipts, and a later source change broke a rebuild. Therefore neither inspected source nor a successful older binary can establish a green current tree or same-source all-tier behavior. Exact probe status belongs in `probes.json`; no performance or productivity result is claimed here.

**Capture integrity.** The original worked-facts packet materially rewrote several snippets while carrying the original files' hashes. Whole-file hashes did not authenticate those transcriptions. The blanket verbatim assertions are withdrawn in all three Jet packets; normalized/partial snippets are locator-derived evidence only. Three complete current Jet examples and three corrected Rust source witnesses are independently byte-bound in [capture-errata.json](#artifact-3b3cc0cad5ff). In particular, the old `for`, `task.spawn`, `Channel` and `match` snippets do not establish stale current source. All 15 executed receipts remain unchanged. Unavailable historical diagnostic-fixture identity is an authentication gap, not a demonstrated fabrication.

### 1. Source identity, coverage and attribution

The assigned source is [Kantan Coding, *Linus's Laws of Writing Readable Code*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d6PG6xdoU4c), published **2024-10-27**, duration **242 seconds**, source identity `youtube:d6PG6xdoU4c`. This is a narrator's presentation, not a recording of Linus giving these instructions.

I read all **78 nonempty English auto-caption cues**, covering speech from 00:00.040 through 03:55.879. I also inspected all **14 available storyboard contact-sheet images**, which sample the 00:00–04:02 timeline. They are low-resolution miniature panels, not continuous video. Short C expressions are readable and independently checked below; several small Go tokens, quote delimiters and long messages are not reliable enough to transcribe exactly. Creator captions and chapters were unavailable. Full video retrieval failed; the later storyboard fallback improved the earlier visual gap without eliminating it.

The description links a Go course site, not the original laws. The closest authenticated textual lineage is [Linux v6.10 `Documentation/process/coding-style.rst`](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v6.10/process/coding-style.html), pinned to commit **`0c3836482481200ead7b416ca80c68a29cfdaabd`**. Its wording closely matches all four spoken lessons. The release tag is associated with Linus, but that does not establish personal authorship of every sentence in this collective document. I attribute those passages to **the Linux kernel coding-style document**, not as newly authenticated personal quotations.

For a genuinely Linus-attributed original statement, I also read [his 2012 Slashdot answer, “favorite hack”](https://meta.slashdot.org/story/12/10/11/0030249/linus-torvalds-answers-your-questions). It is supplemental: the assigned video's speech does not discuss linked-list deletion. The original answer favors a better pointer representation that removes a head-node special case. It is useful evidence against interpreting Linus as banning every compact or expert idiom.

#### Every substantive video law

| Video segment | What the narrator actually argues | Original source and correction | Concrete Jet translation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 00:00–00:46 | Eight-column indentation improves visibility and warns about deep nesting. The images show nesting and large horizontal drift. | Kernel §1 contains the same fatigue/nesting argument. ### 2. Correct the examples before extracting policy

#### 2.1 Source wrapping is not the same as an output newline

There are at least four distinct operations:

1. An editor visually wraps a line without changing source bytes.
2. Source contains adjacent literals or an expression that combines fragments.
3. A literal contains an explicit newline escape.
4. A multiline/raw literal contains actual newline content under that language's rules.

They need not produce the same output, and equal output does not make their source equally searchable. In C, [N1570 §5.1.1.2 phase 6 and §6.4.5](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf) concatenate adjacent literal tokens during translation. This C example has one output line despite two physical source lines:

```c
/* Language-law illustration, not a transcription of the Go video. */
printf("READ-MSG: "
       "saved row\n");
```

A literal search for `READ-MSG: saved row` still does not find that whole text in these source bytes. The video visibly runs a command shaped as `go run main.go | grep -i ...`; that is output search. It does not test the kernel document's source-search requirement. The Go demonstration may genuinely contain a newline-producing literal; the correction does not require declaring its runtime output fake.

Current Jet already supplies the appropriate one-mechanism contrast:

<a id="input-d5cb94438f6a9a523a11c1bc20c91349869c3ad678fda3e377c139c14643eee4"></a>

```jet
fn run() {
    prefix :: "READ-MSG: "
    detail :: "saved row"
    print("{prefix}{detail}")
    print("READ-MSG: saved row")
    print("READ-MSG:\nsaved row")
}
```

READ-P01 ran on frozen executable `e841…` with exit 0. The first two output lines were `READ-MSG: saved row`; the third print produced `READ-MSG:` and `saved row` on separate lines. The formatter dry-run exited 0 with no output for this input. Only the direct literal stores the complete first message together at its output site. This is a reasoning contrast, not a recommendation to prohibit interpolation. Dynamic fields, localization and redaction can make complete literal search insufficient; a stable event or diagnostic identity is then more useful. Do not add a new logging framework just to fix this video's example.

For compiler diagnostics, Jet already gives users a stable code such as `E0109`. Current source also has an interpolation repair for text `+`. Keep those advantages separate from an unmeasured claim that all messages are easy to locate.

#### 2.2 The C rewrite has a narrower equivalence contract than the presentation implies

Short expressions visible in storyboards 11, 13 and 14 are:

```c
/* Compact form shown by the video. */
while (*dest++ = *src++);
```

```c
/* Expanded form shown by the video. */
while (*src != '\0') {
    *dest = *src;
    dest++;
    src++;
}
*dest = *src;
```

For ordinary nonvolatile memory, a valid NUL-terminated source and sufficient valid destination storage, both copy through the terminating zero. The final line is present; the audience's missing-terminator allegation is not a verified defect. One commenter explicitly retracted it.

But the compact form advances both pointers during the terminating assignment. The expansion leaves both pointing at the terminator. For a one-character string, the compact pointers finish two positions past their starting addresses; the expanded pointers finish one position past. They differ if later code observes those pointers. The expansion also rereads source bytes, so this argument must not be generalized to volatile memory. The enclosing program is unavailable; I do **not** claim a demonstrated runtime bug in the video.

This reading follows [N1570 §§6.5.2.4, 6.5.16 and 6.8.5](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf). **BigCodeAstra independently inspected the actual images and confirmed the pointer-state distinction and nonvolatile qualification.** No C compiler run was performed.

The Jet lesson is precise: a readability repair must preserve the agreed observable contract—values, writes, ordering, failure, cleanup and resource ownership—not only a final printed value. Raw sentinel-buffer copying should not be the ordinary Jet text-copy interface. A named, checked collection or text operation can be both shorter and safer than either C spelling. An expert implementation can still document its low-level invariant without violating a comment rule.

#### Same job: keep positive integers, preserve order and the original input

The job is deliberately about a **new result**, not an in-place erase benchmark. Input is `[3, -1, 0, 2]`; result is `[3, 2]`; original input must remain unchanged. All peer snippets below are constructed from the cited language/API contracts, **not run receipts**.

Jet selection example, adapted only for the frozen executable after READ-P03 rejected `for` and the first adaptation rejected `continue`, both with E0003. The distinct second adaptation follows the diagnostic's `loop`/`next` spelling. This does not settle current syntax law; every original input and rejection remains retained:

<a id="input-24f4a11488819756a6abf4f19a29d6474df7cbaac57280f835c98eac5e3d6817"></a>

```jet
fn positive(values: [Int]) [Int] -> {
    kept := [Int]{}
    loop value in values {
        if value <= 0 -> next
        kept.push(value)
    }
    return kept
}
fn run() {
    values :: [3, -1, 0, 2]
    print(positive(values))
    print(values)
}
```

This second adaptation ran with exit 0 and a tier1-native trace. It printed exactly `[3, 2]` followed by `[3, -1, 0, 2]`: the declared new-result/input-preservation job is observed for this one input and frozen path (READ-C040). No peer-runtime, AOT, empty-input or current-source equivalence is inferred.

The equally direct body `if value > 0 { kept.push(value) }` has one more indentation level but no early iteration skip. Neither spelling is universally clearer. Both isolate writes to the result. A source-level readability rule that requires the guard form would enforce taste, not improve this contract.

C++23-style algorithm:

The available [working-draft `copy_if` contract](https://eel.is/c++draft/alg.copy) requires non-overlapping ranges and explicitly states “Stable” in paragraph 25. Its source tree is `c7015b485cc3db8efaa9dfb9ff0809c5394a4ed1`, `algorithms.tex:6507,6609`. This is exact current-draft evidence, not an extracted C++23 release contract. The following is a constructed comparison, not execution proof (READ-C046).

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iterator>
#include <vector>
int main() {
    const std::vector<int> values{3, -1, 0, 2};
    std::vector<int> kept;
    std::ranges::copy_if(values, std::back_inserter(kept),
                         [](int value) { return value > 0; });
}
```

Rust 1.90:

```rust
fn main() {
    let values = vec![3, -1, 0, 2];
    let kept: Vec<i32> = values.iter().copied()
        .filter(|value| *value > 0).collect();
    assert_eq!(kept, vec![3, 2]);
    assert_eq!(values, vec![3, -1, 0, 2]);
}
```

Python 3.14:

```python
values = [3, -1, 0, 2]
kept = [value for value in values if value > 0]
assert kept == [3, 2] and values == [3, -1, 0, 2]
```

Go 1.26-style direct loop:

```go
package main
func main() {
    values := []int{3, -1, 0, 2}
    kept := make([]int, 0, len(values))
    for _, value := range values {
        if value > 0 { kept = append(kept, value) }
    }
    _ = kept
}
```

Java 25:

```java
import java.util.List;
class Positive {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var values = List.of(3, -1, 0, 2);
        var kept = values.stream().filter(value -> value > 0).toList();
    }
}
```

C#14 / .NET10:

```csharp
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
var values = new List<int> { 3, -1, 0, 2 };
var kept = values.Where(value => value > 0).ToList();
```

These programs establish a fair conceptual workload, not identical collection mutability or allocation policies. Java's terminal result and the mutable results elsewhere must not be treated as the same later-mutation contract. No performance comparison is made. If the job changes to **in-place removal**, use the corresponding standard operation—Rust `retain`, C++ `erase_if`, Go `DeleteFunc`, Java `removeIf`, C# `RemoveAll`—and separately state aliasing and return-value obligations. Python rebinding and slice assignment are not interchangeable for observers holding the original list.

For Jet, the collection registry already distinguishes mutators, eager list transformations and lazy iterator transformations. IteratorAstra owns completeness and any missing collection capability; this report does not create a competing `retain`/`filter`/comprehension design. The readability requirement for that stream is exact: state whether the receiver changes, whether evaluation is eager or lazy, whether order is retained, and how a predicate failure affects partial results.
