<a id="owner-choice-directory"></a>
<a id="complete-ballots"></a>
## Appendix D — Complete owner-choice directory

All 124 independent choices below are published in Tower and were read back field-for-field. There are 105 ready owner-review surfaces and 19 complete performance-gated drafts. None is ratified. Full option programs, comparisons, constraints and review summaries live on each linked Tower work home; this directory is not a second ballot.

The 13 full ballots received independent beginner and adversarial review. Final Enum review repaired real type-name, indexing, noncopyable ownership and manual-routing gaps. GPU review retained exact invocation, buffer, scope and numeric contracts without claiming a run or speedup. Shared requirements are not comparative penalties.

<a id="ballots-enums"></a>

### enums

<a id="decision-d-enum-casevalues1"></a>
#### D-ENUM-CASEVALUES1 — One complete iterator of payload-free enum values

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3132](#card-3132).

A case is one named choice. A payload is extra data carried by that choice. In a payload-free enum, each case is one complete value. Jet already records case order, but callers repeat a list today. A adds a typed Direction.cases() iterator; B keeps the list. Neither changes enum identity, matching or wire format.

<a id="decision-d-enum-ingress1"></a>
#### D-ENUM-INGRESS1 — Generate checked decoders for explicitly numbered enums

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3146](#card-3146).

An explicit code is a number assigned to a named enum case. A checked decoder accepts only declared codes and returns a failure for a hole. A generates that lookup from the enum; B keeps an application parser. Both preserve destination-owned conversion and the existing fallible error result.

<a id="decision-d-enum-constructorcall1"></a>
#### D-ENUM-CONSTRUCTORCALL1 — Payload constructors as ordinary callable values

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3161](#card-3161).

A payload constructor combines supplied data with a case name. A callable value is a function that can be stored or passed to another function. Jet can call constructors directly today, but a higher-order use needs a lambda. A makes the qualified constructor itself callable; B keeps the lambda. Unit cases stay values.

<a id="decision-d-enum-evolution1"></a>
#### D-ENUM-EVOLUTION1 — Publisher-required future-case fallback

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3145](#card-3145).

An enum lists named cases. A match chooses a response; else handles the remaining cases. Jet already lets callers use else. Should callers keep that choice, or may a library require it outside its own package? Both choices leave the fallback response with the caller.

<a id="decision-d-enum-casemeta1"></a>
#### D-ENUM-CASEMETA1 — One enum case reflection model

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3147](#card-3147).

An enum selects a case and payload—the attached value. A/C generate complete catalogs or reject inaccessible nested details. A returns a handle holding an independent ordinary value copy. It refuses shared mutable data and unproved field access. Passing a lawful handle exports its captured fields. B writes catalogs and matches. C generates catalogs but keeps runtime matching.

<a id="decision-d-enum-adjacent1"></a>
#### D-ENUM-ADJACENT1 — Adjacent tag and content in Codable

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3148](#card-3148).

A service may send a case name in kind and its payload—the attached value—in body. Codable converts between Jet values and encoded data. A adds this two-field form directly; B builds it explicitly. A unit case has no payload: absent or null body is accepted, then omitted on output. Non-null body fails. Other unit rules need B or a custom codec.

<a id="decision-d-enum-unknown1"></a>
#### D-ENUM-UNKNOWN1 — Typed forwarding of unknown enum variants

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3149](#card-3149).

A tag names a message kind. A stores an unfamiliar kind in a protected enum case. B keeps DataTree—the parsed message—and routes known kinds separately. Neither preserves original bytes; unsupported values fail. A cannot use Untagged, which has no tag, or aliases on its fallback. Core currently keeps the last duplicate tag; that policy decision remains open.

<a id="decision-d-enum-wirealias1"></a>
#### D-ENUM-WIREALIAS1 — Canonical enum output with old input names

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3150](#card-3150).

A wire name is text that identifies a case in stored or sent data. A accepts listed old names whenever this enum is decoded, but writes one current name. B can translate names only at selected calls. Removing an alias later rejects old input. Aliases need a tag and unique names; they cannot mark the Unknown fallback.

<a id="ballots-iterators"></a>

### iterators

<a id="decision-d-iter-resume1"></a>
#### D-ITER-RESUME1 — Keep and resume one iterator

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3315](#card-3315).

Resume means continue the same iterator from its current position. Example: The source is [header, 1, 2, 3]; read the header, then one record. A calls next again on the same owner; B calls next inside two short borrows. Expected output: The next read is 2 and the remaining source is [3]. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-replay1"></a>
#### D-ITER-REPLAY1 — Repeat a replayable source lazily

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3316](#card-3316).

Replay means read a replay-capable source again; it is not reopening arbitrary I/O. Example: The replayable source is [1, 2] and the consumer asks for five values. A restarts copied source state after the first pass; B requires cycle(5). Expected output: The expected prefix is [1, 2, 1, 2, 1]; an empty source ends. Authored NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-iter-size1"></a>
#### D-ITER-SIZE1 — Inspect remaining size without consuming it

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3317](#card-3317).

A size fact reports remaining bounds without pulling the next item. Example: The source contains [10, 20, 30] and the cursor has not advanced. A asks for its declared bounds; B advances and counts when a count is needed. Expected output: A can report 3 without consuming 10; B keeps the existing consuming count. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-back1"></a>
#### D-ITER-BACK1 — Read a source from both ends

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3317](#card-3317).

A backward iterator can take the next item from the remaining back as well as the front. Example: The capable source is [1, 2, 3]. Read from the front, then from the back, without crossing the cursor. Expected output: The reads are 1 then 3, leaving [2]; a one-way source cannot do the back read. Authored NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-iter-fused1"></a>
#### D-ITER-FUSED1 — Make permanent exhaustion explicit

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3317](#card-3317).

A fused iterator stays finished after its first end result. Example: A source returns 1, then no item, then would otherwise return 2. A marks the source finished at the first end; B follows the source-specific end rule. Expected output: A returns 1, then no item forever; B may return 2 only when its source permits resuming. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-borrow1"></a>
#### D-ITER-BORROW1 — Borrow a source without copying its items

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3317](#card-3317).

A borrowed view reads the same source storage without taking ownership of it. Example: The source storage is [10, 20, 30]; read two items through a borrowed adapter. A keeps a checked loan and then resumes the owner; B collects owned adapter input first. Expected output: The borrowed prefix is [10,20] and the owner can continue at 30 after the loan ends. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-scan1"></a>
#### D-ITER-SCAN1 — Keep state separate from scan output

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3326](#card-3326).

A scan keeps private running state and may emit a different output type. Example: Read [1, 2, 3] with private total 0 and emit text labels. Each input updates the total and produces one label without exposing the state type as the item type. Expected output: The intended labels are ["total=1", "total=3", "total=6"]. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-selection1"></a>
#### D-ITER-SELECTION1 — Select absent values without discarding errors

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3327](#card-3327).

Optional selection skips absence, while a returned error remains data or an effect by its declared type. Example: Map [1, 2, 3] so 2 is absent and a separate bad record is an error. A uses the existing filter_map result contract; B gives optional selection its own name. Expected output: The optional path keeps [1,3]; the deliberate error is not silently dropped. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-cmpselect1"></a>
#### D-ITER-CMPSELECT1 — Select extrema with an explicit comparator

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3328](#card-3328).

A comparator is a function that says which of two values comes first. Example: Choose an extreme from ["pear", "fig", "plum"] by string length. A passes the comparator to extrema selection; B writes the same comparison in a fold. Expected output: The shortest item is "fig"; existing empty and last-tie rules remain. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-collect1"></a>
#### D-ITER-COLLECT1 — Choose a destination explicitly

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3329](#card-3329).

Collection construction decides how iterator items become a final destination. Example: Read [1, 2, 1] and request either a List or a Set destination. A lets the destination type construct itself; B passes an owned destination value. Expected output: The List keeps [1,2,1], while the Set applies its existing duplicate rule. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-extend1"></a>
#### D-ITER-EXTEND1 — Grow an existing destination from a source

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3330](#card-3330).

Extend adds source items to an existing destination instead of replacing it. Example: Start values as [1] and feed a lazy source [2, 3]. A inserts directly and reports a prefix if the source fails; B first builds a temporary List. Expected output: On success values become [1,2,3]; a failure may leave the inserted prefix. Authored NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-iter-failconsume1"></a>
#### D-ITER-FAILCONSUME1 — Stop a borrowed consumer on failure

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3331](#card-3331).

A fallible consumer can stop after a prefix and return the existing failure effect. Example: Parse ["1", "oops", "2"] through a borrowed source. The consumer reads 1, fails at "oops", and does not invent a second error hierarchy. Expected output: The error identifies "oops" and the borrowed source still has "2" available. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-lookahead1"></a>
#### D-ITER-LOOKAHEAD1 — Inspect an item without consuming it

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3333](#card-3333).

Lookahead inspects one pending item without consuming it. Example: The source is [1, 2, 3] and a parser needs to check the next token twice. A stores one pending item; B exposes conditional reads through a callback. Expected output: Both inspections see 1, then the consuming read still returns 1. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-sliceproducers1"></a>
#### D-ITER-SLICEPRODUCERS1 — Group borrowed slices without copying them

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3340](#card-3340).

A view is a window onto existing storage; exact and reverse grouping set different boundaries. Example: Group [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] with width 2, including its final partial group. A exposes checked borrowed groups; B keeps owned grouping and its existing boundaries. Expected output: The ordinary chunks are [1,2], [3,4], [5]; exact forms report or reject the partial group by contract. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-interop1"></a>
#### D-ITER-INTEROP1 — Give custom sources the standard adapters

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3341](#card-3341).

An adapter lets a custom source use standard operations without changing its source ownership. Example: A custom source yields [1, 2, 3] and the job doubles each item. A applies map directly through the protocol; B converts explicitly before applying adapters. Expected output: The intended result is [2, 4, 6] with no hidden eager collection in the deferred path. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-channelsource1"></a>
#### D-ITER-CHANNELSOURCE1 — Drain ready channel items without waiting

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3343](#card-3343).

A live channel can be empty now without being closed. Example: The receiver has 1 queued item, then is empty, then receives 2 later. A drains ready values and returns; B reports ready, empty-now, or closed as separate states. Expected output: The first drain returns [1]; a later poll can still return 2 instead of treating empty as closed. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-parallel1"></a>
#### D-ITER-PARALLEL1 — Keep indexed facts in parallel traversal

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3344](#card-3344).

Indexed means the source can name stable positions for splitting; parallel does not mean automatic. Example: Square [1, 2, 3] with a work limit of 2. A extends existing para_map to lawful generic sources; B creates an explicit parallel view. Expected output: The source-order values are [1,4,9]; the measured scheduler gate may still choose serial work. Authored NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): A, B. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-iter-concurrent1"></a>
#### D-ITER-CONCURRENT1 — Bound concurrent work on a live source

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3346](#card-3346).

A concurrency limit bounds unfinished started work and retained completed results. Example: A live source yields 1, 2, 3, 4 and the worker returns x*x with limit 2. A extends para_map for deferred streams; B gives the same task model a new name. Expected output: Ordered output is [1,4,9,16]; an earlier slow task may delay later output, while unordered mode may differ. Authored NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): A, B. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-iter-keyruns1"></a>
#### D-ITER-KEYRUNS1 — Group adjacent equal keys

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3347](#card-3347).

A keyed run is one consecutive stretch with the same key, not a global bucket. Example: For keys A,A,B,A, read one item from the first A run, then request the next group. The child drains to its boundary before the parent reaches B. Expected output: groups A:[A,A], B:[B], A:[A]. Authored NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-iter-unique1"></a>
#### D-ITER-UNIQUE1 — Select distinct keys in encounter order

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3349](#card-3349).

Global uniqueness remembers keys already seen, while adjacent dedup only compares neighbors. Example: Read [a, b, a, c] and keep the first item for each key. A emits the first encounter and remembers keys; B writes the same membership loop with a Set. Expected output: The encounter-order result is [a, b, c]. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-sortedmerge1"></a>
#### D-ITER-SORTEDMERGE1 — Merge sorted sources without sorting them again

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3351](#card-3351).

A sorted merge requires each input source to be sorted before the merge begins. Example: Merge sorted sources [1, 3] and [2, 4] in ascending order. A checks or accepts the sorted-source capability and keeps one frontier per source; B concatenates and sorts all values. Expected output: The intended output is [1,2,3,4]; unsorted input is rejected or diagnosed, never silently resorted by A. Authored NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-iter-combinations1"></a>
#### D-ITER-COMBINATIONS1 — Select finite combinations lazily

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3353](#card-3353).

A combination chooses positions without changing their order; replacement is a separate rule. Example: Choose width-2 combinations from [1, 2, 3]. A uses the stock combinations source; B writes the fixed-width selection loops. Expected output: The intended values are [1,2], [1,3], [2,3]. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-permutations1"></a>
#### D-ITER-PERMUTATIONS1 — Visit finite permutations lazily

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3353](#card-3353).

A permutation chooses distinct positions and changes their order. Example: Choose width-2 permutations from [1, 2, 3]. A uses the stock source; B writes explicit selection loops while preserving ownership. Expected output: The six ordered pairs are produced; output count grows factorially with input size. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-powerset1"></a>
#### D-ITER-POWERSET1 — Visit all finite subsets lazily

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3353](#card-3353).

A powerset contains every positional subset, including the empty subset. Example: Enumerate subsets of [a, b]. A uses the stock lazy source; B writes a fixed-input generator. Expected output: The intended subsets are [], [a], [b], [a,b]; two inputs produce four subsets. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-branchpartition1"></a>
#### D-ITER-BRANCHPARTITION1 — Build different outputs in one partition pass

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3354](#card-3354).

Partition sends each input to one of two outputs while preserving encounter order. Example: Parse ["1", "bad", "2"] into successful numbers and error records. A returns both transformed branches; B writes the two destination updates explicitly. Expected output: The number branch is [1,2] and the error branch is ["bad"]. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-exactgroup1"></a>
#### D-ITER-EXACTGROUP1 — Keep incomplete fixed-width reads

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3355](#card-3355).

An exact group is complete only when it has the requested width. Example: Read width-2 groups from [1, 2, 3]. A returns the consumed partial [3]; B keeps the cursor unchanged until a full group exists. Expected output: The first group is [1,2]; the final [3] is either returned as partial or retained by the chosen contract. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-nested1"></a>
#### D-ITER-NESTED1 — Flatten the existing iterable protocol

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3358](#card-3358).

Flatten visits each child source in order and finishes or drops it before starting the next. Example: The parent is [1,2] and each finite child yields [x,x]. A accepts any lawful child iterator; B requires each child to be a List. Expected output: The finite result is [1,1,2,2]; an endless first child prevents reaching child 2 under either contract. Authored NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-iter-mapown1"></a>
#### D-ITER-MAPOWN1 — Let a mapper consume an owned item

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3359](#card-3359).

An owning callback can consume an item; a borrowed view cannot transfer storage it does not own. Example: Map move-only records [r1, r2] to their ids. A follows the ordinary callback ownership convention; B adds a method that explicitly names moving. Expected output: The callback receives each owned record once; a borrowed source remains borrowed. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-readymerge1"></a>
#### D-ITER-READYMERGE1 — Merge items as their sources become ready

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3365](#card-3365).

Ready merge pulls whichever source has a value now while preserving each source order. Example: Source one is slow and will yield 1; source two is ready with 2. A emits ready values without serially waiting; B reads source one completely before source two. Expected output: A may emit 2 before 1; B emits 1 before 2, and each source keeps its own order. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-endless1"></a>
#### D-ITER-ENDLESS1 — Explain a result that needs an endless source to finish

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3368](#card-3368).

An endless source has no end, so a full collected result cannot finish without a bound or cancellation. Example: The source yields 1 forever; compare to take(3). A warns only when endless production is proven; B emits no new warning. Expected output: to_list() cannot finish, while take(3) can produce [1,1,1]. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-drain1"></a>
#### D-ITER-DRAIN1 — Own a removal range while iterating it

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3371](#card-3371).

Drain removes a chosen range and yields its old items while the collection is borrowed. Example: Drain indexes 1..<3 from [1, 2, 3, 4]. A transfers removed values directly; B copies/replaces through an explicit temporary. Expected output: The removed values are [2,3] and the collection becomes [1,4], even if unread removed values are dropped. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-extract1"></a>
#### D-ITER-EXTRACT1 — Remove only the visited selected items

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3371](#card-3371).

Incremental extraction commits visited removals and leaves unvisited items alone when stopped. Example: Visit [1,2,3,4] and stop after extracting the first odd item. A visits until the caller stops; B rebuilds an explicit List from the chosen predicate. Expected output: A extracts 1 and leaves unvisited 2,3,4 in place; prior removals are not rolled back on later failure. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-splice1"></a>
#### D-ITER-SPLICE1 — Replace a range while yielding its old values

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3371](#card-3371).

Splice yields removed values and inserts replacements at one explicit finish boundary. Example: Replace 2,3 in [1,2,3,4] with [8,9]. A requires the caller to finish or cancel the replacement; B permits only restricted drop-time commit. Expected output: After a successful finish the collection is [1,8,9,4] and removed values are [2,3]. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-remainder1"></a>
#### D-ITER-REMAINDER1 — Borrow the storage that has not been read

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3375](#card-3375).

A remainder view exposes the source storage after the cursor without copying it. Example: Start with data [1,2,3] and advance one item. A returns a checked view of the unconsumed storage; B keeps the cursor offset for the caller. Expected output: The remainder view reads [2,3]; conflicting advancement is rejected while the view is live. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-interleave1"></a>
#### D-ITER-INTERLEAVE1 — Alternate between source items

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3377](#card-3377).

Interleave alternates pulls from sources; its end rule decides what happens to a longer source. Example: Alternate [1,3] with [2,4]. A uses explicit alternating composition; B zips and flattens with the existing shortest rule. Expected output: The equal-length result is [1,2,3,4]; a longer input follows the selected end policy. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-cartesian1"></a>
#### D-ITER-CARTESIAN1 — Generate a Cartesian grid

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3379](#card-3379).

A Cartesian product pairs every value from each dimension. Example: Use [1,2] and [10,20] in both candidate and plain paths. The candidate lists tuples; nested loops print the same tuples. Expected output: (1,10), (1,20), (2,10), (2,20). Reused dimensions must be replayable or materialized. Authored NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-iter-separator1"></a>
#### D-ITER-SEPARATOR1 — Create separators only when demanded

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3384](#card-3384).

A separator factory creates a fresh separator only when another source item is demanded. Example: Intersperse [1,2,3] with a factory that returns a fresh marker. A calls the factory between items; B inserts one constant separator value. Expected output: The intended sequence is [1,marker,2,marker,3]; empty and singleton inputs call the factory zero times. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-setops1"></a>
#### D-ITER-SETOPS1 — Apply keyed set rules to lazy sequences

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3390](#card-3390).

Keyed sequence set operations keep a chosen source representative and encounter order. Example: Combine left [a,b,a] with right [b,c] using first-source representatives. A applies named keyed union/intersection/exclusion; B writes membership loops with a Set. Expected output: Union is [a,b,c] under the stated key rule; other operations use their declared side and finish rules. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-rng1"></a>
#### D-ITER-RNG1 — Shuffle through one explicit random state

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3392](#card-3392).

An explicit random handle owns the seed and the next random state. Example: Shuffle [1,2,3] twice with one Rng handle. A advances the existing Rng state; B resets a private demo seed for each call. Expected output: The second A shuffle observes the advanced state; B repeats its fixed demonstration sequence. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-itdep1"></a>
#### D-ITER-ITDEP1 — Choose itertools dependency scope

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3380](#card-3380).

A dependency choice changes how Jet implements a feature, not what the public iterator means. Example: Deduplicate [1,1,2] and inspect the same output under each package policy. A keeps native code; B permits an optional bridge; C adopts the pinned package by default. Expected output: The intended public result is [1,2] in every case; bridge behavior remains unproved. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-rayondep1"></a>
#### D-ITER-RAYONDEP1 — Choose Rayon dependency scope

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3381](#card-3381).

A dependency bridge is internal; it does not create a second public scheduler. Example: Square [1,2,3] through the existing explicit parallel operation. A stays native; B allows an optional Rayon bridge; C adopts Rayon by default while retaining Jet scheduler rules. Expected output: The public result remains [1,4,9]; no automatic parallelism is inferred. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-futdep1"></a>
#### D-ITER-FUTDEP1 — Choose futures dependency scope

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3382](#card-3382).

A futures dependency can support an internal stream bridge without changing Jet polling law. Example: Map a four-item stream with buffer limit 2. A stays native; B permits an optional futures bridge; C adopts it by default while preserving Jet ownership. Expected output: The intended ordered values are [1,4,9,16]; the bridge is not runtime proof. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-tokiodep1"></a>
#### D-ITER-TOKIODEP1 — Choose tokio-stream dependency scope

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3383](#card-3383).

A tokio-stream bridge is an implementation choice, not a second public runtime. Example: Merge the same ready streams while preserving source order and cancellation. A stays native; B permits an optional tokio-stream bridge; C adopts it by default under existing Jet scheduler rules. Expected output: The intended merged values and cleanup remain the same; no compatibility proof is claimed. Authored NOT RUN.

<a id="decision-d-iter-viewcollect1"></a>
#### D-ITER-VIEWCOLLECT1 — Collect explicit borrowed views

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3393](#card-3393).

A borrowed view points into source storage. Example: Collect views of [1,2,3], read them, then release them before appending 4. A returns [View<T>] headers without payload copies; a conflicting resize while views live is rejected. B copies values. Expected: Views read [1,2,3]; after release, data can become [1,2,3,4]. NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-iter-copy1"></a>
#### D-ITER-COPY1 — Copy a capable iterator position

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3394](#card-3394).

Copying a copyable iterator preserves its cursor position; rebuilding a source may repeat earlier work or effects. Example: Advance a over [1,2,3] once, then set b = ~a. A gives independent cursors: both next() calls return 2. B rebuilds from the source recipe, not the saved position. Expected; NOT RUN.

<a id="ballots-corelib"></a>

### corelib

<a id="decision-d-core-json-dup1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSON-DUP1 — Reject duplicate JSON keys by default

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3234](#card-3234).

A repeated key can hide one value behind another. The frozen decoder keeps the later count. Unknown-field rejection already exists and is separate. Either choice must keep whole-value and streaming input consistent.

<a id="decision-d-core-json-pointer1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSON-POINTER1 — Select data by a standard pointer

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3237](#card-3237).

A pointer is a string path such as /user/name. Core already has field and index access. No standard pointer entrypoint appeared in the bounded capture. Either choice must distinguish missing data from JSON null.

<a id="decision-d-core-json-schema1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSON-SCHEMA1 — Export schema from codec metadata

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3238](#card-3238).

A schema describes accepted data for editors and other tools. Jet already records typed decoding rules. Its captured HTTP and command schemas serve narrower jobs. Either choice must avoid inventing rules that decoding does not enforce.

<a id="decision-d-core-json-patch1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSON-PATCH1 — Apply atomic JSON Patch to data

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3278](#card-3278).

A patch lists edits to a data value. Core has the value and accessors, but no patch entrypoint appeared in the bounded capture. Either choice must define failed edits and preserve the original value.

<a id="decision-d-core-json-merge1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSON-MERGE1 — Apply JSON Merge Patch explicitly

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3279](#card-3279).

Merge Patch updates object members and uses null to delete them. Arrays are replaced, not edited element by element. Existing schema-evolution merging means something else. Either choice must make these rules explicit.

<a id="decision-d-core-args-completion1"></a>
#### D-CORE-ARGS-COMPLETION1 — Make direct completion output usable

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3241](#card-3241).

The direct builder method currently formats a label and words in captured source. A separate tool path already reads embedded command metadata without running the program. Both paths should share command facts.

<a id="decision-d-core-glaze-dependency1"></a>
#### D-CORE-GLAZE-DEPENDENCY1 — Choose the Glaze dependency boundary

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3246](#card-3246).

Useful peer capabilities do not require copying a peer runtime. Core already owns data meaning. The choice is whether a pinned native Glaze adapter should implement approved codec jobs behind that same public surface.

<a id="decision-d-core-bson1"></a>
#### D-CORE-BSON1 — Choose BSON availability in Core

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3267](#card-3267).

First decide codec admission in D-CORE-BSON-ADOPT1. If admitted, this vote chooses stock or an optional first-party package. It changes no wire profile, API semantics or vendor dependency. D-CORE-BSON-PROFILE1 selects the complete wire/API profile independently.

<a id="decision-d-core-msgpack1"></a>
#### D-CORE-MSGPACK1 — Choose MessagePack availability in Core

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3312](#card-3312).

First decide codec admission in D-CORE-MSGPACK-ADOPT1. If admitted, this vote chooses stock or an optional first-party package. It changes no wire profile, API semantics or vendor dependency. D-CORE-MSGPACK-PROFILE1 selects the complete wire/API profile independently.

<a id="decision-d-core-json-diff1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSON-DIFF1 — Generate bounded JSON Patch

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3296](#card-3296).

Applying a patch and finding a patch are different jobs. A generated patch must reproduce the target, but need not be the smallest possible edit list. Either choice must bound comparison work and output.

<a id="decision-d-core-json-mergediff1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSON-MERGEDIFF1 — Generate representable Merge Patch

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3297](#card-3297).

Merge Patch uses an object member’s null value to delete that member. Some desired null assignments therefore cannot be expressed. An unchanged null can remain unchanged. Either choice must report unrepresentable updates instead of losing data.

<a id="decision-d-core-typed-update1"></a>
#### D-CORE-TYPED-UPDATE1 — Choose atomic typed-record updates

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3299](#card-3299).

Ordinary decode constructs a value. A partial update keeps omitted fields from an existing value. These are different jobs. Either choice must preserve validation and define unsupported custom mappings, rather than silently turning decode into mutation.

<a id="decision-d-core-jsonc1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSONC1 — Choose an explicit commented-JSON codec

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3300](#card-3300).

Comments help hand-edited configuration, but they are not ordinary JSON. A separate entrypoint can accept them without weakening network JSON. Either choice must fix the dialect and make output behavior clear.

<a id="decision-d-core-config-layers1"></a>
#### D-CORE-CONFIG-LAYERS1 — Load rooted configuration layers explicitly

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3251](#card-3251).

File-backed configuration can remove repeated loading, merging and provenance code. Its IO must be visible in the loader call, never activated by ordinary decode. A hostname is a caller-selected input, not hidden ambient policy.

<a id="decision-d-core-template1"></a>
#### D-CORE-TEMPLATE1 — Render bounded data templates in Core

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3252](#card-3252).

Runtime templates are a real library job, not ordinary literal formatting. The useful parts are checked fields, sections, iteration and deliberate escaping; they do not justify arbitrary evaluation or another reflection system.

<a id="decision-d-core-jmespath1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JMESPATH1 — Offer a named standard JSON query adapter

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3277](#card-3277).

JMESPath is a wire-data query language, not a synonym for Jet iteration, SQL or a JSON Pointer. Its filters, projections, functions and missing-value rules must travel together if Core claims compatibility.

<a id="decision-d-core-ini1"></a>
#### D-CORE-INI1 — Support an explicit INI configuration profile

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3283](#card-3283).

INI is still a common configuration interchange job. It needs a stated profile: section names, key normalization, duplicates, interpolation and textual scalar conversion cannot be guessed from a generic format label.

<a id="decision-d-core-plist1"></a>
#### D-CORE-PLIST1 — Support typed XML and binary property lists

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3284](#card-3284).

Property lists carry bytes, dates and UIDs beyond an untagged JSON tree. Keep typed values or reject unsupported values explicitly.

<a id="decision-d-core-catalog1"></a>
#### D-CORE-CATALOG1 — Translate through explicit local message catalogs

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3289](#card-3289).

Localization is more than choosing singular or plural in English. Catalogs add languages, context, plural formulas and fallbacks. Those do not require global installation or hidden environment-based language selection.

<a id="decision-d-core-cli-rest1"></a>
#### D-CORE-CLI-REST1 — Generate ReST command reference from metadata

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3292](#card-3292).

A command reference should share names, defaults and validation with the command itself. ReST is independently useful for documentation systems and is not the same output contract as Markdown or man pages.

<a id="decision-d-core-cli-yaml1"></a>
#### D-CORE-CLI-YAML1 — Export machine-readable command documentation

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3293](#card-3293).

A machine-readable command document lets other tools build references without scraping help. It must stay a projection of the checked schema rather than another command-definition format.

<a id="decision-d-core-cli-menu1"></a>
#### D-CORE-CLI-MENU1 — Choose commands through an existing metadata-driven prompt

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3294](#card-3294).

Interactive tools should not repeat a command tree or invoke arbitrary reflected functions. Selection can reuse the same metadata and parsing, while the application keeps explicit control of business execution.

<a id="decision-d-core-json-select1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSON-SELECT1 — Serialize selected fields without an intermediate tree

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3298](#card-3298).

Selective output aims to remove DTO copying and avoid serializing unused large fields. The claimed performance benefit remains unproven. It must use the existing Encode view and must not sacrifice exact numbers or turn duplicate selectors into duplicate JSON keys. A cannot be ratified before its strict candidate/plain win. No matching pair or win is recorded in gauntlet/measurement-manifest.json. Proof remains on #3298 (core-f078).

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-core-json-exclude1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSON-EXCLUDE1 — Serialize explicit top-level exclusions

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3306](#card-3306).

Exclusion is useful when most fields should be retained. It is not equivalent to a safe published allowlist: a newly added field is included unless existing Encode metadata omits it. A cannot be ratified before its strict candidate/plain win. No matching pair or win is recorded in gauntlet/measurement-manifest.json. Proof remains on #3306 (core-f083).

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-core-eetf1"></a>
#### D-CORE-EETF1 — Convert standalone ETF to a checked JSON view

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3270](#card-3270).

ETF contains more than JSON: atoms, lists, process identities and executable-function descriptions have distinct meanings. A useful JSON view must define losses and reject unsupported identities, not advertise a complete bidirectional codec.

<a id="decision-d-core-jsonb1"></a>
#### D-CORE-JSONB1 — Keep SQLite JSONB at the database boundary

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3268](#card-3268).

SQLite recommends treating JSONB as an opaque database blob. Glaze exposes byte-level encoding, but that does not make an internal format a general interchange promise. The owner should decide this separately from ordinary JSON support.

<a id="decision-d-core-beve1"></a>
#### D-CORE-BEVE1 — Support the exact BEVE Version2 profile

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3269](#card-3269).

BEVE adds compact typed arrays and explicit numeric widths to a JSON-like format. Its version, endianness, extension rules and precision boundaries must be part of the contract rather than a speed slogan.

<a id="decision-d-core-cli-markdown1"></a>
#### D-CORE-CLI-MARKDOWN1 — Generate Markdown command reference from metadata

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3242](#card-3242).

A command reference should share names, defaults and validation with the command itself. Markdown output is a data projection, not a second command definition or a reason to execute a target binary.

<a id="decision-d-core-cli-man1"></a>
#### D-CORE-CLI-MAN1 — Generate man pages from command metadata

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3291](#card-3291).

Manual output has its own escaping, headings and section rules. It should share the same command data as help and other references, not require a second source of option names and defaults.

<a id="decision-d-core-etf-codec1"></a>
#### D-CORE-ETF-CODEC1 — Support typed ETF values without a node runtime

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3270](#card-3270).

ETF preserves atoms, tuples and binary values that a JSON view cannot. Glaze provides typed readers and writers with separate limits and gaps. Keep native values typed and reject unsupported identities.

<a id="ballots-readability"></a>

### readability

<a id="decision-d-read-local1"></a>
#### D-READ-LOCAL1 — Local callable reading view

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3168](#card-3168).

A checked consequence is a fact the checker derived, such as a possible failure or an effect. A runtime observation is what actually happened. Jet records these facts, but separate views make Mina join them. A adds an optional summary; B keeps separate views. Neither changes source syntax or checking.

<a id="decision-d-read-state1"></a>
#### D-READ-STATE1 — Checked local obligations in existing tooling

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3175](#card-3175).

A local obligation is a checked duty at one source point, such as whether a name is being read before a write. A read window is the period in which that read still matters. A exposes the checker’s bounded record; B keeps today’s public facts. Neither turns missing data into permission.

<a id="decision-d-read-logsite1"></a>
#### D-READ-LOGSITE1 — Program source sites in core.log records

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3182](#card-3182).

A source site is the exact program location that made a log call. A message is its text, and an event field is an author-chosen label. Jet records structured fields, but current evidence points to the library emitter rather than the Jet call. A adds compiler-bound site data; B keeps event fields only. Redaction and source policy stay in force.

<a id="ballots-gpu"></a>

### gpu

<a id="decision-d-gpu-packaging1"></a>
#### D-GPU-PACKAGING1 — Where should approved GPU compiler components ship?

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3220](#card-3220).

A provider compiler turns checked Jet code into instructions for one GPU provider. Stock means every Jet installation carries the selected compiler; optional means an application installs it when needed. A keeps Core meaning and acquires a provider compiler explicitly. B bundles the approved compiler closure. Both keep offline identity, explicit acquisition and platform drivers.

<a id="decision-d-gpu-f32-storage1"></a>
#### D-GPU-F32-STORAGE1 — How should a typed F32 list become a Tensor?

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3026](#card-3026).

F32 is a 32-bit floating-point value. A Tensor owns an array of such values. The current ordinary constructor follows Float/F64 source behavior. A preserves the input type through from_list; B adds from_list_f32. Both promise typed F32 storage and readback for the same one-value job, but neither has physical-storage proof yet.

<a id="decision-d-gpu-indexed-resource1"></a>
#### D-GPU-INDEXED-RESOURCE1 — How should checked kernels place several results?

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3026](#card-3026).

A kernel calculation runs at each grid position. `Invocation.linear` numbers runs from zero; `extent` counts them. A writes two output places per run; B returns one value per run. The compiler checks bounds and collisions; launch checks actual shapes. `^` moves the output owner, even if launch returns an error. A's required candidate/plain performance proof is missing.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-gpu-group-scope1"></a>
#### D-GPU-GROUP-SCOPE1 — How should kernels share a temporary array?

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3212](#card-3212).

`grid:[256]` starts 256 runs; `workgroup:[256]` puts them in one cooperating group. `local_linear` numbers members; `workgroup_linear` numbers groups. A needs indexed-resource A's writable output. Its barrier waits for every member before shared reads. Moving `buffer` consumes it even on a returned error; retry needs new output storage. B sums axis zero into shape `[1]`, intending `[5559680]`.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-gpu-subgroup-scope1"></a>
#### D-GPU-SUBGROUP-SCOPE1 — Should kernels name lane-to-lane exchange?

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3213](#card-3213).

A subgroup is a set of runs exchanging values. B numbers its complete 32-member subgroup in input order, so lane zero handles input zero. All members must call the same shuffle together; one member calling alone rejects. A instead reads the neighboring input directly. B's required candidate/plain performance proof is missing. Both programs are NOT RUN.

Gated option(s): B. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-gpu-atomic-scope1"></a>
#### D-GPU-ATOMIC-SCOPE1 — How should checked kernels count shared buckets?

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3214](#card-3214).

A counts each input into a shared cell. B scans inputs once for each bucket. Both intend `[1,3]`. `^` moves owned cells: construction takes `cells`, launch takes `counts`, and readback takes `out`. `output:^counts` supplies the kernel's final parameter. A returned error still consumes the moved owner. A's required candidate/plain performance proof is missing.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-gpu-tile-scope1"></a>
#### D-GPU-TILE-SCOPE1 — Should matrix tiles become public kernel values?

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3215](#card-3215).

A uses existing matrix operations. B's tile is one table value shared by a complete workgroup, not four independent stores. `grid:[4]` and `workgroup:[4]` make one four-member group. Four members need not mean four tile cells. The matrix product is `[[-9,-10],[-13,-14]]`; adding ten and replacing negatives with zero gives `[1,0,0,0]`.

Gated option(s): B. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-gpu-u32-scope1"></a>
#### D-GPU-U32-SCOPE1 — Should authored kernels preserve unsigned integers?

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3216](#card-3216).

U32 stores whole numbers from zero through 4294967295. Wrapping removes complete groups of 4294967296 after each operation. Checked arithmetic instead rejects results outside that range. A admits this integer job on a real GPU; B runs explicitly on the CPU. The frozen receipt covers only CPU work. Neither choice permits floating conversion or altered answers.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-gpu-ranked-scope1"></a>
#### D-GPU-RANKED-SCOPE1 — How should kernels keep image dimensions?

Complete draft; candidate performance gate remains open. Work home: [#3217](#card-3217).

Rank counts dimensions. Shape `[2,3]` means two rows of three columns; this job exchanges rows, not axes. `coord(0)` is the zero-based row and `coord(1)` the column. `linear` numbers all six positions; `%` gives division's remainder. A reads row/column places; B flattens positions and restores shape. A's required candidate/plain performance proof must include non-contiguous layouts; it is missing.

Gated option(s): A. No canonical matched-pair strict win is claimed.

<a id="decision-d-gpu-helper-scope1"></a>
#### D-GPU-HELPER-SCOPE1 — How should a kernel reuse an ordinary helper?

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3218](#card-3218).

A helper is reusable calculation. A’s compiler checks it while checking a kernel that may call it. B checks marked declarations even without a GPU caller. Both perform four rounds of double-plus-one. `inputs:(xs,)` supplies one scalar input per list position; results keep that order. These authored GPU programs are NOT RUN; both still owe the same safe behavior.

<a id="ballots-scripting"></a>

### scripting

<a id="decision-d-script-plugin-close1"></a>
#### D-SCRIPT-PLUGIN-CLOSE1 — Release a plugin before its host stops

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3072](#card-3072).

A plugin is a separately loaded extension. A Close protocol is the existing operation for releasing an owned resource. The host can call checked exports today, but the public inventory does not show release. A releases one finished plugin; B keeps it until host shutdown. Both preserve authority checks, ownership and execution limits.

<a id="decision-d-script-http-decode1"></a>
#### D-SCRIPT-HTTP-DECODE1 — Keep typed JSON errors in HTTP

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3071](#card-3071).

JSON decoding turns response text into a typed value. A field error names the bad field and explains the mismatch. The canonical Jet decoder has that detail, but the HTTP helper currently collapses it into InvalidFraming. A carries the field errors; B makes callers read text and decode separately. Both use the same decoder and transport.

<a id="ballots-bigcode"></a>

### bigcode

<a id="decision-d-big-signature1"></a>
#### D-BIG-SIGNATURE1 — Preview a signature change with explicit caller values

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3187](#card-3187).

A signature is a function’s name, parameters and result. Adding a parameter changes the function and every caller. Jet already knows checked symbol identities and typed edits. A previews those edits after Mira chooses each value; B leaves the multi-file migration manual. Both require correct identities, source locations and document versions.

<a id="decision-d-big-diagorigin1"></a>
#### D-BIG-DIAGORIGIN1 — Locate public compiler diagnostics in their source snapshot

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3202](#card-3202).

A byte span says which bytes were involved, but not which source file or text supplied them. A source snapshot is that exact checked input. Jet’s diagnostic has code, message, cause, fix and span, while imported diagnostics can lose their source identity. A stores optional origin data with the row; B keeps source context beside it. Neither changes program validity or the read-only facade.

<a id="decision-d-big-diagdiff1"></a>
#### D-BIG-DIAGDIFF1 — Compare diagnostics while a change is still incomplete

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3203](#card-3203).

A source snapshot is one checked version of a program. An issue relation says whether a report is new, existing, resolved or unknown between versions. A changed program can have errors before it is complete. A compares reports with explicit validity and coverage; B leaves Mira to compare two reports. Neither adds another checker or guesses from error codes alone.

<a id="decision-d-big-revieworigin1"></a>
#### D-BIG-REVIEWORIGIN1 — Keep a review attached to its exact checked inputs

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3204](#card-3204).

A semantic review is a saved conclusion about two source versions. Provenance means the identities of the inputs and proof records used. Jet already records hashes and authenticated claims, but the captured review object does not state both complete input sets. A stores paired provenance with the review; B keeps it in a sidecar. Neither uploads source or calls an unknown closure complete.

<a id="decision-d-big-cause1"></a>
#### D-BIG-CAUSE1 — Preserve the locations of diagnostic causes

Ready for owner review. Work home: [#3205](#card-3205).

A diagnostic cause explains why a reported error exists. A location identifies the source occurrence that supplies that cause. Jet keeps cause spans internally, but the current canonical report serializes only code strings. A keeps each code with its location; B keeps strings. Both retain registered codes and existing editor-related locations.

```jet
// Same Iterable/Iterator protocol as examples/features/collections/iter_hook.jet.
struct Crate {
    data: [Int]
}

struct BagIter {
    bag: Crate
    idx: Int
}

impl BagIter.Iterator {
    type Item = Int
    fn next(&self) ?Int -> {
        if self.idx >= self.bag.data.len() -> return None
        v :: self.bag.data[self.idx]
        self.idx += 1
        return Val(v)
    }
}

impl Crate.Iterable {
    type Iter = BagIter
    fn iter(^self) BagIter -> { return BagIter{bag: self, idx: 0} }
}

fn run() {
    b :: Crate{data: [10, 20, 30]}
    held :: b.iter()
    print(held.next())
    print(held.next())
}
```

**Original path(s) as provenance:** `examples/features/collections/lazy_iter.jet`.

**Complete literal input:**

```jet
// D-LOOPMAP1=B: in-memory `.map`/`.filter` return lists; `.lazy()` opts into Iter pipelines.
fn run() {
    nums :: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    // Eager adapters — no middle Iter, no to_list.
    ids :: nums.filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).map(n -> n * 10)
    print(ids)
    // Eager map + terminal reducer.
    print(nums.map(n -> n * n).sum())
    // Eager flatten/flat_map return Lists; `.lazy()` keeps the one-pass plane.
    nested :: [[1, 2], [3], [4, 5]]
    print(nested.flatten())
    print(nested.flat_map((xs: [Int]) -> xs))
    print(nested.lazy().flatten().to_list())
    print(nested.lazy().flat_map((xs: [Int]) -> xs).to_list())
    // Opt into one-pass lazy pipelines when chaining many adapters.
    hot :: nums.lazy().filter(n -> n > 2).map(n -> n * 10).to_list()
    print(hot)
    // String split stays lazy (iterator source).
    parts :: "a,b,c".split(",")
    print(parts.to_list())
    loop p in "x y z".split(" ") -> print(p)
}
```

**Complete literal input:**

```jet
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> nums = {5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3};
    auto library = nums;
    // Transcribed algorithm from the 15s frame; whitespace normalized.
    for (int i = 1; i < nums.size(); ++i) {
        int key = nums[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && nums[j] > key) {
            nums[j + 1] = nums[j];
            j--;
        }
        nums[j + 1] = key;
    }
    std::sort(library.begin(), library.end());
    for (int n : nums) std::cout << n << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
    for (int n : library) std::cout << n << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
    return nums == library ? 0 : 1;
}
```

```jet
use core.compute as compute

fn run() {
    plain :: compute.full([1, 1], 2.0) ?? panic("plain")
    if compute.on_device(plain, compute.device_vulkan()) == {
        .Ok(_) -> panic("F64 unexpectedly accepted")
        .Err(_) -> print("vulkan-f64:rejected")
    }
    f32_value :: compute.matmul_f32_tile(plain, plain) ?? panic("f32")
    if compute.on_device(f32_value, compute.device_vulkan()) == {
        .Ok(device_value) -> {
            print("vulkan-placement:{compute.placement(device_value)}")
            doubled :: compute.add(device_value, device_value) ?? panic("add")
            print("vulkan-values:{compute.to_list(doubled)}")
            print("vulkan-result-placement:{compute.placement(doubled)}")
        }
        .Err(_) -> print("vulkan-f32:rejected")
    }
    if compute.on_device(f32_value, compute.device_webgpu()) == {
        .Ok(_) -> print("webgpu:available")
        .Err(_) -> print("webgpu:rejected")
    }
}
```

**Complete literal input:**

```jet
// 67 — scope-exit cleanup via core.mem.scope.guard (D-DEFER1 option B).
// Guard fires on every exit path — normal return, early return, and `?`
// propagation. Multiple guards in the same scope drop LIFO.
use core.mem.scope as scope

#Error
enum Fail {
    Bad
}

fn with_guards(succeed: Bool) Int !Fail -> {
    _g1 :: scope.guard(() -> print("guard 1 runs"))
    _g2 :: scope.guard(() -> print("guard 2 runs"))
    if succeed -> return Ok(42)
    return Err(Fail.Bad)
}

fn question_path() Int !Fail -> {
    _cleanup :: scope.guard(() -> print("cleanup before ?"))
    n :: with_guards(false)
    return Ok(n)
}

fn run() {
    r1 :: with_guards(true) ?? 0
    print(r1)
    r2 :: question_path() ?? -1
    print(r2)
}
```
