## Stencil/Mustache

**Tag source:** `https://github.com/stephenberry/glaze/blob/v8.3.0/docs/stencil-mustache.md`, tag `v8.3.0`, retrieved 2026-09-11.  
**Rendered page:** `https://stephenberry.github.io/glaze/stencil-mustache/`, retrieved 2026-09-11; rendered edit/source link points to `main`.

### Documented purpose and basic API

The tag source opens: “Glaze provides string interpolation for C++ structs through the `stencil` and `mustache` formats. These provide templating mechanisms for formatting structured data into strings, inspired by the Mustache templating language. This enables the generation of dynamic output by combining predefined templates with C++ structs.”

The source's `Basic Usage` example is:

```cpp
struct person
{
   std::string first_name{};
   std::string last_name{};
   uint32_t age{};
   bool hungry{};
   bool employed{};
};

// Basic interpolation
std::string_view layout = R"({{first_name}} {{last_name}} is {{age}} years old)";
person p{"Henry", "Foster", 34};
auto result = glz::stencil(layout, p);
// Result: "Henry Foster is 34 years old"
```

The source note says:

> `result` in these examples is a `std::expected<std::string, glz::error_ctx>`. Like most functions in Glaze (e.g. `glz::write_json`) you can also pass in your own string buffer as the last argument, in which case the return type is `glz::error_ctx`.

### Stencil syntax and exact examples

The source's `Template Syntax Specification` documents:

```text
{{key}} - Replaces with the value of the specified field from the struct
{{{key}}} - Triple braces for unescaped output (mustache format only)
{{#boolean_key}} CONTENT {{/boolean_key}} - Shows CONTENT if the boolean field is true
{{^boolean_key}} CONTENT {{/boolean_key}} - Shows CONTENT if the boolean field is false (inverted section)
{{#container_key}} TEMPLATE {{/container_key}} - Iterates over container elements, applying TEMPLATE to each item
{{^container_key}} CONTENT {{/container_key}} - Shows CONTENT if the container is empty
{{! This is a comment}} - Comments are ignored during template processing
```

Boolean sections:

```cpp
std::string_view layout = R"({{first_name}} {{last_name}} {{#employed}}Status: Employed, Age: {{age}}{{/employed}})";
person p{"Carol", "Davis", 30, true, true};
auto result = glz::stencil(layout, p);
// Result: "Carol Davis Status: Employed, Age: 30"
```

Inverted sections:

```cpp
std::string_view layout = R"({{first_name}} {{last_name}} {{^hungry}}I'm not hungry{{/hungry}})";
person p{"Henry", "Foster", 34, false}; // hungry is false
auto result = glz::stencil(layout, p);
// Result: "Henry Foster I'm not hungry"
```

Container iteration:

```cpp
struct TodoItem {
   std::string text;
   bool completed;
   std::string priority;
   size_t id;
};

struct TodoList {
   std::string title;
   std::vector<TodoItem> items;
   bool has_items;
};

std::string_view layout = R"({{title}}: {{#items}}{{text}} ({{priority}}) {{/items}})";
TodoList list{
   "My Tasks", 
   {{"Buy milk", false, "normal", 1}, {"Call mom", true, "high", 2}}, 
   true
};
auto result = glz::stencil(layout, list);
// Result: "My Tasks: Buy milk (normal) Call mom (high) "
```

Nested sections:

```cpp
std::string_view layout = R"({{#items}}{{text}} {{#completed}}✓{{/completed}}{{^completed}}○{{/completed}} {{/items}})";
TodoList list{"Mixed Tasks", {{"Task 1", false, "high", 1}, {"Task 2", true, "low", 2}}, true};
auto result = glz::stencil(layout, list);
// Result: "Task 1 ○Task 2 ✓"
```

Empty-container handling:

```cpp
std::string_view layout = R"({{title}}{{^items}} - No items found{{/items}})";
TodoList empty_list{"Empty List", {}, false};
auto result = glz::stencil(layout, empty_list);
// Result: "Empty List - No items found"
```

### Mustache and HTML escaping

The source says Glaze provides `glz::mustache` with the same interface as `glz::stencil`, but with HTML escaping behavior:

- **Double braces** `{{key}}` - HTML-escaped output (safe for HTML)
- **Triple braces** `{{{key}}}` - Unescaped output (raw HTML)

Exact HTML examples:

```cpp
struct html_content {
   std::string title;
   std::string raw_html;
};

// Double braces escape HTML
std::string_view layout = R"(<h1>{{title}}</h1>)";
html_content content{"My <Script> Title", ""};
auto result = glz::mustache(layout, content);
// Result: "<h1>My &lt;Script&gt; Title</h1>"

// Triple braces preserve HTML
std::string_view layout2 = R"(<div>{{{raw_html}}}</div>)";
html_content content2{"", "<strong>Bold text</strong>"};
auto result2 = glz::mustache(layout2, content2);
// Result: "<div><strong>Bold text</strong></div>"
```

The source lists these escaped entities:

```text
< → &lt;
> → &gt;
& → &amp;
" → &quot;
' → &#x27;
```

The complex-template source example uses `title`, `description`, `raw_html`, `has_items`, `items`, `css_class`, and `completed`:

```cpp
std::string_view blog_template = R"(
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>{{title}}</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>{{title}}</h1>
    <p>{{description}}</p>
    <div class="content">
        {{{raw_html}}}
    </div>
    {{#has_items}}
    <ul>
        {{#items}}
        <li class="{{css_class}}">{{text}} {{#completed}}✓{{/completed}}</li>
        {{/items}}
    </ul>
    {{/has_items}}
</body>
</html>)";
```

### Errors and constraints

The source states that stencil/mustache functions return `std::expected<std::string, glz::error_ctx>`. Its common errors are:

- `glz::error_code::unknown_key` - Referenced field doesn't exist in struct
- `glz::error_code::unexpected_end` - Mismatched or missing closing tags
- `glz::error_code::syntax_error` - Malformed template syntax

The source's formatting example is:

```cpp
std::string_view layout = R"({{bad_key}} {{last_name}} {{age}})";

person p{"Henry", "Foster", 34};
auto result = glz::stencil(layout, p);
expect(result.error());
auto error_msg = glz::format_error(result, layout);
```

The stated `error_msg` shape is:

```text
1:10: unknown_key
   {{bad_key}} {{last_name}} {{age}}
            ^
```

The page does not publish a numeric template-size, recursion-depth, output-size, allocation, ownership, or async limit. It does state that StencilCount structs must be reflectable or glaze objects, Boolean fields are used for section conditions, and all field names in templates must exist.

### StencilCount

The source names `glz::stencilcount` and requires:

```cpp
#include "glaze/stencil/stencilcount.hpp"
```

Exact example:

```cpp
std::string_view layout = R"(# About
## {{+}} {{first_name}} {{last_name}}
{{++}} {{first_name}} is {{age}} years old.

## {{+}} Hobbies
{{++}} Outdoor
{{+++}} Running
{{+++}} Hiking
)";

person p{"Henry", "Foster", 34};
auto result = glz::stencilcount(layout, p);
// Result:
// # About
// ## 1. Henry Foster
// 1.1 Henry is 34 years old.
// 
// ## 2. Hobbies
// 2.1 Outdoor
// 2.1.1 Running
// 2.1.2 Hiking
```

The source's StencilCount syntax is:

- `{{+}}` - Major section number (1, 2, 3, ...)
- `{{++}}` - Sub-section number (1.1, 1.2, 2.1, ...)
- `{{+++}}` - Sub-sub-section number (1.1.1, 1.1.2, ...)
- And so on for deeper nesting levels

Requirements listed by the source:

- Structs must be reflectable (using Glaze reflection) or be glaze objects
- Boolean fields are used for section conditions
- All field names in templates must exist in the struct

## EETF (Erlang External Term Format)

**Tag source:** `https://github.com/stephenberry/glaze/blob/v8.3.0/docs/EETF/erlang-external-term-format.md`, tag `v8.3.0`, retrieved 2026-09-11.  
**Rendered page:** `https://stephenberry.github.io/glaze/EETF/erlang-external-term-format/`, retrieved 2026-09-11; rendered edit/source link points to `main`.

### Enablement and dependency controls

The tag source states:

> Glaze optionally supports the [Erlang External Term Format](https://www.erlang.org/doc/apps/erts/erl_ext_dist.html), abbreviated as EETF.

The Glaze CMake option is `glaze_EETF_FORMAT`. The source says this option links in the required Erlang libraries:

> In the long term the goal is to remove the requirement on the Erlang libraries, but they are required for now.

If CMake is not used, the source requires:

```cpp
#define GLZ_ENABLE_EETF
```

The `glaze_EETF_FORMAT` option adds the `GLZ_ENABLE_EETF` macro when selected. The page links the unit test source at `https://github.com/stephenberry/glaze/blob/main/tests/eetf_test/eetf_test.cpp`.

### EETF-to-JSON conversion

The exact source example is:

```cpp
std::string json{};
auto ec = glz::eetf_to_json(term, json);
```

`binary_as_base64` is off by default, so an Erlang binary is written as a JSON string. Binaries hold arbitrary bytes, and a control character (0x00–1F) among them has no short JSON escape, so the conversion fails with `error_code::invalid_control_character`.

The source's two option paths are:

```cpp
// binary_as_base64 is a member of eetf_opts, so set it inline.
// Usually the right answer for a binary: no raw bytes end up in a JSON string.
glz::eetf_to_json<glz::eetf::eetf_opts{.binary_as_base64 = true}>(term, json);

// escape_control_characters is inheritable, so add it to a custom opts struct.
// Keeps the bytes as JSON string content, escaped.
struct escaping : glz::eetf::eetf_opts {
   bool escape_control_characters = true;
};
glz::eetf_to_json<escaping{}>(term, json);
```

The source links `String Escaping` at `https://stephenberry.github.io/glaze/binary/#string-escaping`.

Only strings, atoms, and binaries work as object keys, since a JSON key must be a string. The atoms `true` and `false` are written as bare JSON literals, except as a key, where they stay quoted.

### Errors, limits, and unknowns

The page exposes the conversion call and option controls above. It does not give a complete EETF reader/writer symbol inventory, full term-type table, binary-reader/writer signatures, allocation/ownership rules, recursion or input-size limits, async behavior, or a complete malformed-term error table. Those details are explicit page-level unknowns in this capture. No runtime conversion or EETF implementation claim is made.

## Partial Read

**Tag source:** `https://github.com/stephenberry/glaze/blob/v8.3.0/docs/partial-read.md`, tag `v8.3.0`, retrieved 2026-09-11.  
**Rendered page:** `https://stephenberry.github.io/glaze/partial-read/`, retrieved 2026-09-11; rendered edit/source link points to `main`.

The page says that it can be unnecessary to read an entire JSON document when only an initial header or fields are needed. It describes a limited approach with the `partial_read` option and links to compile-time/run-time JMESPath for more advanced partial reading.

### `glz::opts::partial_read`

The source definition is:

> `partial_read` is a compile time flag in `glz::opts` that indicates only existing array and object elements should be read into, and once the memory has been read, parsing returns without iterating through the rest of the document.

The page note is:

> Once any sub-object is read, the parsing will finish. This ensures high performance with short circuiting.

A wrapper by the same name is also documented.

### Exact examples

Read only the first two tuple elements:

```cpp
std::string s = R"(["hello",88,"a string we don't care about"])";
std::tuple<std::string, int> obj{};
expect(!glz::read<glz::opts{.partial_read = true}>(obj, s));
expect(std::get<0>(obj) == "hello");
expect(std::get<1>(obj) == 88);
```

Read only the first two preallocated vector elements:

```cpp
std::string s = R"([1,2,3,4,5])";
std::vector<int> v(2);
expect(!glz::read<glz::opts{.partial_read = true}>(v, s));
expect(v.size() == 2);
expect(v[0] = 1);
expect(v[1] = 2);
```

The tag source itself uses assignment (`=`), not comparison (`==`), in these two `expect` lines; no correction is made here.

Read only the allocated map element:

```cpp
std::string s = R"({"1":1,"2":2,"3":3})";
std::map<std::string, int> obj{{"2", 0}};
expect(!glz::read<glz::opts{.partial_read = true}>(obj, s));
expect(obj.size() == 1);
expect(obj.at("2") = 2);
```

The tag source also uses assignment in `expect(obj.at("2") = 2)`; it is retained exactly.

Read fields present in a struct and short-circuit:

```cpp
struct partial_struct
{
   std::string string{};
   int32_t integer{};
};
```

```cpp
std::string s = R"({"integer":400,"string":"ha!",ignore})";
partial_struct obj{};
expect(!glz::read<glz::opts{.partial_read = true}>(obj, s));
expect(obj.string == "ha!");
expect(obj.integer == 400);
```

### Unit-test source examples and observed documented rails

The tag source defines:

```cpp
struct Header
{
   std::string id{};
   std::string type{};
};

struct HeaderFlipped
{
   std::string type{};
   std::string id{};
};

struct NestedPartialRead
{
   std::string method{};
   Header header{};
   int number{};
};

suite partial_read_tests = [] {
   using namespace ut;
   
   static constexpr glz::opts partial_read{.partial_read = true};
```

The complete source cases cover these behaviors:

```cpp
   "partial read"_test = [] {
      Header h{};
      std::string buf = R"({"id":"51e2affb","type":"message_type","unknown key":"value"})";

      expect(!glz::read<partial_read>(h, buf));
      expect(h.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(h.type == "message_type");
   };

   "partial read 2"_test = [] {
      Header h{};
      // closing curly bracket is missing
      std::string buf = R"({"id":"51e2affb","type":"message_type","unknown key":"value")";

      expect(!glz::read<partial_read>(h, buf));
      expect(h.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(h.type == "message_type");
   };

   "partial read unknown key"_test = [] {
      Header h{};
      std::string buf = R"({"id":"51e2affb","unknown key":"value","type":"message_type"})";

      expect(glz::read<partial_read>(h, buf) == glz::error_code::unknown_key);
      expect(h.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(h.type.empty());
   };

   "partial read unknown key 2"_test = [] {
      Header h{};
      std::string buf = R"({"id":"51e2affb","unknown key":"value","type":"message_type"})";

      expect(!glz::read<glz::opts{.error_on_unknown_keys = false, .partial_read = true}>(h, buf));
      expect(h.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(h.type == "message_type");
   };

   "partial read don't read garbage"_test = [] {
      Header h{};
      std::string buf = R"({"id":"51e2affb","unknown key":"value","type":"message_type"garbage})";

      expect(!glz::read<glz::opts{.error_on_unknown_keys = false, .partial_read = true}>(h, buf));
      expect(h.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(h.type == "message_type");
   };

   "partial read missing key"_test = [] {
      Header h{};
      std::string buf = R"({"id":"51e2affb","unknown key":"value"})";

      expect(glz::read<glz::opts{.error_on_unknown_keys = false, .partial_read = true}>(h, buf) != glz::error_code::missing_key);
      expect(h.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(h.type.empty());
   };

   "partial read missing key 2"_test = [] {
      Header h{};
      std::string buf = R"({"id":"51e2affb","unknown key":"value"})";

      expect(!glz::read<glz::opts{.error_on_unknown_keys = false, .partial_read = true}>(h, buf));
      expect(h.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(h.type.empty());
   };
```

The source also has reversed member order and additional unknown-key cases:

```cpp
   "partial read HeaderFlipped"_test = [] {
      HeaderFlipped h{};
      std::string buf = R"({"id":"51e2affb","type":"message_type","unknown key":"value"})";

      expect(not glz::read<partial_read>(h, buf));
      expect(h.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(h.type == "message_type");
   };

   "partial read HeaderFlipped unknown key"_test = [] {
      HeaderFlipped h{};
      std::string buf = R"({"id":"51e2affb","unknown key":"value","type":"message_type"})";

      expect(glz::read<partial_read>(h, buf) == glz::error_code::unknown_key);
      expect(h.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(h.type.empty());
   };

   "partial read unknown key 2 HeaderFlipped"_test = [] {
      HeaderFlipped h{};
      std::string buf = R"({"id":"51e2affb","unknown key":"value","type":"message_type","another_field":409845})";

      expect(glz::read<glz::opts{.error_on_unknown_keys = false, .partial_read = true}>(h, buf) == glz::error_code::none);
      expect(h.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(h.type == "message_type");
   };
};
```

Nested object cases are:

```cpp
suite nested_partial_read_tests = [] {
   using namespace ut;
   
   static constexpr glz::opts partial_read{.partial_read = true};

   "nested object partial read"_test = [] {
      NestedPartialRead n{};
      std::string buf =
         R"({"method":"m1","header":{"id":"51e2affb","type":"message_type","unknown key":"value"},"number":51})";

      expect(not glz::read<partial_read>(n, buf));
      expect(n.method == "m1");
      expect(n.header.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(n.header.type == "message_type");
      expect(n.number == 0);
   };

   "nested object partial read, don't read garbage"_test = [] {
      NestedPartialRead n{};
      std::string buf =
         R"({"method":"m1","header":{"id":"51e2affb","type":"message_type","unknown key":"value",garbage},"number":51})";

      expect(not glz::read<partial_read>(n, buf));
      expect(n.method == "m1");
      expect(n.header.id == "51e2affb");
      expect(n.header.type == "message_type");
      expect(n.number == 0);
   };
};
```

The source examples therefore expose `glz::error_code::unknown_key`, `glz::error_code::missing_key`, and `glz::error_code::none` in the option combinations shown. No numeric document-size, nesting, allocation, ownership, or async bound is stated by this page. The examples are source evidence, not executed-test claims.

## Partial Write

**Tag source:** `https://github.com/stephenberry/glaze/blob/v8.3.0/docs/partial-write.md`, tag `v8.3.0`, retrieved 2026-09-11.  
**Rendered page:** `https://stephenberry.github.io/glaze/partial-write/`, retrieved 2026-09-11; rendered edit/source link points to `main`.

The page defines three approaches: compile-time partial write with JSON pointers, runtime partial write as a whitelist, and runtime exclude write as a blacklist.

### Compile-time partial write

The exact source example is:

```cpp
struct animals_t
{
   std::string lion = "Lion";
   std::string tiger = "Tiger";
   std::string panda = "Panda";

   struct glaze
   {
      using T = animals_t;
      static constexpr auto value = glz::object(&T::lion, &T::tiger, &T::panda);
   };
};

struct zoo_t
{
   animals_t animals{};
   std::string name{"My Awesome Zoo"};

   struct glaze
   {
      using T = zoo_t;
      static constexpr auto value = glz::object(&T::animals, &T::name);
   };
};

"partial write"_test = [] {
    static constexpr auto partial = glz::json_ptrs("/name", "/animals/tiger");

    zoo_t obj{};
    std::string s{};
    const auto ec = glz::write_json<partial>(obj, s);
    expect(!ec);
    expect(s == R"({"animals":{"tiger":"Tiger"},"name":"My Awesome Zoo"})") << s;
 };
```

This approach supports nested paths, uses `glz::json_ptrs`, and is documented as having zero runtime overhead.

### Runtime whitelist: `glz::write_json_partial`

Basic source example:

```cpp
struct my_struct
{
   int x = 10;
   std::string name = "example";
   double value = 3.14;
   bool active = true;
};

my_struct obj{};
std::string buffer;

// Specify keys at runtime
std::vector<std::string> keys = {"name", "x"};
auto ec = glz::write_json_partial(obj, keys, buffer);
// Result: {"name":"example","x":10}
```

Output key order follows the input key container:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string_view> keys = {"value", "name", "x"};
glz::write_json_partial(obj, keys, buffer);
// Result: {"value":3.14,"name":"example","x":10}
```

The source lists these string-like key containers:

```cpp
// std::vector<std::string>
std::vector<std::string> keys1 = {"x", "name"};

// std::vector<std::string_view>
std::vector<std::string_view> keys2 = {"x", "name"};

// std::array
std::array<std::string_view, 2> keys3 = {"x", "name"};
```

An unknown key returns `error_code::unknown_key`:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> keys = {"x", "nonexistent"};
auto ec = glz::write_json_partial(obj, keys, buffer);
if (ec.ec == glz::error_code::unknown_key) {
    // Handle unknown key error
}
```

An empty key container writes `{}`:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> keys = {};
glz::write_json_partial(obj, keys, buffer);
// Result: {}
```

Duplicate keys are allowed and are emitted repeatedly:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> keys = {"x", "x"};
glz::write_json_partial(obj, keys, buffer);
// Result: {"x":10,"x":10}
```

The page shows `prettify` support:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> keys = {"x", "name"};
glz::write_json_partial<glz::opts{.prettify = true}>(obj, keys, buffer);
// Result:
// {
//    "x": 10,
//    "name": "example"
// }
```

The three documented overload forms are:

```cpp
// 1. Write to resizable buffer (std::string, std::vector<char>)
error_ctx write_json_partial(T&& value, const Keys& keys, Buffer&& buffer);

// 2. Write to raw buffer (char*)
expected<size_t, error_ctx> write_json_partial(T&& value, const Keys& keys, Buffer&& buffer);

// 3. Return a new string
expected<std::string, error_ctx> write_json_partial(T&& value, const Keys& keys);
```

Pure reflection is documented:

```cpp
// No glz::meta needed - pure reflection
struct reflectable_struct
{
   int field1 = 100;
   std::string field2 = "test";
};

reflectable_struct obj{};
std::vector<std::string> keys = {"field2"};
glz::write_json_partial(obj, keys, buffer);
// Result: {"field2":"test"}
```

### Runtime blacklist: `glz::write_json_exclude`

Basic source example:

```cpp
struct my_struct
{
   int x = 10;
   std::string name = "example";
   double value = 3.14;
   bool active = true;
   std::string password = "secret";  // Don't serialize this!
};

my_struct obj{};
std::string buffer;

// Exclude specific keys at runtime
std::vector<std::string> exclude = {"password"};
auto ec = glz::write_json_exclude(obj, exclude, buffer);
// Result: {"x":10,"name":"example","value":3.14,"active":true}
```

Output key order follows struct definition order, not exclude-list order:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> exclude = {"name"};
glz::write_json_exclude(obj, exclude, buffer);
// Result: {"x":10,"value":3.14,"active":true,"password":"secret"}
// Keys appear in struct order: x, value, active, password (name excluded)
```

The source lists these string-like exclude containers:

```cpp
// std::vector<std::string>
std::vector<std::string> exclude1 = {"password", "internal_id"};

// std::vector<std::string_view>
std::vector<std::string_view> exclude2 = {"password", "internal_id"};

// std::array
std::array<std::string_view, 2> exclude3 = {"password", "internal_id"};
```

An unknown exclude key returns `error_code::unknown_key`:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> exclude = {"nonexistent"};
auto ec = glz::write_json_exclude(obj, exclude, buffer);
if (ec.ec == glz::error_code::unknown_key) {
    // Handle unknown key error
}
```

An empty exclude list writes all fields:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> exclude = {};
glz::write_json_exclude(obj, exclude, buffer);
// Result: {"x":10,"name":"example","value":3.14,"active":true,"password":"secret"}
```

Excluding every field writes `{}`:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> exclude = {"x", "name", "value", "active", "password"};
glz::write_json_exclude(obj, exclude, buffer);
// Result: {}
```

Duplicate exclude keys are handled once:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> exclude = {"password", "password"};
glz::write_json_exclude(obj, exclude, buffer);
// Result: {"x":10,"name":"example","value":3.14,"active":true}
```

The page shows `prettify` support:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> exclude = {"password"};
glz::write_json_exclude<glz::opts{.prettify = true}>(obj, exclude, buffer);
// Result:
// {
//    "x": 10,
//    "name": "example",
//    "value": 3.14,
//    "active": true
// }
```

The three documented overload forms are:

```cpp
// 1. Write to resizable buffer (std::string, std::vector<char>)
error_ctx write_json_exclude(T&& value, const Keys& exclude_keys, Buffer&& buffer);

// 2. Write to raw buffer (char*)
expected<size_t, error_ctx> write_json_exclude(T&& value, const Keys& exclude_keys, Buffer&& buffer);

// 3. Return a new string
expected<std::string, error_ctx> write_json_exclude(T&& value, const Keys& exclude_keys);
```

Pure reflection is documented:

```cpp
// No glz::meta needed - pure reflection
struct reflectable_struct
{
   int field1 = 100;
   std::string field2 = "test";
   std::string internal = "hidden";
};

reflectable_struct obj{};
std::vector<std::string> exclude = {"internal"};
glz::write_json_exclude(obj, exclude, buffer);
// Result: {"field1":100,"field2":"test"}
```

### Documented comparison table

| Feature | Compile-Time | Runtime Partial (Whitelist) | Runtime Exclude (Blacklist) |
|---------|--------------|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Function | `write_json<partial>` | `write_json_partial` | `write_json_exclude` |
| Key specification | `constexpr` JSON pointers | Runtime container | Runtime container |
| Nested paths | Supported | Top-level keys only | Top-level keys only |
| Performance | Zero overhead | Hash lookup per key | Hash lookup per exclude key |
| Output order | Specified order | Input container order | Struct definition order |
| Use case | Fixed field sets | Include specific fields | Exclude specific fields |

The source then gives per-approach usage guidance. It is retained here only as official source context, not as a lane recommendation:

```text
Use compile-time partial write when:
- The fields to serialize are known at compile time
- You need nested JSON pointer paths
- Maximum performance is critical

Use runtime partial write (whitelist) when:
- The fields to serialize depend on runtime conditions
- Different message types need different field subsets
- User configuration determines which fields to include
- You want control over the output key order

Use runtime exclude write (blacklist) when:
- You want to serialize most fields but exclude a few
- Excluding sensitive fields (passwords, tokens, internal IDs)
- The set of excluded fields is smaller than the set of included fields
- You want keys in struct definition order
```

The page does not state numeric input/output-size, nesting, allocation, ownership, or async limits beyond the overload and key-container behavior shown above. It names `error_ctx`, `expected<size_t, error_ctx>`, `expected<std::string, error_ctx>`, and `error_code::unknown_key` as the visible return/error surface.

## JSON Include

**Tag source:** `https://github.com/stephenberry/glaze/blob/v8.3.0/docs/json-include.md`, tag `v8.3.0`, retrieved 2026-09-11.  
**Rendered page:** `https://stephenberry.github.io/glaze/json-include/`, retrieved 2026-09-11; rendered edit/source link points to `main`.

### `glz::file_include`

The tag source says:

> Glaze provides a `glz::file_include` type that can be added to your struct (or glz::meta). The key may be anything, in this example we use choose `include` to mimic C++.

```cpp
struct includer_struct {
  glz::file_include include{};
  std::string str = "Hello";
  int i = 55;
};
```

When this object is parsed, when the key `include` is encountered the associated file will be read into the local object.

```cpp
includer_struct obj{};
std::string s = R"({"include": "./obj.json", "i": 100})";
glz::read_json(obj, s);
```

This will read the `./obj.json` file into the `obj` as it is parsed. Since glaze parses in sequence, the order in which includes are listed in the JSON file is the order in which they will be evaluated. The `file_include` will only be read into the local object, so includes can be deeply nested.

> Paths are always relative to the location of the previously loaded file. For nested includes this means the user only needs to consider the relative path to the file in which the include is written.

### Hostname Include

Similar to `glz::file_include`, glaze provides `glz::hostname_include`. This is used for host-specific configuration files.

> You must explicitly include the header file `#include "glaze/file/hostname_include.hpp"`

In use:

```cpp
std::string s = R"({"hostname_include": "../{}_config.json", "i": 100})";
auto ec = glz::read_json(obj, s);
```

Note how the provided path contains `{}`, which will be replaced with the hostname when the file is read. Other than this, the `hostname_include` behaves the same as `file_include`.

### `glz::raw_or_file`

`glz::raw_or_file` is somewhat like a `glz::file_include`, but also handles serialization. The purpose is to allow JSON files to be optionally referred to within higher level configuration files, but once loaded, the files behave as glz::raw_json, where the format does not need to be understood until deserialized.

> Note that his approach only allows a single layer of includes. It does not allow infinitely deep includes like `glz::file_include` and `glz::hostname_include` support.

**How glz::raw_or_file behaves:**  
If the input is a valid file path within a string, the entire file will be read into a std::string within the glz::raw_or_file member. The internal buffer does not escape characters, as it is handled like glz::raw_json.  
If the input is not a valid file path or not a string, the value is simply validated and stored like glz::raw_json  
When serialized, the value is dumped like glz::raw_json, which means it will look like the input file was copied and pasted into the higher level document.

Benefits of this approach include:

- The layout for the file loaded into glz::raw_or_file does not need to be known by the program. As long as it is valid JSON it can be passed along.
- The serialized output after loading the file looks like a combined file, which is easier to read and format than an escaped string version of the file. It is also more efficient because escaping/unescaping doesn't need to be performed, only validation.

### Errors, limits, ownership, and async unknowns

The page does not publish a complete error-code table, path-validation grammar, file-size/recursion/depth limit, allocation or ownership rule, symlink/security rule, or async behavior. Those details are explicit page-level unknowns. No file read or serialization runtime claim was made here.

## CLI Menu

**Tag source:** `https://github.com/stephenberry/glaze/blob/v8.3.0/docs/cli-menu.md`, tag `v8.3.0`, retrieved 2026-09-11.  
**Rendered page:** `https://stephenberry.github.io/glaze/cli-menu/`, retrieved 2026-09-11; rendered edit/source link points to `main`.

### Purpose and clearing the screen

The page states that Glaze generates command-line menus from nested structs. Callable structs combine to form the menu hierarchy, and command names are reflected from function names or supplied via `glz::meta`.

To bring the menu to the forefront, the page instructs: type `cls` or `clear` and press `ENTER`.

### Exact source example

```cpp
struct my_functions
{
   std::function<void()> hello = [] { std::printf("Hello\n"); };
   std::function<void()> world = [] { std::printf("World\n"); };
};

// This glz::meta is optional unless you need to change the function name in the menu
template <>
struct glz::meta<my_functions>
{
   using T = my_functions;
   static constexpr auto value = object("hi", &T::hello, &T::world);
};

struct four_t
{
   four_t(glz::make_reflectable) {} // required for reflection since this struct has no members

   std::pair<std::string, int> operator()() { return {"four", 4}; }
};

struct more_functions
{
   std::function<std::string()> one = [] { return "one"; };
   std::function<int()> two = [] { return 2; };
   std::function<std::string_view()> three = [] { return "three"; };
   four_t four{};
};

struct a_special_function
{
   a_special_function(glz::make_reflectable) {}

   glz::raw_json operator()(const std::tuple<int, bool>& in)
   {
      return std::to_string(std::get<0>(in)) + " | " + std::to_string(std::get<1>(in));
   }
};

struct my_nested_menu
{
   my_functions first_menu{};
   more_functions second_menu{};
   std::function<int(int)> user_number = [](int x) { return x; };
   std::function<std::string(const std::string&)> user_string = [](const auto& str) { return str; };
   a_special_function special{};
};

void nested_menu()
{
   my_nested_menu menu{};
   glz::run_cli_menu(menu); // show the command line interface menu
}
```

The exact top-level printed menu is:

```text
================================
  1   first_menu
  2   second_menu
  3   user_number
  4   user_string
  5   special
  6   Exit Menu
--------------------------------
cmd> 
```

The page contains no API signature table and does not state menu error codes, input/argument limits, allocation/ownership behavior, async behavior, or platform restrictions. Those are explicit page-level unknowns.

## JSONC controls retained from the tag-pinned JSON page

**Tag source:** `https://github.com/stephenberry/glaze/blob/v8.3.0/docs/json.md`, tag `v8.3.0`, retrieved 2026-09-11.  
**Rendered page:** `https://stephenberry.github.io/glaze/json/`, retrieved 2026-09-11; rendered edit/source link points to `main`.

### Exact JSONC body example

Under `Advanced Features > JSON with Comments (JSONC)`, the tag source gives:

```cpp
std::string jsonc_data = R"({
    "name": "John", // Person's name
    /* Multi-line comment
       about age */
    "age": 30
})";

Person person{};
auto ec = glz::read_jsonc(person, jsonc_data);
// Or: glz::read<glz::opts{.comments = true}>(person, jsonc_data);
```

### Conformance and control quote

The tag source states:

> Glaze is RFC 8259 compliant. UTF-8 encoding is validated when reading unless you opt out with `validate_utf8 = false`. Two further checks are off by default for performance:
>
> - `validate_skipped = false`: Faster parsing by not fully validating skipped values (does not affect resulting C++ objects)
> - `validate_trailing_whitespace = false`: Stops parsing after the target object
>
> For strict compliance, it gives:

```cpp
struct strict_opts : glz::opts {
    bool validate_skipped = true;
    bool validate_trailing_whitespace = true;
};

auto ec = glz::read<strict_opts{}>(obj, json_data);
```

The source then states that `glz::validate_json` and `glz::validate_jsonc` enable both checks, so a document passing them is fully RFC 8259 conformant.

The UTF-8 section states that JSONC comments are skipped without validation because comments are not part of RFC 8259 and their bytes never reach the program. The page's visible API/control evidence is therefore `glz::read_jsonc`, `glz::opts{.comments = true}`, `validate_utf8`, `validate_skipped`, `validate_trailing_whitespace`, `glz::validate_json`, and `glz::validate_jsonc`. This capture does not infer additional comment grammar, ownership, allocation, or async semantics.

## Independent normative JMESPath specification (current observed source)

**Canonical URL:** `https://jmespath.org/specification.html`  
**Retrieved:** 2026-09-11  
**Version/tag:** the page does not expose a release tag or version; this is current observed official specification evidence.  
**Boundary:** this is the independent JMESPath language specification. It is not a claim that Glaze implements the complete language. Glaze's own current page says: “Glaze currently has limited support for partial reading with JMESPath. Broader support will be added in the future.” The Glaze page and examples are captured in `data-operations.md`, lines 516–571, with include `glaze/json/jmespath.hpp`, compile-time `glz::read_jmespath<...>`, runtime `glz::read_jmespath`, reusable `glz::jmespath_expression`, and slices. The normative scope below must remain separate from that limited selector subset.

### Evaluation contract and JSON types

The specification's example function is:

```text
search(<jmespath expr>, <JSON document>) -> <return value>
```

Example:

```text
search(foo, {"foo": "bar"}) -> "bar"
```

It states that applying a JMESPath expression to a JSON document always results in valid JSON when there are no evaluation errors: “Structured data in, structured data out.” Apart from JMESPath expression types, the JSON types are number (integers and double-precision floating-point format), string, boolean, array, object, and null. Implementations may map those JSON types to language equivalents.

### Grammar (ABNF excerpt, complete top-level production set)

The specification says the grammar uses ABNF as described by RFC4234. Its top-level grammar is:

```abnf
expression        = sub-expression / index-expression  / comparator-expression
expression        =/ or-expression / identifier
expression        =/ and-expression / not-expression / paren-expression
expression        =/ "*" / multi-select-list / multi-select-hash / literal
expression        =/ function-expression / pipe-expression / raw-string
expression        =/ current-node
sub-expression    = expression "." ( identifier /
                                     multi-select-list /
                                     multi-select-hash /
                                     function-expression /
                                     "*" )
pipe-expression   = expression "|" expression
or-expression     = expression "||" expression
and-expression    = expression "&&" expression
not-expression    = "!" expression
paren-expression  = "(" expression ")"
index-expression  = expression bracket-specifier / bracket-specifier
multi-select-list = "[" ( expression *( "," expression ) ) "]"
multi-select-hash = "{" ( keyval-expr *( "," keyval-expr ) ) "}"
keyval-expr       = identifier ":" expression
bracket-specifier = "[" (number / "*" / slice-expression) "]" / "[]"
bracket-specifier =/ "[?" expression "]"
comparator-expression = expression comparator expression
slice-expression  = [number] ":" [number] [ ":" [number] ]
comparator        = "<" / "<=" / "==" / ">=" / ">" / "!="
function-expression = unquoted-string  (
                        no-args  /
                        one-or-more-args )
no-args             = "(" ")"
one-or-more-args    = "(" ( function-arg *( "," function-arg ) ) ")"
function-arg        = expression / expression-type
current-node        = "@"
expression-type     = "&" expression

raw-string        = "'" *raw-string-char "'"
raw-string-char   = (%x20-26 / %x28-5B / %x5D-10FFFF) / preserved-escape /
                      raw-string-escape
preserved-escape  = escape (%x20-26 / %28-5B / %x5D-10FFFF)
raw-string-escape = escape ("'" / escape)
literal           = "`" json-value "`"
unescaped-literal = %x20-21 /       ; space !
                        %x23-5B /       ; # - [
                        %x5D-5F /       ; ] ^ _
                        %x61-7A /       ; a-z
                        %x7C-10FFFF     ; |}~ ...
escaped-literal   = escaped-char / (escape %x60)
number            = ["-"]1*digit
digit             = %x30-39
identifier        = unquoted-string / quoted-string
unquoted-string   = (%x41-5A / %x61-7A / %x5F) *(  ; A-Za-z_
                        %x30-39  /  ; 0-9
                        %x41-5A /  ; A-Z
                        %x5F    /  ; _
                        %x61-7A)   ; a-z
quoted-string     = quote 1*(unescaped-char / escaped-char) quote
unescaped-char    = %x20-21 / %x23-5B / %x5D-10FFFF
escape            = %x5C   ; Back slash: \
quote             = %x22   ; Double quote: '"'
escaped-char      = escape (
                        %x22 /          ; "    quotation mark  U+0022
                        %x5C /          ; \    reverse solidus U+005C
                        %x2F /          ; /    solidus U+002F
                        %x62 /          ; b    backspace U+0008
                        %x66 /          ; f    form feed U+000C
                        %x6E /          ; n    line feed U+000A
                        %x72 /          ; r    carriage return U+000D
                        %x74 /          ; t    tab U+0009
                        %x75 4HEXDIG )  ; uXXXX U+XXXX

json-value = false / null / true / json-object / json-array /
             json-number / json-quoted-string
false = %x66.61.6c.73.65   ; false
null  = %x6e.75.6c.6c      ; null
true  = %x74.72.75.65      ; true
json-quoted-string = %x22 1*(unescaped-literal / escaped-literal) %x22
begin-array     = ws %x5B ws  ; [ left square bracket
begin-object    = ws %x7B ws  ; { left curly bracket
end-array       = ws %x5D ws  ; ] right square bracket
end-object      = ws %x7D ws  ; } right curly bracket
name-separator  = ws %x3A ws  ; : colon
value-separator = ws %x2C ws  ; , comma
ws              = *(%x20 /              ; Space
                    %x09 /              ; Horizontal tab
                    %x0A /              ; Line feed or New line
                    %x0D                ; Carriage return
                   )
json-object = begin-object [ member *( value-separator member ) ] end-object
member = quoted-string name-separator json-value
json-array = begin-array [ json-value *( value-separator json-value ) ] end-array
json-number = [ minus ] int [ frac ] [ exp ]
decimal-point = %x2E       ; .
digit1-9 = %x31-39         ; 1-9
e = %x65 / %x45            ; e E
exp = e [ minus / plus ] 1*DIGIT
frac = decimal-point 1*DIGIT
int = zero / ( digit1-9 *DIGIT )
minus = %x2D               ; -
plus = %x2B                ; +
zero = %x30                ; 0
```

The listed binding precedence is weakest to tightest: pipe `|`, or `||`, and `&&`, unary not `!`, and rbracket `]`.

### Identifiers, indexing, slices, and projections

Identifiers are `unquoted-string` or `quoted-string`. An unquoted identifier must start with `A-Za-z_`; identifiers with other starting characters must be quoted. If an identifier does not exist in the JSON document, its value is `null`.

Exact identifier examples from the specification include:

```text
search(foo, {"foo": "value"}) -> "value"
search(bar, {"foo": "value"}) -> null
search(foo, {"foo": [0, 1, 2]}) -> [0, 1, 2]
search("with space", {"with space": "value"}) -> "value"
search("special chars: !@#", {"special chars: !@#": "value"}) -> "value"
search("quote\"char", {"quote\"char": "value"}) -> "value"
search("\u2713", {"\u2713": "value"}) -> "value"
```

Indexing is zero-based. Negative indices are relative to the end, using `length of array + negative-index`; an out-of-range index returns `null`.

Slices have the form `[start:stop:step]`, with optional components and Python-like semantics. The specification requires:

- Negative start/stop positions are calculated from array length.
- Omitted start defaults to `0` for positive step or the array end for negative step.
- Omitted stop defaults to array length for positive step or `0` for negative step.
- Omitted step defaults to `1`.
- A zero step MUST raise `invalid-value`.
- Slicing a non-array returns `null`.
- A slice of an array yielding no results MUST return an empty array.

Examples:

```text
search([0:4:1], [0, 1, 2, 3]) -> [0, 1, 2, 3]
search([0:4], [0, 1, 2, 3]) -> [0, 1, 2, 3]
search([0:3], [0, 1, 2, 3]) -> [0, 1, 2]
search([:2], [0, 1, 2, 3]) -> [0, 1]
search([::2], [0, 1, 2, 3]) -> [0, 2]
search([::-1], [0, 1, 2, 3]) -> [3, 2, 1, 0]
search([-2:], [0, 1, 2, 3]) -> [2, 3]
```

The flatten operator `[]` merges sublists in the current result into a single list, then projects subsequent expressions over that flattened list. Wildcards `[*]` apply to arrays and `*` to objects; a wildcard on the wrong JSON type returns `null`, and a projection that yields `null` omits that result. Object wildcard order is unspecified because JSON objects are unordered.

### Operators and selections

The specification defines:

- `||`: return the left value if truth-like, otherwise the right; false-like values include empty list, empty object, empty string, false, and null; if both are false-like, return null.
- `&&`: return the right value for a truth-like left value, otherwise the left value.
- `!`: negate truth-like/false-like values.
- Multi-select list `[expr-1,expr-2,...]`: evaluate each expression and return a list with one result per expression, including null results.
- Multi-select hash `{key: expression,...}`: evaluate each expression and create an object with those keys.
- Literal expressions use backticks around JSON values; the backtick itself must be escaped inside the JSON value.
- Raw string literals use single quotes and do not expand Unicode, newline, tab, or other JSON escape sequences.
- Filter expressions `[? expression]` are defined only for arrays; a non-array input returns `null`. Equality is exact for strings/numbers/booleans/null, arrays compare ordered elements, and objects compare key/value sets. Ordering operators are only valid for numbers; applying them to other types yields `null` and excludes the item.

### Function/type system

Function grammar:

```abnf
function-expression = unquoted-string  (
                        no-args  /
                        one-or-more-args )
no-args             = "(" ")"
one-or-more-args    = "(" ( function-arg *( "," function-arg ) ) ")"
function-arg        = expression / current-node / expression-type
current-node        = "@"
expression-type     = "&" expression
```

The JSON data types are number, string, boolean, array, object, and null. The additional JMESPath function type is `expression`, denoted by `&expression`. Function arguments are evaluated in applicative order before the function call. Unknown functions MUST be indicated as `unknown-function`; wrong fixed/variadic arity MUST be indicated as `invalid-arity`; violated argument types MUST be indicated as `invalid-type`. No implicit type conversion occurs; explicit `to_string` and `to_number` are provided.

The function signature notation is:

```text
return_type function_name(type $argname)
return_type function_name2(type1|type2 $argname)
```

`array[type]` constrains array element type, `any` means any JSON type, and `expression->type` constrains the resolved type of a deferred expression. String functions operate on Unicode code points and do not account for normalization.

### Complete built-in function inventory and signatures

The specification's built-in inventory and signatures are:

```text
number abs(number $value)
number avg(array[number] $elements)
boolean contains(array|string $subject, any $search)
number ceil(number $value)
boolean ends_with(string $subject, string $prefix)
number floor(number $value)
string join(string $glue, array[string] $stringsarray)
array keys(object $obj)
number length(string|array|object $subject)
array[any] map(expression->any->any expr, array[any] elements)
number max(array[number]|array[string] $collection)
max_by(array elements, expression->number|expression->string expr)
object merge([object *argument, [, object $...]])
number min(array[number]|array[string] $collection)
min_by(array elements, expression->number|expression->string expr)
any not_null([any $argument [, any $...]])
array reverse(string|array $argument)
array sort(array[number]|array[string] $list)
sort_by(array elements, expression->number|expression->string expr)
boolean starts_with(string $subject, string $prefix)
number sum(array[number] $collection)
array to_array(any $arg)
string to_string(any $arg)
number to_number(any $arg)
string type(array|object|string|number|boolean|null $subject)
array values(object $obj)
```

The source's visible behavior/edge examples include:

```text
abs(1) -> 1
abs(-1) -> 1
abs('abc') -> <error: invalid-type>

avg([10, 15, 20]) -> 15
avg([]) -> null

contains('foobar', 'foo') -> true
contains('foobar', 'not') -> false
contains(["a", "b"], 'a') -> true

join(', ', ["a", "b"]) -> "a, b"
join(', ', ["a", false, "b"]) -> <error: invalid-type>

length('abc') -> 3
length([]) -> 0
length({}) -> 0

max([10, 15]) -> 15
max(["a", "b"]) -> "b"
min([10, 15]) -> 10
sum([10, 15]) -> 25
sum([]) -> 0

reverse([0, 1, 2, 3, 4]) -> [4, 3, 2, 1, 0]
to_array(`0`) -> [0]
to_array(`true`) -> [true]
to_string(`2`) -> "2"
type(@) -> one of "number", "string", "boolean", "array", "object", or "null"
```

Additional function semantics recorded by the page are: `avg`, `max`, and `min` return null for empty arrays; `map` retains a result for every input element even when the result is null; `sort` accepts homogeneous strings or numbers and sorts strings by code points without locale; `sort_by`, `max_by`, and `min_by` require expression results of number or string; `not_null` returns the first non-null argument or null; `to_number` parses strings conforming to `json-number`, returns numbers unchanged, and returns null for arrays, objects, booleans, or null; `keys` and `values` have unspecified object order; and `type` returns the six JSON type names.

### Errors and implementation boundary

The specification defines these errors:

- `invalid-type`: an invalid type is encountered during evaluation.
- `invalid-value`: an invalid value is encountered during evaluation.
- `unknown-function`: an unknown function is encountered.
- `invalid-arity`: a function receives an invalid number of arguments.

It states that error timing is implementation-specific, but implementations should indicate the specific error to the caller. Floating-number support in `to_number` is also implementation-specific, with support for at least IEEE 754-2008 binary64 recommended. The specification does not define a computational complexity, step-count, timeout, memory, allocation, recursion-depth, document-size, or other resource-cost bound. This is an explicit cost-boundary gap in this source, not a claim that implementations have no limits.

### Pipe expressions

The grammar is:

```abnf
pipe-expression  = expression "|" expression
```

A pipe combines two expressions. Any expression can be on its right-hand side, and a pipe stops projections on the left from propagating to the right. The source examples are:

```text
search(foo | bar, {"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}) -> "baz"
search(foo[*].bar | [0], {
    "foo": [{"bar": ["first1", "second1"]},
            {"bar": ["first2", "second2"]}]}) -> ["first1", "second1"]
search(foo | [0], {"foo": [0, 1, 2]}) -> [0]
```

## `configparser` — INI configuration parser

### Pinned source and capability identity

Canonical page: https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.2/Doc/library/configparser.rst

Locator: page title/module declaration, lines 1-20 in the pinned raw page.

Exact page header and capability statement:

```rst
:mod:`!configparser` --- Configuration file parser
==================================================

.. module:: configparser
   :synopsis: Configuration file parser.

**Source code:** :source:`Lib/configparser.py`

This module provides the :class:`ConfigParser` class which implements a basic
configuration language which provides a structure similar to what's found in
Microsoft Windows INI files.  You can use this to write Python programs which
can be customized by end users easily.
```

The page states that the module does not interpret or write Windows Registry extended-INI value-type prefixes. It points to `tomllib`, `shlex`, and `json` as related documented formats/tools; those are references only and are not part of this capture's API inventory.

### Public constructor, defaults, and parser configuration

Locator: `ConfigParser Objects`, page lines 939-1051.

Exact constructor declaration:

```rst
.. class:: ConfigParser(defaults=None, dict_type=dict, allow_no_value=False, *, \
                        delimiters=('=', ':'), comment_prefixes=('#', ';'), \
                        inline_comment_prefixes=None, strict=True, \
                        empty_lines_in_values=True, \
                        default_section=configparser.DEFAULTSECT, \
                        interpolation=BasicInterpolation(), converters={}, \
                        allow_unnamed_section=False)
```

The page documents these constructor semantics:

- `defaults=None` initializes intrinsic defaults.
- `dict_type=dict` creates section, option, and default dictionaries and controls insertion order/write appearance.
- `delimiters=('=', ':')` separates keys and values; the first occurrence on a line is the delimiter.
- `comment_prefixes=('#', ';')` marks comments on otherwise empty lines; `inline_comment_prefixes=None` disables inline comments by default.
- `strict=True` rejects duplicate sections/options from one source (`read_file`, `read_string`, or `read_dict`) with `DuplicateSectionError` or `DuplicateOptionError`.
- `empty_lines_in_values=True` keeps internal empty lines in indented multiline values; `False` ends an option at an empty line.
- `allow_no_value=False`; when `True`, valueless options are accepted as `None` and serialize without a trailing delimiter.
- `default_section=configparser.DEFAULTSECT` (normally `"DEFAULT"`) names the special defaults/interpolation section and can be changed at runtime for later writes; already parsed data is not re-evaluated.
- `interpolation=BasicInterpolation()` is the default. `None` disables interpolation; `ExtendedInterpolation()` enables `${section:option}` references.
- `converters={}` adds named conversion callables and corresponding `get*` methods on the parser and section proxies.
- `allow_unnamed_section=False`; when `True`, the first section header may be omitted. The option and `MultilineContinuationError` behavior are documented as Python 3.13 changes.

The page states that reading multiple configurations gives later files higher priority for conflicting keys while retaining prior keys. It also states that mapping access returns a section proxy: values are taken from the original parser on demand rather than copied, and mutations through the proxy mutate the original parser.

### Public parser operations and exact documented behavior

Locator: `ConfigParser` method declarations, page lines 1052-1265.

```rst
.. method:: defaults()
.. method:: sections()
.. method:: add_section(section)
.. method:: has_section(section)
.. method:: options(section)
.. method:: has_option(section, option)
.. method:: read(filenames, encoding=None)
.. method:: read_file(f, source=None)
.. method:: read_string(string, source='<string>')
.. method:: read_dict(dictionary, source='<dict>')
.. method:: get(section, option, *, raw=False, vars=None[, fallback])
.. method:: getint(section, option, *, raw=False, vars=None[, fallback])
.. method:: getfloat(section, option, *, raw=False, vars=None[, fallback])
.. method:: getboolean(section, option, *, raw=False, vars=None[, fallback])
.. method:: items(raw=False, vars=None)
            items(section, raw=False, vars=None)
.. method:: set(section, option, value)
.. method:: write(fileobject, space_around_delimiters=True)
.. method:: remove_option(section, option)
.. method:: remove_section(section)
.. method:: optionxform(option)
```

Exact documented operation facts:

- `defaults()` returns a dictionary of instance-wide defaults.
- `sections()` returns available sections and excludes the default section.
- `add_section(section)` adds a named section; an existing section raises `DuplicateSectionError`, the default section raises `ValueError`, and a non-string name raises `TypeError`.
- `has_section(section)` reports whether a named non-default section exists.
- `options(section)` returns option names available in a section.
- `has_option(section, option)` returns `True` only when the section/option is present; `None` or an empty section name means `DEFAULT`.
- `read(filenames, encoding=None)` attempts an iterable of filenames and returns the successfully parsed filenames. A string, `bytes`, or path-like object is treated as one filename. An unopenable optional file is ignored. If no named file exists, the parser remains empty; the page's example uses `read_file` for required defaults before `read` for optional files.
- `read_file(f, source=None)` parses an iterable yielding Unicode strings. The source label defaults to `f.name` when present, otherwise `'<???>'`.
- `read_string(string, source='<string>')` parses a string and accepts an optional context/source label.
- `read_dict(dictionary, source='<dict>')` loads an object with dict-like `items()`. Section/key order is preserved when the supplied dictionary preserves it; values are automatically converted to strings; the method can copy state between parsers.
- `get(section, option, *, raw=False, vars=None[, fallback])` looks up `vars`, then the named section, then `DEFAULTSECT`. A supplied fallback is used only when no key is found. Interpolation expands unless `raw=True`; interpolation keys use the same lookup order. `raw`, `vars`, and `fallback` are keyword-only.
- `getint`, `getfloat`, and `getboolean` perform the corresponding conversion while accepting the `get` lookup/fallback controls. `getboolean` accepts case-insensitive `'1'`, `'yes'`, `'true'`, `'on'` for `True`, and `'0'`, `'no'`, `'false'`, `'off'` for `False`; other values raise `ValueError`.
- `items()` without a section returns section-name/section-proxy pairs including `DEFAULTSECT`; with a section it returns option/value pairs using the `get` controls. Values supplied in `vars` no longer appear in the result as of Python 3.8.
- `set(section, option, value)` sets a string option/value in an existing section; a missing section raises `NoSectionError`, and non-string option/value raises `TypeError`.
- `write(fileobject, space_around_delimiters=True)` writes a parseable text representation. With the default, delimiters are surrounded by spaces. Original comments are not preserved.
- `remove_option(section, option)` raises `NoSectionError` for a missing section; returns `True` when an option was removed and `False` otherwise.
- `remove_section(section)` returns `True` when the section existed and `False` otherwise.
- `optionxform(option)` canonicalizes names for read/get/set. Its default returns lowercase; it may be overridden or assigned, for example to `str` for case-sensitive names. Whitespace is stripped before transformation, and the page notes the transform should be idempotent.

The mapping protocol additionally documents case-insensitive option membership by default, default-section values visible through every section, inability to delete `DEFAULTSECT` (`ValueError`), and section-proxy mutation of parser-owned state. The mapping implementation adheres to `collections.abc.MutableMapping`.

### Interpolation, constants, and compatibility class

The page documents these public interpolation classes:

- `BasicInterpolation()`: default handler; `%(option)s` references values in the same section or defaults, and `%%` escapes `%`; interpolation is performed on demand.
- `ExtendedInterpolation()`: `${section:option}` references can span levels and can omit the section name for the current section/defaults; `$$` escapes `$`.

Public data declarations and limits:

```rst
.. data:: UNNAMED_SECTION

   A special object representing a section name used to reference the unnamed section.

.. data:: MAX_INTERPOLATION_DEPTH

   The maximum depth for recursive interpolation for ConfigParser.get when raw
   is false. This is relevant only when the default interpolation is used.
```

The page names `RawConfigParser` with the same constructor shape. It is the legacy variant: interpolation is disabled by default, and its unsafe `add_section`/`set` methods permit non-string internal values; writing or non-raw access can then fail. The page records `ConfigParser(interpolation=None)` as the non-interpolating alternative.

### Exceptions and documented error surface

Locator: `Exceptions`, page lines 1339-1411.

```rst
Error
NoSectionError
DuplicateSectionError
DuplicateOptionError
NoOptionError
InterpolationError
InterpolationDepthError
InterpolationMissingOptionError
InterpolationSyntaxError
MissingSectionHeaderError
ParsingError
MultilineContinuationError
```

Exact documented roles: `Error` is the base for module exceptions; `NoSectionError` marks an absent section; `DuplicateSectionError` marks duplicate section creation/input; `DuplicateOptionError` marks duplicate options in strict input; `NoOptionError` marks an absent option; `InterpolationError` is the interpolation base with depth, missing-option, and syntax subclasses; `MissingSectionHeaderError` marks input without section headers; `ParsingError` marks parse failures; and Python 3.13 `MultilineContinuationError` marks an indented continuation after a key without a value. The page also records `ValueError`, `TypeError`, and `NoSectionError` at the individual operations above.

### Official usage evidence

Locator: `Quick Start`, page lines 63-216.

```python
import configparser
config = configparser.ConfigParser()
config['DEFAULT'] = {'ServerAliveInterval': '45',
                     'Compression': 'yes',
                     'CompressionLevel': '9'}
config['forge.example'] = {}
config['forge.example']['User'] = 'hg'
config['topsecret.server.example'] = {}
topsecret = config['topsecret.server.example']
topsecret['Port'] = '50022'
topsecret['ForwardX11'] = 'no'
config['DEFAULT']['ForwardX11'] = 'yes'
with open('example.ini', 'w') as configfile:
  config.write(configfile)

config = configparser.ConfigParser()
config.read('example.ini')
config['forge.example']['User']
# 'hg'
topsecret['ForwardX11']
# 'no'
```

The same page's typed-getter evidence uses `topsecret.getboolean('ForwardX11')`, `config.getboolean('forge.example', 'Compression')`, `getint`, and `getfloat`; the documented boolean vocabulary is recorded above.

- The documented input is an INI-like text format and text file/string/dictionary sources; the page explicitly distinguishes this from Windows Registry extended-INI value prefixes.
- No asynchronous constructor, read/write, interpolation, or mapping operation is listed on this page.
- Section proxies are views into parser-owned state, not copied dictionaries. The page does not state a general allocation cost.
- `MAX_INTERPOLATION_DEPTH` is named as a limit, but the numeric value is not given in the captured page section; no number is inferred.
- The page's `read` behavior intentionally ignores unopenable optional files, while `read_file` is shown for required input; this is a documented distinction, not an execution result.

## `plistlib` — XML/binary property-list serialization

### Pinned source and supported value domain

Canonical page: https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.2/Doc/library/plistlib.rst

Locator: module header and overview, pinned raw page lines 8-57.

Exact page identity and capability statement:

```rst
:mod:`!plistlib` --- Generate and parse Apple ``.plist`` files
==============================================================

.. module:: plistlib
   :synopsis: Generate and parse Apple plist files.

**Source code:** :source:`Lib/plistlib.py`

This module provides an interface for reading and writing the "property list"
files used by Apple, primarily on macOS and iOS. This module supports both binary
and XML plist files.

The property list (``.plist``) file format is a simple serialization supporting
basic object types, like dictionaries, lists, numbers and strings. Usually the
top level object is a dictionary.

To write out and to parse a plist file, use the :func:`dump` and
:func:`load` functions.

To work with plist data in bytes or string objects, use :func:`dumps`
and :func:`loads`.
```

Documented supported values are strings, integers, floats, booleans, tuples, lists, dictionaries with string keys, `bytes`, `bytearray`, and `datetime.datetime`. Binary-format UID tokens are supported through `UID`.

### Public functions, defaults, errors, and limits

Locator: function declarations and descriptions, pinned raw page lines 59-145.

Exact declarations:

```rst
.. function:: load(fp, *, fmt=None, dict_type=dict, aware_datetime=False)
.. function:: loads(data, *, fmt=None, dict_type=dict, aware_datetime=False)
.. function:: dump(value, fp, *, fmt=FMT_XML, sort_keys=True, skipkeys=False, aware_datetime=False)
.. function:: dumps(value, *, fmt=FMT_XML, sort_keys=True, skipkeys=False, aware_datetime=False)
```

Exact documented behavior:

- `load` reads a readable binary file object and returns the unpacked root object, usually a dictionary. `fmt=None` autodetects; `FMT_XML` and `FMT_BINARY` select XML or binary. `dict_type` controls dictionaries produced while reading. `aware_datetime=True` creates timezone-aware datetimes with `datetime.UTC`. XML parsing uses Expat; unknown XML elements are ignored by the plist parser. Ill-formed XML may raise Expat-documented exceptions; malformed binary input raises `InvalidFileException`.
- `loads` accepts bytes, and Python 3.13 additionally accepts a string when `fmt=FMT_XML`; it has the same format/dictionary/aware-datetime controls as `load`.
- `dump` writes a value to a writable binary file object. `fmt=FMT_XML` is the default; `FMT_BINARY` selects binary output. `sort_keys=True` sorts dictionary keys (the default); `False` preserves iteration order. `skipkeys=False` (the default) raises `TypeError` for non-string dictionary keys; `True` skips such keys. `aware_datetime=True` converts aware datetimes to UTC before writing. Unsupported values or containers raise `TypeError`; binary integers that cannot be represented raise `OverflowError`.
- `dumps` returns plist-formatted bytes and has the same format/sorting/key-skipping/aware-datetime controls as `dump`.

Public constants:

```rst
.. data:: FMT_XML
   The XML format for plist files.

.. data:: FMT_BINARY
   The binary format for plist files
```

Public class and exact limit:

```rst
.. class:: UID(data)

   Wraps an :class:`int`.  This is used when reading or writing NSKeyedArchiver
   encoded data, which contains UID.

   It has one attribute, :attr:`data`, which can be used to retrieve the int value
   of the UID.  :attr:`data` must be in the range ``0 <= data < 2**64``.
```

The page records the old API as removed in Python 3.9, binary plist support as added in 3.4, UID token support as added in 3.8, and the `aware_datetime` keyword as added in 3.13.

### Official usage examples

Locator: `Examples`, pinned raw page lines 173-209.

Generating a plist:

```python
import datetime
import plistlib

pl = dict(
    aString = "Doodah",
    aList = ["A", "B", 12, 32.1, [1, 2, 3]],
    aFloat = 0.1,
    anInt = 728,
    aDict = dict(
        anotherString = "<hello & hi there!>",
        aThirdString = "M\xe4ssig, Ma\xdf",
        aTrueValue = True,
        aFalseValue = False,
    ),
    someData = b"<binary gunk>",
    someMoreData = b"<lots of binary gunk>" * 10,
    aDate = datetime.datetime.now()
)
print(plistlib.dumps(pl).decode())
```

Parsing a plist:

```python
import plistlib

plist = b"""<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>foo</key>
    <string>bar</string>
</dict>
</plist>"""
pl = plistlib.loads(plist)
print(pl["foo"])
```

### Platform, async, ownership, and capture limits

- The page names Apple macOS/iOS as the primary property-list users, and documents XML and binary formats. It does not claim that the API is limited to those operating systems.
- `load`/`dump` use caller-supplied readable/writable binary file objects; `loads`/`dumps` use bytes/string values and return in-memory values/bytes. No separate ownership-transfer or disposal protocol is documented on this page.
- No asynchronous operation is listed.
- The explicit numeric limit captured is `UID.data` in `[0, 2**64)`. The page gives no general plist size/depth/allocation limit; no such limit is inferred.

## `gettext` — GNU and class-based translation services

### Pinned source and API families

Canonical page: https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.2/Doc/library/gettext.rst

Locator: module header and overview, pinned raw page lines 8-40.

Exact page identity and capability statement:

```rst
:mod:`!gettext` --- Multilingual internationalization services
==============================================================

.. module:: gettext
   :synopsis: Multilingual internationalization services.

**Source code:** :source:`Lib/gettext.py`

The :mod:`gettext` module provides internationalization (I18N) and localization
(L10N) services for your Python modules and applications. It supports both the
GNU :program:`gettext` message catalog API and a higher level, class-based API.
```

The page distinguishes the GNU API's process-global translation state from the class-based API, which supports modules or applications that switch languages without changing global state.

### GNU API: exact functions and lookup behavior

Locator: `GNU gettext API`, pinned raw page lines 31-109.

Exact public declarations:

```rst
.. function:: bindtextdomain(domain, localedir=None)
.. function:: textdomain(domain=None)
.. function:: gettext(message)
.. function:: dgettext(domain, message)
.. function:: ngettext(singular, plural, n)
.. function:: dngettext(domain, singular, plural, n)
.. function:: pgettext(context, message)
.. function:: dpgettext(domain, context, message)
.. function:: npgettext(context, singular, plural, n)
.. function:: dnpgettext(domain, context, singular, plural, n)
```

Exact documented behavior:

- `bindtextdomain(domain, localedir=None)` binds a domain to a locale directory. On Unix, the lookup path is `{localedir}/{language}/LC_MESSAGES/{domain}.mo`; language is searched in `LANGUAGE`, `LC_ALL`, `LC_MESSAGES`, then `LANG`. With omitted/`None` `localedir`, the current binding is returned.
- `textdomain(domain=None)` queries the current global domain when `None`, or sets and returns a new global domain.
- `gettext(message)` returns the localized message using current global domain/language/locale directory and is commonly aliased to `_`.
- `dgettext(domain, message)` performs the lookup in an explicit domain.
- `ngettext(singular, plural, n)` uses the catalog plural formula when translated; if no translation exists, it returns `singular` for `n == 1` and `plural` otherwise. The formula is a C or Python expression from the catalog header and can select more than two forms.
- `dngettext(domain, singular, plural, n)` is the domain-explicit plural variant.
- The `pgettext`/`dpgettext`/`npgettext`/`dnpgettext` family restricts lookup to a message context and was added in Python 3.8.
- GNU `dcgettext` is explicitly documented as unimplemented.

Exact global-API usage example:

```python
import gettext
gettext.bindtextdomain('myapplication', '/path/to/my/language/directory')
gettext.textdomain('myapplication')
_ = gettext.gettext
# ...
print(_('This is a translatable string.'))
```

### Class-based API: search, translation construction, installation

Locator: `find`, `translation`, and `install`, pinned raw page lines 111-190.

Exact public declarations:

```rst
.. function:: find(domain, localedir=None, languages=None, all=False)
.. function:: translation(domain, localedir=None, languages=None, class_=None, fallback=False)
.. function:: install(domain, localedir=None, *, names=None)
```

Exact documented behavior:

- `find` implements the standard `.mo` search algorithm. If `localedir` is omitted, the system locale directory is used. If `languages` is omitted, the first non-empty value among `LANGUAGE`, `LC_ALL`, `LC_MESSAGES`, and `LANG` supplies a colon-separated language list. Languages are expanded/normalized and searched as `{localedir}/{language}/LC_MESSAGES/{domain}.mo`. It returns the first existing path, `None` if none exists, or all paths in search order when `all=True`.
- `translation` passes the domain/locale/languages to `find`. It caches instances by identical `.mo` filenames. `class_` selects the class (default `GNUTranslations`) and its constructor must accept one file-object argument. For multiple files, later files are fallbacks for earlier files; `copy.copy` clones each cached object while sharing actual instance data with the cache. If no `.mo` file exists, default `fallback=False` raises `OSError`; `fallback=True` returns `NullTranslations`.
- `install(domain, localedir=None, *, names=None)` installs `_` in Python's builtins using `translation`. The optional `names` sequence may additionally install `gettext`, `ngettext`, `pgettext`, or `npgettext`; `names` became keyword-only in Python 3.11.

### `NullTranslations` and `GNUTranslations` classes

Locator: class sections, pinned raw page lines 191-362.

Exact base constructor and method declarations:

```rst
.. class:: NullTranslations(fp=None)

   .. method:: _parse(fp)
   .. method:: add_fallback(fallback)
   .. method:: gettext(message)
   .. method:: ngettext(singular, plural, n)
   .. method:: pgettext(context, message)
   .. method:: npgettext(context, singular, plural, n)
   .. method:: info()
   .. method:: charset()
   .. method:: install(names=None)
```

`NullTranslations(fp=None)` ignores the optional file object in the base class, initializes protected `_info`, `_charset`, and `_fallback` state, and calls `_parse(fp)` when `fp` is not `None`. `_parse` is a no-op base hook for custom catalog formats. `add_fallback` installs a fallback object. Without a fallback, base `gettext` returns the message; base `ngettext` returns singular only for `n == 1` and plural otherwise. The context methods forward to fallback when present. `info()` returns catalog metadata; `charset()` returns the catalog encoding. `install(names=None)` installs gettext callables into builtins; the page explicitly lists supported extra names and notes the global side effect.

`GNUTranslations` derives from `NullTranslations` and overrides `_parse` to read GNU `.mo` files in big- and little-endian forms. It reads optional RFC 822-style metadata from the empty-string translation, uses `Content-Type` to initialize charset (or `None` when absent), assumes ASCII when no charset is specified, and stores metadata in `_info`.

Exact overridden lookup declarations:

```rst
.. class:: GNUTranslations

   .. method:: gettext(message)
   .. method:: ngettext(singular, plural, n)
   .. method:: pgettext(context, message)
   .. method:: npgettext(context, singular, plural, n)
```

Documented lookup behavior: `GNUTranslations.gettext` returns the catalog translation, forwards missing entries to a fallback when configured, and otherwise returns the message ID. `ngettext` uses singular as the lookup ID and `n` to choose the plural; absent entries use singular only for `n == 1`, plural otherwise. Context variants perform the analogous context-restricted lookup and fallback.

### Translation examples and lifecycle facts

Locator: localized module/application/language-switching examples, pinned raw page lines 463-519.

```python
import gettext
t = gettext.translation('spam', '/usr/share/locale')
_ = t.gettext
```

```python

gettext.install('myapplication')
```

```python
import gettext

lang1 = gettext.translation('myapplication', languages=['en'])
lang2 = gettext.translation('myapplication', languages=['fr'])
lang3 = gettext.translation('myapplication', languages=['de'])

lang1.install()
lang2.install()
lang3.install()
```

The page's GNU plural example constructs `GNUTranslations(somefile)` and calls `cat.ngettext(...) % {'num': n}`. The page also documents message extraction into `.po` files and compilation into `.mo` files; those tools/files are documented ecosystem constraints, not executed operations.

### Errors, platform, async, ownership, and limits

- `GNUTranslations` construction can raise `OSError` when the `.mo` magic number is invalid, the major version is unexpected, or another file-reading problem occurs.
- With no catalog, `translation(..., fallback=False)` raises `OSError`; with `fallback=True`, it returns `NullTranslations`.
- The Solaris operating system's distinct binary `.mo` format is explicitly unsupported because no format documentation is available.
- The default locale directory is system-dependent. The page gives `/usr/share/locale` on Red Hat and `/usr/lib/locale` on Solaris as examples, and states Python's default is `{sys.base_prefix}/share/locale`; it recommends no default path value beyond this documented fact.
- Global GNU functions and `install` mutate process-global/builtins state. The class-based API stores fallback/catalog state; `translation` caches by `.mo` filename and shares actual cached instance data while cloning objects for fallback setup.
- No asynchronous gettext API is listed. No general catalog-size, recursion-depth, or allocation limit is stated in the captured page; no such limit is inferred.

```go
// GenMarkdown creates markdown output.
func GenMarkdown(cmd *cobra.Command, w io.Writer) error {
	return GenMarkdownCustom(cmd, w, func(s string) string { return s })
}

// GenMarkdownTree will generate a markdown page for this command and all
// descendants in the directory given. The header may be nil.
func GenMarkdownTree(cmd *cobra.Command, dir string) error {
	identity := func(s string) string { return s }
	emptyStr := func(s string) string { return "" }
	return GenMarkdownTreeCustom(cmd, dir, emptyStr, identity)
}
```

`GenMarkdownCustom` calls `InitDefaultHelpCmd` and `InitDefaultHelpFlag`, writes command headings/synopsis/examples/options/SEE ALSO, and appends an auto-generated date tag unless `DisableAutoGenTag`; `GenMarkdownTreeCustom` recursively visits available descendants and creates `<command_path_with_underscores>.md` below the supplied directory. These statements are source-behavior descriptions, not execution claims.

Exact source excerpts:

```go
// GenManTree will generate a man page for this command and all descendants
// in the directory given. The header may be nil.
func GenManTree(cmd *cobra.Command, header *GenManHeader, dir string) error {
	return GenManTreeFromOpts(cmd, GenManTreeOptions{
		Header:           header,
		Path:             dir,
		CommandSeparator: "-",
	})
}

// GenMan will generate a man page for the given command and write it to
// w. The header argument may be nil, however obviously w may not.
func GenMan(cmd *cobra.Command, header *GenManHeader, w io.Writer) error {
	if header == nil {
		header = &GenManHeader{}
	}
	if err := fillHeader(header, cmd.CommandPath(), cmd.DisableAutoGenTag); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	b := genMan(cmd, header)
	_, err := w.Write(md2man.Render(b))
	return err
}
```

`GenManTreeFromOpts` recursively emits a man page per available descendant, uses `Header.Section` or `1`, uses `CommandSeparator` or `_`, and creates files under `opts.Path`; `GenMan` renders Cobra's generated markdown through `github.com/cpuguy83/go-md2man/v2/md2man`. Header defaults and `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` parsing are implemented in the same pinned source.
