## Existing ordinary file-reader composition

These excerpts are included only to identify already-existing reader ownership and line-read composition. They do not introduce a new API.

### `JetFileReader`/`JetFileWriter` handles

**EXACT.** Source: `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/HandlesRaylib.rs`, lines 13-23.

```rust
// ── Streaming file handles (E2-M7, D-IO2) ────────────────────────────────────
// FileReader / FileWriter are RAII: Drop closes (and flushes) them
// on every exit path — including `?` early returns and panics.
struct JetFileReader {
    inner: std::io::BufReader<std::fs::File>,
    path: String,
}
struct JetFileWriter {
    inner: std::io::BufWriter<std::fs::File>,
    path: String,
}
```

### File open and line read

**EXACT.** Source: `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/FileStream.rs`, lines 1-21 and 65-92.

```rust
pub(crate) fn jet_std_files_open(path: &String) -> Result<JetFileReader, jet_std::IOError> {
    if jet_fault_should_fail("FS.Read") {
        return Err(jet_std::IOError::other(
            jet_std::IOOperation::Read,
            Some(path.clone()),
            "fault injected: FS.Read",
        ));
    }
    let file = jet_fs_open(path)
        .map_err(|error| jet_std::io_error_at(jet_std::IOOperation::Read, path, error))?;
    Ok(JetFileReader {
        inner: std::io::BufReader::new(file),
        path: path.clone(),
    })
}

pub(crate) fn jet_std_file_reader_read_line(
    reader: &mut JetFileReader,
) -> Result<Option<String>, jet_std::IOError> {
    use std::io::BufRead;

    if jet_fault_should_fail("FS.Read") {
        return Err(jet_std::IOError::other(
            jet_std::IOOperation::Read,
            Some(reader.path.clone()),
            "fault injected: FS.Read",
        ));
    }
    let mut line = String::new();
    match reader.inner.read_line(&mut line) {
        Ok(0) => Ok(None),
        Ok(_) => {
            while line.ends_with('\n') || line.ends_with('\r') {
                line.pop();
            }
            Ok(Some(line))
        }
        Err(error) => Err(jet_std::io_error_at(
            jet_std::IOOperation::Read,
            &reader.path,
            error,
        )),
    }
}
```

```rust
// D-STDIN1=A: streaming line-by-line stdin.
// Stdin owns the shared buffer. A loop-local BufReader would discard unread
// bytes when a sentinel breaks the loop before a subsequent readline call.
struct JetStdinReader {
    inner: std::io::Stdin,
}
fn jet_std_io_stdin() -> JetStdinReader {
    JetStdinReader {
        inner: std::io::stdin(),
    }
}
fn jet_std_io_stdin_read_line(r: &mut JetStdinReader) -> Result<Option<String>, jet_std::IOError> {
    if jet_fault_should_fail("IO.Read") {
        return Err(jet_std::IOError::other(
            jet_std::IOOperation::Read,
            Some("stdin".to_string()),
            "fault injected: IO.Read",
        ));
    }
    let mut line = String::new();
    match r.inner.read_line(&mut line) {
        Ok(0) => Ok(None),
        Ok(_) => {
            while line.ends_with('\n') || line.ends_with('\r') {
                line.pop();
            }
            Ok(Some(line))
        }
        Err(e) => Err(jet_std::IOError::other(
            jet_std::IOOperation::Read,
            Some("stdin".to_string()),

        )),
    }
}
```

### Ordinary terminal line-read delegation

**EXACT.** Source: `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/IoLineStream.rs`, lines 1-44.

```rust
fn jet_std_io_input(prompt: Option<&String>) -> Result<String, jet_std::IOError> {
    if let Some(p) = prompt {
        if jet_fault_should_fail("IO.Write") {
            return Err(jet_std::IOError::other(
                jet_std::IOOperation::Write,
                Some("stdout".to_string()),
                "fault injected: IO.Write",
            ));
        }
        if jet_fault_should_fail("IO.Flush") {
            return Err(jet_std::IOError::other(
                jet_std::IOOperation::Flush,
                Some("stdout".to_string()),
                "fault injected: IO.Flush",
            ));
        }
        jet_term_write_stdout(p, true)
            .map_err(|e| jet_std::IOError::other(jet_std::IOOperation::Flush, None, e))?;
    }
    if jet_fault_should_fail("IO.Read") {
        return Err(jet_std::IOError::other(
            jet_std::IOOperation::Read,
            Some("stdin".to_string()),
            "fault injected: IO.Read",
        ));
    }
    // #2009: the shared reader owns the line read and the trailing-newline
    // trim. `io.input` answers with text, so a closed stream reads as an empty
    // line here; the prompt kernels take the sharper `JetTermRead` fact.
    let line = jet_term_read_stdin_line().map_err(|e| {
        jet_std::IOError::other(jet_std::IOOperation::Read, Some("stdin".to_string()), e)
    })?;
    Ok(jet_term_read_text(line))
}

// #1480: free-function spellings the Core surface ledger scores against peers.
fn jet_std_io_readline() -> Result<String, jet_std::IOError> {
    jet_std_io_input(None)
}
```

# Erlang External Term Format wire evidence

**Capture date:** 2026-09-11  
**Canonical URL:** `https://www.erlang.org/doc/apps/erts/erl_ext_dist.html`  
**Source identity:** Erlang/OTP 29.0.6, ERTS `v17.0.6` (`meta-major-vsn: 29`, page title `External Term Format — OTP 29.0.6 (erts 17.0.6)`)  
**Pinned source link exposed by the page:** `https://github.com/erlang/otp/blob/OTP-29.0.6/erts/doc/guides/erl_ext_dist.md#L1`  
**Source locator:** `#introduction`, `#encoding-atoms`, `#distribution-header`, and every tag heading listed in the index below.

This is official wire-format evidence only. No Erlang runtime, dependency, compiler, or network fetch was run. The Glaze page linked this canonical ETF document, but Glaze's documented `glz::eetf_to_json` path is a checked, one-way ETF-to-JSON conversion. This file does not claim a full bidirectional ETF codec, term identity preservation, or Glaze support for every tag below.

## Introduction and format envelope

The page states that the external term format is mainly used by Erlang's distribution mechanism. All Erlang terms have an external representation, and interpretation is application-specific.

The Erlang conversion BIFs named by the source are:

```text
erlang:term_to_binary/1,2
erlang:binary_to_term/1
```

The source also refers to `erlang:term_to_iovec/1,2`. Distribution applies the conversion implicitly when messages cross node boundaries.

The overall term format is:

```text
| 131 | Tag | Data |
```

where `131` is one byte, followed by one-byte `Tag` and tag-specific `Data`. When a distribution header is used between connected nodes, the version byte `131` is omitted from terms following that header because the distribution header carries the implied version.

The compressed term format is:

```text
| 131 | 80 | UncompressedSize | Zlib-compressedData |
```

`UncompressedSize` is an unsigned 32-bit integer in big-endian byte order. After expansion, the compressed data is:

```text
| Tag | Data |
```

## Atom encoding and atom limits

As from ERTS 9.0 (OTP 20), atoms may contain any Unicode characters. Atoms sent over node distribution are always UTF-8 using `ATOM_UTF8_EXT`, `SMALL_ATOM_UTF8_EXT`, or `ATOM_CACHE_REF`. Atoms encoded by `erlang:term_to_binary/1,2` or `erlang:term_to_iovec/1,2` are by default also UTF-8 using `ATOM_UTF8_EXT` or `SMALL_ATOM_UTF8_EXT`.

The maximum allowed number of characters in an atom is 255; in UTF-8 each character can require four bytes.

## Distribution headers are protocol framing, not ordinary term payload tags

The page gives separate distribution-header formats. These headers carry metadata for a control message and payload, primarily for atom-cache handling. Since OTP-22 they can fragment large distribution messages. An `ATOM_CACHE_REF` in a term following a distribution header refers to the corresponding cache entry.

The atom-cache reference index range is `0 <= AtomCacheReferenceIndex < 255`, allowing at most 255 different cache references from following terms. The normal non-fragmented header uses tag byte `68`:

```text
| 131 | 68 | NumberOfAtomCacheRefs | Flags | AtomCacheRefs |
```

When `NumberOfAtomCacheRefs` is zero, `Flags` and `AtomCacheRefs` are omitted. `LongAtoms` selects two-byte atom lengths instead of one-byte lengths in the distribution header. The atom cache has 8 segments of 256 entries, for 2048 entries.

Fragmented messages use a starting header tag `69`:

```text
| 131 | 69 | SequenceId (8) | FragmentId (8) | NumberOfAtomCacheRefs | Flags | AtomCacheRefs |
```

Continuation fragments use tag `70`:

```text
| 131 | 70 | SequenceId (8) | FragmentId (8) |
```

A fragmented sequence's `FragmentId` starts at the total number of fragments and decrements to 1, the final fragment. Fragments must be delivered in order. The page's example uses fragment size 128 and explicitly notes that 128 is only an example; any fragment size may be used.

These distribution-header tags and atom-cache rules are protocol framing. They are not evidence that a Glaze JSON conversion accepts or preserves distribution control messages.

## Complete term-tag index

The following index records every term-tag heading exposed by the OTP 29.0.6 page, including deprecated/removed tags and the page's wire fields. Widths in parentheses are the page-table widths in bytes; `N` means variable length as defined by the fields.

| Tag name | Decimal tag | Wire fields / exact page shape | Documented format facts and status |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `ATOM_CACHE_REF` | `82` | `82` + `AtomCacheReferenceIndex` (1) | Refers to an atom at `AtomCacheReferenceIndex` in a distribution header. Distribution framing, not a standalone atom text. |
| `SMALL_INTEGER_EXT` | `97` | `97` + `Int` (1) | Unsigned 8-bit integer. |
| `INTEGER_EXT` | `98` | `98` + `Int` (4) | Signed 32-bit integer, big-endian. |
| `FLOAT_EXT` | `99` | `99` + `Float string` (31) | Finite float in string format; source says sprintf format `"%.20e"` and sscanf format `"%lf"`. Minor version 0; superseded by `NEW_FLOAT_EXT`. |
| `PORT_EXT` | `102` | `102` + `Node` (N) + `ID` (4) + `Creation` (1) | Same as `NEW_PORT_EXT`, but one-byte `Creation` with only two significant bits. |
| `NEW_PORT_EXT` | `89` | `89` + `Node` (N) + `ID` (4) + `Creation` (4) | Same as `V4_PORT_EXT`, but four-byte `ID` with only 28 significant bits. Introduced OTP 19 for decode/echo; not encoded for local ports. OTP 23 makes it the normal port encoding under `DFLAG_BIG_CREATION`. |
| `V4_PORT_EXT` | `120` | `120` + `Node` (N) + `ID` (8) + `Creation` (4) | Port identifier from `erlang:open_port/2`; node is an atom; ID is unsigned 64-bit big-endian; port operations are not allowed across node boundaries. OTP 26 requires `DFLAG_V4_NC` and accepts full 64-bit ports for decode/echo. |
| `PID_EXT` | `103` | `103` + `Node` (N) + `ID` (4) + `Serial` (4) + `Creation` (1) | Same as `NEW_PID_EXT`, but one-byte `Creation` with only two significant bits. |
| `NEW_PID_EXT` | `88` | `88` + `Node` (N) + `ID` (4) + `Serial` (4) + `Creation` (4) | Encodes an Erlang process identifier. Node is an atom; ID and Serial are unsigned 32-bit big-endian; Creation is unsigned 32-bit and distinguishes node incarnations. Introduced OTP 19 for decode/echo; OTP 23 makes it normal under `DFLAG_BIG_CREATION`; OTP 26 requires `DFLAG_V4_NC` and accepts full 64-bit pids for decode/echo. |
| `SMALL_TUPLE_EXT` | `104` | `104` + `Arity` (1) + `Elements` (N) | Tuple; unsigned one-byte arity. |
| `LARGE_TUPLE_EXT` | `105` | `105` + `Arity` (4) + `Elements` (N) | Tuple; unsigned four-byte big-endian arity. |
| `MAP_EXT` | `116` | `116` + `Arity` (4) + `Pairs` (N) | Map; unsigned four-byte big-endian pair count. Pairs are `K1,V1,K2,V2,...,Kn,Vn`; duplicate keys are not allowed. As from Erlang/OTP 17.0. |
| `NIL_EXT` | `106` | `106` | Empty list, Erlang syntax `[]`. |
| `STRING_EXT` | `107` | `107` + `Length` (2) + `Characters` (N) | Optimization for lists of bytes (0–255), not a distinct Erlang type. Length is unsigned two-byte big-endian; lists longer than 65535 must use `LIST_EXT`. |
| `LIST_EXT` | `108` | `108` + `Length` (4) + `Elements` (N) + `Tail` (N) | List; length is element count. Tail is `NIL_EXT` for a proper list and any type for an improper list such as `[a|b]`. |
| `BINARY_EXT` | `109` | `109` + `Len` (4) + `Data` (N) | Binary; length is unsigned four-byte big-endian. |
| `SMALL_BIG_EXT` | `110` | `110` + `n` (1) + `Sign` (1) + `d(0)...d(n-1)` (N) | Bignum; sign 0 positive/1 negative; digits are least-significant byte first, base 256. |
| `LARGE_BIG_EXT` | `111` | `111` + `n` (4) + `Sign` (1) + `d(0)...d(n-1)` (N) | Same as `SMALL_BIG_EXT`, with unsigned four-byte big-endian length. |
| `REFERENCE_EXT` (deprecated) | `101` | `101` + `Node` (N) + `ID` (4) + `Creation` (1) | Same as `NEW_REFERENCE_EXT`, but one ID word (`Len = 1`); deprecated. |
| `NEW_REFERENCE_EXT` | `114` | `114` + `Len` (2) + `Node` (N) + `Creation` (1) + `ID...` (N) | Same as `NEWER_REFERENCE_EXT` except first ID word has only 18 significant bits and Creation is one byte with only two significant bits. |
| `NEWER_REFERENCE_EXT` | `90` | `90` + `Len` (2) + `Node` (N) + `Creation` (4) + `ID...` (N) | Reference from `erlang:make_ref/0`; Len is unsigned 16-bit and no greater than 5; ID is Len uninterpreted four-byte big-endian words; Creation follows `NEW_PID_EXT`. Introduced OTP 19 for decode/echo; OTP 23 normalizes references under `DFLAG_BIG_CREATION`; OTP 26 allows up to five ID words under `DFLAG_V4_NC`. |
| `FUN_EXT` (removed) | `117` | `117` + `NumFree` (4) + `Pid` + `Module` + `Index` + `Uniq` + `Free vars...` | Not emitted since OTP R8 and not decoded since OTP 23. |
| `NEW_FUN_EXT` | `112` | `112` + `Size` (4) + `Arity` (1) + `Uniq` (16) + `Index` (4) + `NumFree` (4) + `Module` + `OldIndex` + `OldUniq` + `Pid` + `Free Vars` | Internal fun encoding (`fun F/A` and anonymous funs). Size includes its Size field; Uniq is 16-byte MD5; free variables are terms. |
| `EXPORT_EXT` | `113` | `113` + `Module` (N) + `Function` (N) + `Arity` (N) | External fun encoding `fun M:F/A`; Module and Function are atoms; Arity uses `SMALL_INTEGER_EXT`. |
| `BIT_BINARY_EXT` | `77` | `77` + `Len` (4) + `Bits` (1) + `Data` (N) | Bitstring whose length need not be a multiple of 8. Len is unsigned four-byte big-endian; Bits is 1–8 bits used in the final byte, counted from most to least significant. |
| `NEW_FLOAT_EXT` | `70` | `70` + `IEEE float` (8) | Finite float as eight-byte big-endian IEEE format; minor version 1. |
| `ATOM_UTF8_EXT` | `118` | `118` + `Len` (2) + `AtomName` (N) | Atom with unsigned two-byte big-endian byte length and UTF-8 bytes. |
| `SMALL_ATOM_UTF8_EXT` | `119` | `119` + `Len` (1) + `AtomName` (N) | Atom with unsigned one-byte length and UTF-8 bytes; longer atoms use `ATOM_UTF8_EXT`. |
| `ATOM_EXT` (deprecated) | `100` | `100` + `Len` (2) + `AtomName` (N) | Atom with unsigned two-byte big-endian length and Latin-1 bytes; maximum Len 255; deprecated. |
| `SMALL_ATOM_EXT` (deprecated) | `115` | `115` + `Len` (1) + `AtomName` (N) | Atom with unsigned one-byte length and Latin-1 bytes; deprecated. Introduced ERTS 5.7.2 and requires `DFLAG_SMALL_ATOM_TAGS` exchange. |
| `LOCAL_EXT` | `121` | `121` + unspecified local-format bytes | Alternative local external term format for a matching local decoder only. Runtime uses it for `term_to_binary/2` with `local`; introduced OTP 26.0. |
| `RECORD_EXT` | `67` | `67` + `#Fields` (4) + `Flags` (1) + `Module` + `Name` + `Field Names` + `Values` | Native record encoding; fields and names are atoms, values are recursively encoded terms; introduced OTP 29.0. |

The official fragment locator for each row is the lower-case tag heading (for example, `#small_integer_ext`, `#map_ext`, or `#record_ext`). The deprecated/removed rows use the page's exact suffixes: `#reference_ext-deprecated`, `#fun_ext-removed`, `#atom_ext-deprecated`, and `#small_atom_ext-deprecated`.

## Wire facts grouped by Erlang value family

### Numbers and strings

`SMALL_INTEGER_EXT` is an unsigned 8-bit integer. `INTEGER_EXT` is a signed 32-bit big-endian integer. `FLOAT_EXT` stores finite floats as string format using sprintf `"%.20e"` and is the minor-version-0 form; `NEW_FLOAT_EXT` stores finite floats as eight-byte big-endian IEEE values and is the minor-version-1 form. The source excludes infinity, negative infinity, and NaN from both float encodings.

`SMALL_BIG_EXT` and `LARGE_BIG_EXT` store arbitrary bignums with a sign byte (`0` positive, `1` negative) and least-significant-byte-first base-256 digits. The small form has a one-byte digit count; the large form has a four-byte big-endian count.

`STRING_EXT` is an optimization for a list of bytes in the range 0–255, not a separate Erlang string type. Its two-byte big-endian length means lists longer than 65535 elements must be encoded as `LIST_EXT`. `LIST_EXT` carries a four-byte element count and a final tail; `NIL_EXT` is the proper-list tail, while an improper list may have any tail term.

`BINARY_EXT` carries an unsigned four-byte big-endian byte length and data. `BIT_BINARY_EXT` carries an unsigned four-byte big-endian `Len` byte count, a one-byte `Bits` count of bits used in the final byte (1–8), and `Len` data bytes; its bitstring need not have a byte-multiple length.

### Tuples, maps, and object-key-relevant terms

`SMALL_TUPLE_EXT` has an unsigned one-byte arity; `LARGE_TUPLE_EXT` has an unsigned four-byte big-endian arity. Each tuple element is recursively encoded as a term.

`MAP_EXT` has an unsigned four-byte big-endian pair count and encodes pairs in order `K1, V1, K2, V2, ..., Kn, Vn`. Duplicate keys are not allowed within one map. The page marks this map format “As from Erlang/OTP 17.0.”

For JSON conversion, the Glaze EETF page independently documents only strings, atoms, and binaries as usable object keys because a JSON key must be a string. That Glaze statement is narrower than this ETF wire inventory and does not establish a mapping for every ETF term category.

### Atoms and atom cache

`ATOM_UTF8_EXT` uses a two-byte big-endian byte length and UTF-8 atom bytes. `SMALL_ATOM_UTF8_EXT` uses a one-byte length and UTF-8 bytes; longer UTF-8 atoms use `ATOM_UTF8_EXT`. `ATOM_EXT` and `SMALL_ATOM_EXT` are deprecated Latin-1 encodings with two-byte and one-byte lengths respectively. The page records the `DFLAG_SMALL_ATOM_TAGS` handshake requirement for `SMALL_ATOM_EXT`.

`ATOM_CACHE_REF` is a one-byte cache index used with distribution headers. It does not carry atom text in the term itself.

### Process, port, reference, and function terms

`PID_EXT`/`NEW_PID_EXT` encode process identifiers with node, ID, serial, and creation fields. `PORT_EXT`/`NEW_PORT_EXT`/`V4_PORT_EXT` encode port identifiers with node, ID, and creation fields. The page identifies node names as atoms and records the OTP 19/23/26 decode/echo and distribution-flag transitions in the table above.

`REFERENCE_EXT`, `NEW_REFERENCE_EXT`, and `NEWER_REFERENCE_EXT` encode reference terms. `REFERENCE_EXT` is deprecated. `NEWER_REFERENCE_EXT` is generated by `erlang:make_ref/0`, permits at most five ID words, and records the OTP 19/23/26 compatibility transitions.

`FUN_EXT` is removed: it has not been emitted since OTP R8 and has not been decoded since OTP 23. `NEW_FUN_EXT` encodes internal funs and `EXPORT_EXT` encodes external funs `fun M:F/A`; the latter uses atom-encoded module/function names and `SMALL_INTEGER_EXT` for arity.

These PID, port, reference, and fun/export tags are ordinary ETF term tags in the OTP index. They are not evidence that Glaze's documented JSON conversion preserves process identity, node identity, references, closures, or distribution behavior.

### Local and record extensions

`LOCAL_EXT` marks an alternative local external format whose following bytes are unspecified and must be decoded only by a matching local decoder. The Erlang runtime uses it for `term_to_binary/2` with the `local` option; the page records introduction in OTP 26.0.

`RECORD_EXT` encodes a native record using field count, flags, module atom, name atom, field-name atoms, and recursively encoded values. The page records introduction in OTP 29.0.

## Glaze conversion boundary

The Glaze `v8.3.0` EETF page (`https://github.com/stephenberry/glaze/blob/v8.3.0/docs/EETF/erlang-external-term-format.md`, retrieved 2026-09-11) exposes `glz::eetf_to_json(term, json)` and the options `binary_as_base64` and inheritable `escape_control_characters`. It documents that `binary_as_base64` is off by default, control bytes `0x00–1F` can return `error_code::invalid_control_character`, and only strings/atoms/binaries work as JSON object keys. The page does not expose a bidirectional API or a complete tag-to-JSON identity table.

Accordingly, the boundary recorded here is deliberately one-way and checked: ETF term bytes → JSON bytes through the documented Glaze conversion. No claim is made that JSON → ETF is available, that unsupported PID/reference/fun/distribution terms round-trip, or that all ETF tags are accepted by Glaze.

## Explicit evidence gaps

1. The OTP page provides the complete term-tag heading index and wire fields above, but this capture does not reproduce every long distribution-fragment example byte-for-byte.

## JSONB profile: Glaze v8.3.0 documentation

The tag-pinned heading and opening text are:

```text
# JSONB (SQLite Binary JSON)

Glaze provides read/write support for the SQLite JSONB binary JSON format. JSONB is the native on-disk representation that SQLite uses for its `jsonb_*` functions — producing it directly from C++ avoids a JSON → JSONB conversion pass inside SQLite.
```

The linked specification in that paragraph is `https://sqlite.org/jsonb.html`.

### Tag-pinned public entry points and exact basic usage

The selected source examples are:

```c++
#include "glaze/jsonb.hpp"

my_struct s{};
std::string buffer{};
auto ec = glz::write_jsonb(s, buffer);
if (!ec) {
   // buffer now contains a valid SQLite JSONB blob, ready to INSERT.
}
```

```c++
my_struct s{};
auto ec = glz::read_jsonb(s, buffer);
if (!ec) {
   // Success
}
```

```c++
auto json = glz::jsonb_to_json(buffer);
if (json) {
   // json.value() is a std::string containing JSON text
}
```

The tag-pinned high-level API index is:

```c++
// Write
error_ctx         glz::write_jsonb<T>(T&& value, Buffer& buffer);
expected<string>  glz::write_jsonb<T>(T&& value);   // returns a new string
error_code        glz::write_file_jsonb<T>(T&& value, sv filename, Buffer& scratch);

// Read
error_ctx         glz::read_jsonb<T>(T& value, const Buffer& buffer);
expected<T>       glz::read_jsonb<T>(const Buffer& buffer);
error_ctx         glz::read_file_jsonb<T>(T& value, sv filename, Buffer& scratch);

// Convert
error_ctx         glz::jsonb_to_json(const Buffer& jsonb, std::string& out);
expected<string>  glz::jsonb_to_json(const Buffer& jsonb);
```

The same page states that `glz::set_jsonb<Opts>()` composes JSONB with other `glz::opts` fields. The exceptions include `glaze/exceptions/jsonb_exceptions.hpp`; the throwing names are `glz::ex::write_jsonb`, `glz::ex::read_jsonb`, `glz::ex::write_file_jsonb`, `glz::ex::read_file_jsonb`, and `glz::ex::jsonb_to_json`, available only when `__cpp_exceptions` is set.

### JSONB element codes and payload categories

The tag-pinned documentation states: “JSONB encodes every value with a 1–9 byte header (type nibble + payload-size nibble) followed by the payload bytes.” Its complete code table is:

| Code | Name | Glaze writes from | Glaze reads into |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 0 | `NULL` | `std::nullptr_t`, empty optional | any `null`-compatible type |
| 1 | `TRUE` | `bool{true}` | `bool` |
| 2 | `FALSE` | `bool{false}` | `bool` |
| 3 | `INT` | `std::integral` types | `std::integral`, `std::floating_point` |
| 4 | `INT5` | not emitted | `std::integral`, `std::floating_point` |
| 5 | `FLOAT` | finite `float`, `double` | `std::floating_point`, `std::integral` |
| 6 | `FLOAT5` | `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity` | `std::floating_point` |
| 7 | `TEXT` | `std::string`, string literals, reflected field names when no JSON escape is needed | `std::string`, `std::string_view` |
| 8 | `TEXTJ` | not emitted | `std::string` with JSON escape decoding |
| 9 | `TEXT5` | not emitted | `std::string` with JSON5 escape decoding |
| 10 | `TEXTRAW` | `std::string`, string literals, reflected field names when any byte `<0x20`, `"`, or `\\` is present | `std::string`, `std::string_view` |
| 11 | `ARRAY` | `std::vector`, tuples, ranges, `std::array`, reflected `glaze_array` | same |
| 12 | `OBJECT` | `std::map`, `std::unordered_map`, `std::pair`, reflected structs | same |

The docs state that codes `13–15` are reserved by the spec and Glaze returns `error_code::syntax_error` on read if any appear.

For strings, the source says the writer pre-scans every string and picks the tightest spec-conformant type:

- `TEXT (7)` has a payload already valid as a JSON string body, so downstream JSON emitters can wrap it in quotes and `memcpy` it.
- `TEXTRAW (10)` has at least one byte requiring JSON escaping: any byte `<0x20`, an unescaped `"`, or an unescaped `\\`; downstream JSON emitters run the full escape writer.

The reader handles all four text types for interoperability with SQLite or hand-crafted blobs. The docs state that `TEXTJ` and `TEXT5` are never emitted by Glaze, while they remain readable for interoperability.

### Numeric, container, variant, and option constraints

The tag-pinned docs state that SQLite JSONB does not cap `INT`/`INT5` at 64 bits or `FLOAT`/`FLOAT5` at IEEE-754 binary64 because payloads are ASCII text and magnitude is open-ended. Glaze parses integers through `int64_t`/`uint64_t` and floats through `double`, then bounds-checks the destination; a payload exceeding those intermediates returns `error_code::parse_number_failure`. The page gives the integer range `[INT64_MIN, UINT64_MAX]`, target-type bounds checks, and the negative `INT5` two's-complement edge case.

Container readers and the JSONB-to-JSON converter cap recursion at `max_recursive_depth_limit` (`256`) and return `error_code::exceeded_max_recursive_depth` on overflow.

Arrays and objects store a **payload size in bytes**, not a child count. The tag-pinned docs state that Glaze reserves a 9-byte header slot (`u64_follows`), writes children, and patches the header with the actual payload size. The spec permits non-minimal headers. The same page records the SQLite interop statement that `json_valid(blob, 4)` accepts Glaze's well-formed non-minimal output while `json_valid(blob, 8)` requires canonical minimal-header form and rejects it; this is a source claim, not a run in this capture.

For variants, the docs state that the active alternative is serialized directly, with no wrapping array or index prefix; read deduces the alternative from the JSONB type code. Auto-deduction permits at most one alternative per JSONB category. Internal tagging uses an `OBJECT` with the tag pair first; adjacent `content` tagging is not implemented for JSONB and is rejected at compile time; an external producer whose tag is not the first object key receives `no_matching_variant_type`.

The documented JSONB options are `error_on_unknown_keys=true`, `error_on_missing_keys=false`, `skip_null_members=true`, and custom options `error_on_const_read`, `skip_default_members`, `max_string_length`, and `write_function_pointers`. Text-only options have no effect on JSONB itself; `jsonb_to_json` emits JSON text and therefore applies text options, with fixed escaping of control characters and UTF-8 validation unless `validate_utf8` is off.

## JSONB profile: official SQLite specification

### Version and intended use

The official `https://sqlite.org/jsonb.html` page says:

```text
Beginning with version 3.45.0 (pending), SQLite supports an
alternative binary encoding of JSON which we call "JSONB". JSONB is
a binary format that stored as a BLOB.
```

It says SQLite's JSONB is not binary-compatible with PostgreSQL's JSONB. It also says JSONB is designed for internal use by SQLite only, applications should access it through the JSON SQL functions rather than individual BLOB bytes, and the representation is documented for portability/backward compatibility rather than for application byte-level writers.

The current `json1.html#the_jsonb_format` page separately says JSONB support begins with SQLite version `3.45.0 (2024-01-15)`, says SQLite JSONB makes no O(1) lookup claim and is O(N) for most operations, and repeats that applications should treat JSONB as an opaque BLOB rather than reverse-engineer it. These are two official pages with different release wording; this capture does not strengthen them into a single unobserved release assertion.

### Header and payload-size definition

The SQLite specification says each JSON element is a header followed by a payload; the header is 1–9 bytes and identifies element type and payload size. Its payload-size rules are:

- The upper four bits of the first header byte determine the header size and, for values `0–11`, the payload size itself.
- Upper nibble `0–11`: one-byte header; payload size is that nibble.
- Upper nibble `12`: total header 2 bytes; one following unsigned byte is the payload size.
- Upper nibble `13`: total header 3 bytes; two following unsigned big-endian bytes are the payload size.
- Upper nibble `14`: total header 5 bytes; four following unsigned big-endian bytes are the payload size.
- Upper nibble `15`: total header 9 bytes; eight following unsigned big-endian bytes are the payload size.
- The header need not use the simplest form. The current SQLite implementation does not support BLOBs larger than 2 GiB, so the eight-byte size form is reserved for future expansion.

The official page's exact non-minimal-equivalent examples for numeric text `"1"` are:

```text
0x13 0x31
0xc3 0x01 0x31
0xd3 0x00 0x01 0x31
0xe3 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x01 0x31
0xf3 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x01 0x31
```

### Element type definitions

The least-significant four bits of the first header byte determine element type. The official SQLite type definitions are:

| Code | Name | Official payload meaning |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | `NULL` | JSON `null`; true null payload size is zero; non-zero payload is reserved for future expansion and legacy readers interpret nominal null. |
| 1 | `TRUE` | JSON `true`; true value payload size is zero; non-zero payload is reserved and legacy readers interpret nominal true. |
| 2 | `FALSE` | JSON `false`; true value payload size is zero; non-zero payload is reserved and legacy readers interpret nominal false. |
| 3 | `INT` | Canonical RFC 8259 JSON integer; payload is ASCII numeric text. |
| 4 | `INT5` | Non-canonical/JSON5 integer; payload is ASCII numeric text and needs translation to RFC 8259 JSON text. |
| 5 | `FLOAT` | Canonical RFC 8259 JSON floating-point value; payload is ASCII numeric text. |
| 6 | `FLOAT5` | Non-canonical/JSON5 floating-point value; payload is ASCII numeric text and needs translation to RFC 8259 JSON text. |
| 7 | `TEXT` | JSON string with no escapes or characters needing escaping for SQL/JSON; payload is UTF-8 text without string delimiters. |
| 8 | `TEXTJ` | JSON string containing RFC 8259 escapes; payload is UTF-8 escaped text without string delimiters. |
| 9 | `TEXT5` | JSON string containing JSON5/non-canonical escapes; payload is UTF-8 escaped text without string delimiters. |
| 10 | `TEXTRAW` | JSON string containing UTF-8 characters needing escaping in standard JSON text; payload has no string delimiters. |
| 11 | `ARRAY` | JSON array; payload contains the JSONB elements of the array. |
| 12 | `OBJECT` | JSON object; payload contains pairs of JSONB elements. First element of each pair must be a string (types 7–10); second may be any type, including nested arrays/objects. |
| 13 | `RESERVED-13` | Reserved; legacy implementations should raise an error. |
| 14 | `RESERVED-14` | Reserved; legacy implementations should raise an error. |
| 15 | `RESERVED-15` | Reserved; legacy implementations should raise an error. |

The SQLite page states that numeric values remain text to defer conversion, and that the four text representations preserve whether escaping came from RFC 8259 JSON, JSON5, or SQL string values.

### Malformed/opaque-format warnings

The official SQLite JSONB pages state that malformed JSONB may cause a malformed-JSON error, return a correct answer when malformed bytes do not affect the query, or return a nonsensical answer. Handling may change between SQLite versions. The documented promise is that malformed JSONB will not cause a memory error or similar vulnerability; it may produce a bad answer or abort, but it will not crash. `json_valid()` is the documented validity check.

The SQLite JSONB format page says the name is inspired by PostgreSQL but the formats are not binary-compatible. The JSON functions page says SQLite JSONB currently makes no O(1) lookup claim and is O(N) for most operations. These are compatibility/opaque-format facts, not a claim about Glaze's implementation beyond the Glaze page's own interop statements above.

## JSONB profile: tag-pinned Glaze header definitions

The tag-pinned `include/glaze/jsonb/header.hpp` source defines the element and size codes. The selected definitions below omit include lines and inline attributes while preserving the published constants and bit operations:

```c++
namespace glz::jsonb
{
   namespace type
   {
      inline constexpr uint8_t null_ = 0;
      inline constexpr uint8_t true_ = 1;
      inline constexpr uint8_t false_ = 2;
      inline constexpr uint8_t int_ = 3; // ASCII decimal, RFC 8259 integer
      inline constexpr uint8_t int5 = 4; // ASCII JSON5 integer (hex, leading +, etc.)
      inline constexpr uint8_t float_ = 5; // ASCII decimal float, RFC 8259
      inline constexpr uint8_t float5 = 6; // ASCII JSON5 float (NaN, Infinity, .5, etc.)
      inline constexpr uint8_t text = 7; // UTF-8, no escapes needed
      inline constexpr uint8_t textj = 8; // UTF-8, contains RFC 8259 escapes
      inline constexpr uint8_t text5 = 9; // UTF-8, contains JSON5 escapes
      inline constexpr uint8_t textraw = 10; // Raw UTF-8 bytes, may need escaping to emit JSON
      inline constexpr uint8_t array = 11;
      inline constexpr uint8_t object = 12;
      // 13, 14, 15 reserved
   }

   namespace size_code
   {
      inline constexpr uint8_t u8_follows = 12;
      inline constexpr uint8_t u16_follows = 13;
      inline constexpr uint8_t u32_follows = 14;
      inline constexpr uint8_t u64_follows = 15;
   }

   inline constexpr size_t max_header_bytes = 9;

   [[nodiscard]] constexpr uint8_t get_type(uint8_t initial) noexcept { return initial & 0x0f; }
   [[nodiscard]] constexpr uint8_t get_size_nibble(uint8_t initial) noexcept
   {
      return (initial >> 4) & 0x0f;
   }
   [[nodiscard]] constexpr uint8_t make_initial(uint8_t type_code, uint8_t size_nibble) noexcept
   {
      return static_cast<uint8_t>((size_nibble << 4) | (type_code & 0x0f));
   }
}
```

The same source defines `header_bytes_for_payload` to return `1` for payload sizes `<=11`, `2` for `<=0xFF`, `3` for `<=0xFFFF`, `5` for `<=0xFFFFFFFFull`, and `9` otherwise. `write_header` emits the initial byte with `make_initial`; for extended sizes it writes unsigned big-endian `uint8_t`, `uint16_t`, `uint32_t`, or `uint64_t` payload-size data. The source comment says scalar headers are minimal, while `patch_header_9` always uses the nine-byte `u64_follows` form for a reserved container slot.

The tag-pinned JSONB writer source's relevant scalar decision is captured below; surrounding declarations and buffer checks are omitted:

```c++
// Integer (signed + unsigned)
template <class T>
   requires(std::integral<T> && !std::same_as<T, bool>)
struct to<JSONB, T> final
{
   template <auto Opts>
   static void op(auto&& value, is_context auto&& ctx, auto&& b, auto& ix)
   {
      std::array<char, 32> tmp;
      using X = std::decay_t<decltype(sized_integer_conversion<T>())>;
      auto* end_ptr = glz::to_chars(tmp.data(), static_cast<X>(value));
      const size_t n = static_cast<size_t>(end_ptr - tmp.data());
      jsonb_detail::write_scalar(ctx, jsonb::type::int_, tmp.data(), n, b, ix);
   }
};
```

For strings, the source chooses `jsonb::type::textraw` when `string_needs_json_escape(...)` is true and otherwise `jsonb::type::text`. Reflected object keys are emitted as `jsonb::type::text` payloads. Arrays, maps, pairs, and reflected objects reserve the nine-byte container header, serialize their child payloads, then call `jsonb::patch_header_9` with type `array` or `object` and the resulting payload byte size.

These definitions expose the exact source-level type/header rules needed to inspect a small object profile. This capture intentionally does not calculate or publish a JSONB hex fixture.

## BEVE profile: Glaze v8.3.0 documentation

The tag-pinned BEVE source opens with:

```text
# Binary Format (BEVE)

Glaze provides a binary format to send and receive messages like JSON, but with significantly improved performance and message size savings.

The binary specification is known as [BEVE](https://github.com/beve-org/beve).
```

The exact tag-pinned examples are:

```c++
my_struct s{};
std::vector<std::byte> buffer{};
auto ec = glz::write_beve(s, buffer);
if (!ec) {
   // Success: ec.count contains bytes written
}
```

```c++
my_struct s{};
auto ec = glz::read_beve(s, buffer);
if (!ec) {
   // Success
}
```

The page note is: “Reading binary is safe for invalid input and does not require null terminated buffers.” It states that readers, the value skipper, and `glz::beve_to_json` cap nesting at `max_recursive_depth_limit` (`256` wire levels) and return `error_code::exceeded_max_recursive_depth` beyond it; each object and array counts as a level.

The tag-pinned size helpers are `glz::beve_size`, `glz::beve_size_untagged`, and `glz::compressed_int_size`. The exact documented `compressed_int_size` boundary examples are:

```c++
glz::compressed_int_size(0);           // 1 byte (values < 64)
glz::compressed_int_size(63);          // 1 byte
glz::compressed_int_size(64);          // 2 bytes (values < 16384)
glz::compressed_int_size(16383);       // 2 bytes
glz::compressed_int_size(16384);       // 4 bytes (values < 1073741824)
glz::compressed_int_size(1073741824);  // 8 bytes

static_assert(glz::compressed_int_size<100>() == 2);
```

### Glaze BEVE header-peek profile

The tag-pinned docs define the public return shape:

```c++
struct beve_header {
   uint8_t tag{};        // Raw tag byte
   uint8_t type{};       // Base type (see below)
   uint8_t ext_type{};   // For extensions: subtype (variant, complex, etc.)
   size_t count{};       // Element count, string length, variant index, etc.
   size_t header_size{}; // Bytes consumed by tag + count encoding
};
```

The documented base types are:

| `type` | Name | `count` meaning |
---:|---|---|
| 0 | null/boolean | 0 for null, 1 for boolean |
| 1 | number | 1 |
| 2 | string | string length in bytes |
| 3 | object | number of key-value pairs |
| 4 | typed array | number of elements |
| 5 | generic array | number of elements |
| 6 | extensions | extension-specific |

The documented extension subtypes are delimiter `0`, variant (Version 1 only) `1`, and complex `3`; a single complex has `count == 2` and `header_size == 2`, while a complex array has `header_size > 2`. `glz::beve_peek_header` has a buffer overload and `glz::beve_peek_header(data, size)` raw-pointer overload; `glz::beve_peek_header_at` reads at an arbitrary byte offset without slicing/copying.

The tag-pinned page says buffers written before BEVE Version 2 begin with the `glz::extension::variant` header and still read normally. This is a compatibility note for legacy Version 1 data; it does not change the Version 2 profile below.

## BEVE profile: official Version 2 specification

The official BEVE README and rendered page both identify the profile as **Version 2**. The README states that the endianness must be **little endian**. It defines `SIZE` as a compressed unsigned integer used for array-member count, object-member count, or UTF-8 string byte count; it does not mean raw bytes except for UTF-8 strings.

### Compressed unsigned integers and byte-count indicators

The official compressed-unsigned-integer table is:

| Selector | Number of bytes | Integer value |
|---:|---:|---|
| 0 | 1 | `N < 64` (`[2^6]`) |
| 1 | 2 | `N < 16384` (`[2^14]`) |
| 2 | 4 | `N < 1073741824` (`[2^30]`) |
| 3 | 8 | `N < 4611686018427387904` (`[2^62]`) |

The official `BYTE COUNT` indicator maps `0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,...` to `1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,...` bytes respectively.

### Base header and scalar tags

The official `HEADER` definition says every `VALUE` begins with a byte header and unspecified bits must be zero. Its first three bits denote:

```text
0 -> null or boolean       0b00000'000
1 -> number                0b00000'001
2 -> string                0b00000'010
3 -> object                0b00000'011
4 -> typed array           0b00000'100
5 -> generic array         0b00000'101
6 -> extension             0b00000'110
7 -> reserved              0b00000'111
```

Null is simply `0`. Boolean uses:

```text
false      0b000'01'000
true       0b000'11'000
```

For a number, the next two bits select floating point, signed integer, or unsigned integer:

```text
0 -> floating point      0b000'00'001
1 -> signed integer      0b000'01'001
2 -> unsigned integer    0b000'10'001
```

The next three bits are the `BYTE COUNT`. The official width examples include:

```text
bfloat16_t    0b000'00'001
float16_t     0b001'00'001
float32_t     0b010'00'001
float64_t     0b011'00'001
float128_t    0b100'00'001

int8_t        0b000'01'001
int16_t       0b001'01'001
int32_t       0b010'01'001
int64_t       0b011'01'001
int128_t      0b100'01'001

uint8_t       0b000'10'001
uint16_t      0b001'10'001
uint32_t      0b010'10'001
uint64_t      0b011'10'001
uint128_t     0b100'10'001
```

### Strings, objects, and arrays

The official string rules are:

```text
Strings must be encoded with UTF-8.

Layout: HEADER | SIZE | DATA
```

For object keys and typed string arrays, the string header is omitted:

```text
Layout: SIZE | DATA
```

The official object rules are:

```text
0 -> string
1 -> signed integer
2 -> unsigned integer
```

For integer keys, the next three header bits indicate `BYTE COUNT`. An object key must not contain a header because the key type has already been defined. The object layout is:

```text
HEADER | SIZE | KEY[0] | VALUE[0] | ... KEY[N] | VALUE[N]
```

Typed arrays use a type header and `SIZE`; generic arrays expect each element to have its own header:

```text
Typed array:  HEADER | SIZE | data
Generic array: HEADER | SIZE | VALUE[0] | ... VALUE[N]
```

The typed-array category values are floating point `0`, signed integer `1`, unsigned integer `2`, and boolean/string/aligned `3`. For category `3`, subtype `0` is packed boolean, subtype `1` is an array of strings, and subtype `2` is an aligned numeric array. The official boolean-array rule is LSB-first packing, with `SIZE` equal to the boolean count and final high padding bits zero.

### Version 2 extension compatibility

The official extension table assigns delimiter `0`, type tag `1`, matrices `2`, and complex numbers `3`. It explicitly marks the type-tag extension as **deprecated in Version 2**: Version 2 removes the positional, schema-dependent index and represents variant-like structures as ordinary objects. Extension ID `1` is reserved and must not be reused; Version 2 encoders must not emit it, while decoders should continue reading Version 1 data for backward compatibility.

This is the exact Version 2 compatibility boundary recorded by the normative source. No claim is made here about which extensions a particular Glaze build accepts beyond the tag-pinned Glaze statements above.

## Compatibility, release, and opaque-format boundaries

- **Glaze identity:** all selected Glaze body/source evidence is pinned to tag `v8.3.0`; the lane release record identifies commit `dce5e0f7ec572725ec369a0bc59a00eeb2270a9a`. Current rendered pages expose `main` links without a docs commit and are not asserted byte-identical to the tag.
- **SQLite identity:** the official JSONB page exposes introduction wording `3.45.0 (pending)`; the current JSON functions page states `3.45.0 (2024-01-15)`. No page release/tag was exposed by these reads. SQLite says JSONB is not PostgreSQL-compatible, is intended for SQLite/internal use, and should be treated as an opaque BLOB.
- **SQLite malformed input:** official docs permit error, correct result, or nonsensical result for malformed JSONB, with behavior allowed to change between SQLite versions; they promise no memory-safety crash. This is not a Glaze error contract.
- **Glaze JSONB headers:** Glaze's docs/source state that non-minimal headers are allowed and its container writer reserves the nine-byte form. The current page's `json_valid(blob,4)`/`json_valid(blob,8)` statements are preserved as source claims only; no SQLite execution was performed.
- **BEVE identity:** the official BEVE repository README and rendered specification both state Version 2. The repository/file read exposed branch `main` but no release tag or commit identity. No stronger BEVE release claim is made.
- **BEVE Version 1/2 boundary:** Version 2 reserves extension ID `1` and forbids new type-tag emission; Version 1 decoders should continue reading legacy type-tag data. Glaze's v8.3.0 docs say pre-Version-2 buffers with the variant extension still read normally.
- **No reverse-engineering claim:** SQLite's normative page expressly says applications should not use JSONB outside SQLite or try to reverse-engineer the format. The JSONB header details here are recorded because they are published by the linked normative page and the Glaze v8.3.0 implementation/docs; they do not turn SQLite's opaque internal format into a general-purpose interchange recommendation.

# BSON, MessagePack, and Glaze EETF fixture-wire evidence

**Capture date:** 2026-09-11  
**Scope:** official BSON 1.1 grammar, official MessagePack `master` specification, and the Glaze v8.3.0 EETF test's exact map argument/construction for `glz::eetf_to_json`.  
**Evidence status:** selected exact source text, type/tag values, and wire layouts are reproduced or mechanically normalized below. No bytes are derived, no fixture is constructed, and no encoder/decoder/runtime is run.

## Provenance and version identity

| Evidence | Canonical URL | Exact identity at capture | Locator / capture state |
|---|---|---|---|
| BSON specification | `https://bsonspec.org/spec.html` | Specification Version `1.1`; page title `BSON (Binary JSON): Specification`; page does not expose a release/tag beyond the displayed specification version | `Specification Version 1.1`, `Basic Types`, `Non-terminals`, `More Information`; selected int32/document/cstring grammar below; retrieved 2026-09-11 |
| MessagePack specification | `https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack/blob/master/spec.md` | Official `msgpack/msgpack`, branch `master`; source footer says `MessagePack specification`, last modified `2017-08-09 22:42:07 -0700`; no release/tag claim is made | `Formats > Overview`, `int format family`, `str format family`, `map format family`, `Serialization`; selected fixed-map/fixed-string/positive-fixint wire definitions below; retrieved 2026-09-11 |
| Glaze EETF test source | `https://github.com/stephenberry/glaze/blob/v8.3.0/tests/eetf_test/eetf_test.cpp` | Glaze `v8.3.0`, tag; release record identifies commit `dce5e0f7ec572725ec369a0bc59a00eeb2270a9a` | `eetf_to_json std::map` test; exact map type, initializer, `write_term`, `eetf_to_json` arguments, and expected JSON below; retrieved 2026-09-11 |

The BSON and MessagePack pages are normative/source-format evidence only. The Glaze test is evidence of the pinned test's argument/construction and expected converter output, not a claim that any runtime was exercised in this capture.

## BSON specification Version 1.1

### Basic type widths and byte order

The official page heading is `Specification Version 1.1`. It states that BSON is a binary format in which zero or more ordered key/value pairs are stored as one entity called a *document*. The page's Basic Types table states that each type is serialized in little-endian format:

| Type | Exact size / meaning |
|---|---|
| `signed_byte(n)` | 8-bit, two's-complement signed integer with value `n` |
| `unsigned_byte(n)` | 8-bit unsigned integer with value `n` |
| `int32` | 4 bytes, 32-bit signed integer, two's complement |
| `int64` | 8 bytes, 64-bit signed integer, two's complement |
| `uint64` | 8 bytes, 64-bit unsigned integer |
| `double` | 8 bytes, IEEE 754-2008 binary floating point |
| `decimal128` | 16 bytes, IEEE 754-2008 decimal floating point |

### Document, int32 element, and cstring grammar

The selected official grammar is:

```text
document ::= int32 e_list unsigned_byte(0)
```

The page defines `int32` here as the total number of bytes constituting the document. The element-list production is recursive and may be empty:

```text
e_list ::= element e_list
         | ""
```

The BSON element production for a 32-bit integer is:

```text
signed_byte(16) e_name int32
```

The page labels this “32-bit integer.” An element name is:

```text
e_name ::= cstring
```

A BSON string and cstring are:

```text
string  ::= int32 (byte*) unsigned_byte(0)
cstring ::= (byte*) unsigned_byte(0)
```

The page says the `string` `int32` is the number of bytes in `(byte*)` plus one for the trailing null byte; `(byte*)` is zero or more UTF-8 encoded characters. It says a `cstring` is zero or more modified UTF-8 encoded characters followed by a null byte, and `(byte*)` **MUST NOT** contain `unsigned_byte(0)`, so it is not full UTF-8.

For the requested document/key/value profile, the official grammar therefore identifies the document's total-length `int32`, the terminating `unsigned_byte(0)`, element type `signed_byte(16)` for an int32 value, a cstring key, and the four-byte little-endian int32 payload. This is a grammar inventory only; no bytes are calculated here.

### Other BSON element categories visible in the same grammar

The Version 1.1 page lists element type bytes for double `1`, string `2`, embedded document `3`, array `4`, binary `5`, undefined `6` (deprecated), ObjectId `7`, boolean `8`, UTC datetime `9`, null `10`, regular expression `11`, DBPointer `12` (deprecated), JavaScript `13`, Symbol `14` (deprecated), code-with-scope `15` (deprecated), int32 `16`, timestamp `17`, int64 `18`, decimal128 `19`, MinKey `-1`, and MaxKey `127`. The complete table and subtype grammar remain on the canonical page; the focused prerequisite here is int32/document/cstring.

### BSON compatibility boundary

The page labels Version 1.1 and marks several categories deprecated (`Undefined`, `DBPointer`, `Symbol`, and `Code with scope`). It also states that arrays are BSON documents with integer keys beginning at `0` and continuing sequentially. No BSON driver/runtime version, allocation behavior, or malformed-input behavior is inferred from this grammar page.

## MessagePack specification (`master`)

### Source identity and type-system limits

The official `msgpack/msgpack` `master` `spec.md` describes MessagePack as an object serialization specification like JSON. Its type system includes Integer, Nil, Boolean, Float, Raw/String, Binary, Array, Map, and Extension. The page states these limits:

- Integer values range from `-(2^63)` up to `(2^64)-1`.
- Maximum Binary length is `(2^32)-1`.
- Maximum String byte size is `(2^32)-1`.
- Maximum Array element count is `(2^32)-1`.
- Maximum Map key-value association count is `(2^32)-1`.
- String objects may contain invalid byte sequences; deserializer behavior then depends on the implementation.

The source footer is:

```text
MessagePack specification
Last modified at 2017-08-09 22:42:07 -0700
Sadayuki Furuhashi © 2013-04-21 21:52:33 -0700
```

This is an official `master` branch specification identity, not a release/tag claim.

### Fixed-map, fixed-string, and positive-fixint overview tags

The exact rows from the Formats > Overview table are:

```text
positive fixint | 0xxxxxxx  | 0x00 - 0x7f
fixmap          | 1000xxxx  | 0x80 - 0x8f
fixstr          | 101xxxxx  | 0xa0 - 0xbf
```

The same overview table assigns `0xc0` to nil, `0xc2` false, `0xc3` true, `0xcc`–`0xcf` to unsigned integers, `0xd0`–`0xd3` to signed integers, `0xd9`–`0xdb` to `str 8/16/32`, and `0xde`/`0xdf` to `map 16`/`map 32`.

### Positive-fixint

The exact int-family diagram states:

```text
positive fixint stores 7-bit positive integer
+--------+
|0XXXXXXX|
+--------+
```

The source defines `0XXXXXXX` as an 8-bit unsigned integer. The positive-fixint first byte therefore carries the value in its seven low bits and has no following payload bytes. This is the published format rule; no particular fixture value is encoded here.

### Fixed-map

The exact map-family description and diagram are:

```text
fixmap stores a map whose length is upto 15 elements
+--------+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~+
|1000XXXX|   N*2 objects   |
+--------+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~+
```

The source defines `XXXX` as a 4-bit unsigned integer representing `N`, `N` as the size of a map, odd elements as map keys, and the next element after a key as its associated value. The complete fixed-map layout is therefore one `fixmap` first byte followed by `N` key/value pairs, each key and value represented by its own MessagePack format.

For comparison, the same source defines `map 16` as `0xde` plus a 16-bit big-endian count and `map 32` as `0xdf` plus a 32-bit big-endian count; those extended forms are not needed for a map of one or two entries.

### Fixed-string

The exact string-family description and diagram are:

```text
fixstr stores a byte array whose length is upto 31 bytes:
+--------+========+
|101XXXXX|  data  |
+--------+========+
```

The source defines `XXXXX` as a 5-bit unsigned integer representing `N`, and `N` as the length of the data. `str 8` uses `0xd9` plus one unsigned-byte length, `str 16` uses `0xda` plus a 16-bit big-endian length, and `str 32` uses `0xdb` plus a 32-bit big-endian length. The focused prerequisite is the fixed-string form; no key bytes are calculated here.

The source's serialization table maps String to the str family (`fixstr` or `str 8/16/32`) and Map to the map family (`fixmap` or `map 16/32`). If multiple output formats are possible, serializers **SHOULD** use the smallest format; this is the MessagePack source's serializer guidance, not a recommendation added by this capture.

### Map/string fixture boundary

The official definitions identify the fields needed for a small map whose key is a short UTF-8/byte string and whose value is a positive integer: fixed-map count bits, fixed-string length bits/data, and positive-fixint value byte. This capture intentionally does not derive the resulting bytes or publish a fixture.

## Glaze v8.3.0 EETF test: exact map argument and construction

The tag-pinned test source includes:

```c++
#include "glaze/eetf/eetf_to_json.hpp"
#include "glaze/eetf/read.hpp"
#include "glaze/eetf/wrappers.hpp"
#include "glaze/eetf/write.hpp"
```

The exact `eetf_to_json std::map` test body is:

```c++
"eetf_to_json std::map"_test = [] {
   std::map<std::string, int> v = {{"first", 1}, {"second", 2}, {"third", 3}};
   std::string buffer{};
   expect(not glz::write_term(v, buffer));

   std::string json{};
   expect(!glz::eetf_to_json(buffer, json));
   expect(json == R"({"first":1,"second":2,"third":3})") << json;

   expect(!glz::eetf_to_json<glz::opts{.prettify = true}>(buffer, json));
   expect(json ==
          R"({
   "first": 1,
   "second": 2,
   "third": 3
})") << json;
};
```

The exact argument/ownership shapes visible in this test are:

- Input term construction: `std::map<std::string, int> v` with three initializer-list entries.
- EETF buffer construction: `std::string buffer{}` passed to `glz::write_term(v, buffer)`.
- JSON output construction: `std::string json{}` passed to `glz::eetf_to_json(buffer, json)`.
- Pretty option argument: `glz::eetf_to_json<glz::opts{.prettify = true}>(buffer, json)`.
- Expected compact JSON: `{"first":1,"second":2,"third":3}`.
- Expected pretty JSON has one key/value per line with three-space indentation, as shown in the exact source block.

The same test file contains `term_map_001`, a manually specified `std::array<std::uint8_t, 81>` EETF map fixture, and tests for `std::map<glz::eetf::atom, int>`. Those fixtures are not reproduced here because this lane only needs the exact `eetf_to_json` argument type/construction; no EETF bytes are derived or run.

This source test proves the pinned test's map construction and API call shape. It does not, by itself, establish a general EETF wire-to-JSON identity-preserving codec; the separate Erlang ETF capture records that Glaze's documented path is one-way ETF-to-JSON.

## Cross-format fixture boundary and evidence gaps

1. BSON Version 1.1 provides a little-endian `int32` document length, cstring key, type byte `16`, four-byte int32 value, and trailing document terminator grammar. No BSON bytes are calculated here.
2. MessagePack `master` provides fixed-map (`0x80–0x8f`), fixed-string (`0xa0–0xbf`), and positive-fixint (`0x00–0x7f`) tag definitions. No MessagePack bytes are calculated here.
3. The Glaze v8.3.0 test's exact map constructor is `std::map<std::string, int>` with `first/second/third` entries; the test does not contain an exact key named `count`. Therefore no claim is made that a source test directly constructs a `{"count":2}` map.
4. No compiler, dependency, runtime, SQLite, encoder, decoder, or byte-level execution was performed. No fixture hex is included.
5. BSON and MessagePack source pages do not establish Glaze-specific ownership/allocation/async behavior. The Glaze test establishes only the captured call/construction shape and expected test assertion.

## 2. Sema direct Core-use collection and closure

Source: `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Bundle/Validation/CoreUsage.rs`, SHA-256 `11c5ba16ba3717974fbc2cbddf7b140f49752fa206bdd33e6859b9c2ea08537e4`, lines 1-70.

Source same file, lines 72-514. `collect_used_core` initializes `used`, usage spans, and FFI callback set. If any module state has `exact_int_reachable`, it inserts `core.math::__exact_int__`. It walks every bundle module and its `ModuleState.core_imports`, adds `core.encoding::types` when annotations mention that surface, merges inline re-export/import aliases, then traverses function signatures/bodies, struct fields/methods/trait impls/validation blocks/CLI bindings, enum payloads/discriminants/methods/impls, impl methods/associated types, tests, constants, traits, extern Rust functions, distinct bases, error-conversion bodies, and nested code modules. Source same file, lines 579-704 and 721-761. ## 3. TIR Codable demand and generic method reachability

Source: `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/mod.rs`, SHA-256 `3d736f8ae61217e1cf535bfc3866df0f018511aec4993c39ac5284a825783088`, lines 1496-1610 and 1612-1792.

`collect_serde_codec_demands` walks every lowered TIR function body. It demands `encode` and `decode` for generic `Type::Apply` expression types; recursively walks calls, handle methods, `DecodeUnder`, `Try`, fallbacks, and Core calls. A `SerdeEncode` handle demands the receiver's encode; `DataTreeDecode(target)` demands target decode. Encoding Core calls (`core.encoding.json`, `.toml`, `.yaml`, `.csv`, `.cbor`) with `to_string`, `to_string_pretty`, `to_bytes`, or `to_bytes_canonical` demand encode for their first argument; encoding `decode` result types demand decode for the `ok` type (lines 1496-1610).

`lower_demanded_generic_methods` takes pending JIT method calls, adds these serde demands, processes stable instance keys once, checks generic depth, resolves owner declarations, specializes owner/method parameters, admits generated serde by `is_generated_serde` provenance or the normal TIR coverage gate, lowers the concrete method, gives it a stable key, then recursively collects nested codec demands from the lowered body (lines 1612-1792). The source explicitly says this is the path for generic generated Codable methods and that generated provenance is parser-unforgeable; no fallback implementation is claimed here.

Source same file, lines 5237-5284 and 11725-11729. TIR defines `SerdeCodec::{Encode,Decode}`; the doc says Encode bridges to `jet_encode(&self) -> jet_std::DataTree` and Decode bridges to static `jet_decode(tree: &jet_std::DataTree) -> Result<Self, Vec<FieldError>>`. TIR operation variants are `DataTreeDecode(Type)` and `SerdeEncode`.

## 4. Compile-time fragment callable closure and declaration pruning

Source same `TIR/mod.rs`, lines 2361-2414. `fragment_callable_closure` starts from expressions/statements, calls `collect_fragment_callable`, then follows a pending worklist. For each reachable function/method it calls `collect_fragment_function_dependencies`; newly found dependencies are inserted and queued. It returns a `BTreeSet<FragmentCallable>`.

Source same file, lines 2417-2464. `fragment_declaration_items` clones each `Impl`, `Struct`, or `Enum` and retains only methods whose `(owner,name)` appears in the reachable set; other item kinds are cloned unchanged.

Source same file, lines 2569-2595 and 2881-2904. The fragment builder uses the callable closure, includes reachable free functions, carries shape declarations, clears derives from fragment structures, and builds declarations from `fragment_declaration_items`. It skips unreachable functions and generic/`encode`/`decode` extras in the emitted fragment pass. These lines document source-level fragment pruning; they are not a claim about the whole-program artifact's function graph.

## 5. Runtime-part projection from Core-use labels

Source: `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/mod.rs`, SHA-256 `c98a6fbe2e8c4c68c2b280d6270208b171f80ae40e82563200ca3f3ae4b0bf95`, lines 1935-2050 (continuing source lines 2050 onward).

`runtime_parts_for_used_core(&BTreeSet<String>) -> BTreeSet<MirRuntimePartId>` defines the one lowering-time boundary that inspects legacy Core-use labels. Its `matches` closure accepts exact, `::`-prefixed, or `.`-prefixed labels. The visible mapping is:

- `core.event` → `Event`;
- `core.rt|core.realtime` → `Realtime`;
- `core.hardware|core.embedded|core.board|core.device` → `EmbeddedHardware`;
- `core.ui|core.font|core.web|app` → `Ui` and also `Devtools`;
- `core.ui::gtk_backend|core.ui.gtk_backend` → `Gtk`;
- app/web/http/db/sync/websocket/browser labels → `Apps`;
- `core.email` → `Email`;
- game/raylib labels → `Game`;
- files/watcher/term/sys/process labels → `Files`;
- interrupt-specific sys/process labels → `Interrupt`;
- files/watcher/term/sys/process/args/testing/perf/mem.scope labels → `FsRuntime`;
- `core.crypto` → `Crypto`;
- math/random/time/expiring/units labels → `Math`;
- encoding/json/jsonl/csv/toml/yaml/xml/cbor/hex/archive gzip/zstd labels → `Encoding` (lines 2026-2049 show this encoding set).

The function continues with additional mappings after line 2050; this capture records the exact visible encoding boundary but does not claim the remainder is exhaustively transcribed here. The source comment says runtime adapters consume typed IDs and do not reconstruct selection from strings.

## 6. Artifact planning and MIR projection

Source: `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/artifact_plan.rs`, SHA-256 `ed20c61ac7868269bb159a5911c0d614199a00c715082515110181161e98e03a`, lines 1745-1780. `lower_artifact_plan` creates an artifact key/kind/name/target, copies module/link/job keys, copies `bundle.used_core` labels directly into `runtime_parts`, lowers exports, and records provider/closure/artifact identities.

Source: `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/mir.rs`, SHA-256 `bbb9370daa3b3ab36f5e4eff26e7b16196f72e060930d74a122e9cc34bcafc36`.

- Lines 1441-1456 retain only impl rows whose method IDs resolve to executable function identities.
- Lines 2141-2172 project artifact links/jobs/runtime parts/exports; runtime parts come from `runtime_parts_for_used_core(&row.runtime_parts)` plus parsed typed runtime-part keys, and exports retain only function references resolvable through the registry.
- Lines 2674-2704 project package facts; package runtime parts come from `runtime_parts_for_used_core(&program.facts.used_core)`, and `uses_arrow` is set when `core.data.arrow` or a child label is present.

## 7. Native emission and link-closure output

Source: `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/MIRRust.rs`, SHA-256 `1c79b8a4b4ed7e4fe3181177f9ac3bcb7b415565f38fca93cb2c110bd10b11ad`, lines 475-580. Native emission computes `uses_arrow` from program facts or runtime part `Data`, resolves active OS, emits cached runtime and full Core Prelude using `emitter.artifact.runtime_parts`, conditionally emits the HTTP bridge for three reachable HTTP symbols, then emits selected types/traits/constants and calls `emitter.emit_link_closure()`.

Source same file, lines 6336-6388. `emit_link_closure` starts with an empty `BTreeSet`, visits each artifact link, and recursively emits each dependency before its parent. `emit_link_unit` deduplicates by ID, requires the ID to resolve to a MIR link row, panics if target applicability fails, prints link-unit/cache metadata and search paths, and emits object/static/dynamic/framework artifacts as Rust `#[link] extern "C" {}` declarations; generated-source artifacts are printed as comments. ## Exact release identity and dependencies

Sources:

- https://github.com/lunarmodules/luasec/blob/v1.3.2/README.md (`LuaSec 1.3.2` header and project description).
- https://github.com/lunarmodules/luasec/blob/v1.3.2/luasec-1.3.2-1.rockspec (`package`, `version`, `source`, `description`, `dependencies`, `external_dependencies`, and `build` blocks).

The exact README states: “LuaSec depends on OpenSSL, and integrates with LuaSocket to make it easy to add secure connections to any Lua applications or scripts.” The exact rockspec identifies `package = "LuaSec"`, `version = "1.3.2-1"`, source tag `v1.3.2`, and dependencies `"lua >= 5.1", "luasocket"`.

The exact rockspec declares OpenSSL as an external dependency. On Unix it names header `openssl/ssl.h` and library `ssl`; on Windows it names header `openssl/ssl.h`. The builtin build installs `ssl.so`/`ssl.dll`, Lua module `ssl.lua`, and module `ssl.https` from `src/https.lua`; it links OpenSSL `ssl` and `crypto` on Unix and `libssl`/`libcrypto` on Windows.

## TLS binding surface

Source: https://github.com/lunarmodules/luasec/blob/v1.3.2/src/ssl.lua (`_M` export block; `newcontext`, `wrap`, `loadcertificate`; `wrap(sock, cfg)` function).

The exact `ssl.lua` source exports `_VERSION = "1.3.2"`, `config`, `loadcertificate`, `newcontext`, and `wrap`. Its `wrap(sock, cfg)` function creates an SSL core object, takes the file descriptor from the supplied socket, invalidates the original socket descriptor, and returns the secure connection or an error message. The `newcontext` function creates/configures a context, loads key/certificate and CA locations when provided, applies cipher/verification/options settings, and handles ALPN/PSK/DANE configuration when configured by the input table.

These are source capabilities only. The capture does not assert that any particular OpenSSL version, certificate, platform, or Lua engine was exercised.

## HTTPS companion surface

Source: https://github.com/lunarmodules/luasec/blob/v1.3.2/src/https.lua (`_M` module table; `tcp(params)`; `request(url, body)`; export block).

The exact `https.lua` source exports `_VERSION = "1.3.2"`, `PORT = 443`, and `TIMEOUT = 60`. Its `tcp(params)` helper creates a LuaSocket TCP socket, connects it, wraps it with `ssl.wrap`, sets SNI and timeout, and performs `dohandshake`. Its `request(url, body)` helper accepts a URL string or table, builds the HTTPS URL/request, delegates HTTP transport to `socket.http`, and returns response data/code/headers/status. It explicitly returns `nil, "proxy not supported"` for proxy use, `nil, "redirect not supported"` for redirects, and `nil, "create function not permitted"` when a caller supplies a custom create function.

The exact rockspec maps the module name `ssl.https` to `src/https.lua`, establishing the HTTPS companion file in the requested release artifact.

## Exact HTTPS verification defaults and hostname handling

Sources:

- https://github.com/lunarmodules/luasec/blob/v1.3.2/src/https.lua (TLS configuration table and `tcp(params)`).
- https://github.com/lunarmodules/luasec/blob/v1.3.2/src/ssl.lua (`newcontext(cfg)`).
- https://github.com/lunarmodules/luasec/blob/v1.3.2/src/context.c (`set_verify_flag`, `load_locations`, and `set_verify`).
- https://github.com/lunarmodules/luasec/blob/v1.3.2/src/ssl.c (`meth_sni` and SSL method table).
- https://github.com/lunarmodules/luasec/blob/v1.3.2/src/x509.c (certificate method table).

The exact `https.lua` default configuration table is:

    local cfg = {
      protocol = "any",
      options  = {"all", "no_sslv2", "no_sslv3", "no_tlsv1"},
      verify   = "none",
    }

The exact `tcp(params)` source copies each default only when the corresponding parameter is absent (`params[k] = params[k] or v`), forces `params.mode = "client"`, and, after TCP connect, calls `ssl.wrap(self.sock, params)`, `self.sock:sni(host)`, and `self.sock:dohandshake()`.

The exact `ssl.lua` `newcontext(cfg)` source calls `context.locations(ctx, cfg.cafile, cfg.capath)` only when `cfg.cafile` or `cfg.capath` is present, then calls `context.setverify` with `cfg.verify`. The exact `context.c` source maps `"none"` to `SSL_VERIFY_NONE` and `"peer"` to `SSL_VERIFY_PEER`.

The exact `ssl.c` client `sni` method calls `SSL_set_tlsext_host_name(ssl->ssl, name)`. In the retrieved exact-tag files `src/ssl.c`, `src/x509.c`, `src/ssl.lua`, and `src/https.lua`, no `X509_check_host`, `checkhost`, `hostflags`, or `sethost` token was present. The captured source therefore records SNI transmission, but no exact-tag hostname-certificate matching call.

These are source-text facts only. No certificate-chain or hostname-validation handshake was run.

Source: https://github.com/lunarmodules/luasec/wiki/Home (page displayed as edited Oct 10, 2019; retrieved 2026-09-11; linked by the exact release README/rockspec).

The wiki describes LuaSec as an OpenSSL binding for TLS/SSL communication that takes an established TCP connection and creates a secure session. Its examples use `require("socket")`, `require("ssl")`, `socket.tcp()`, `ssl.wrap(conn, params)`, `conn:dohandshake()`, and `conn:close()`. Example configuration fields include `mode`, `protocol`, `key`, `certificate`, `cafile`, `verify`, and `options`.

The wiki page is not labeled as version 1.3.2; it is retained only as official documentation context. The exact-tag source files above are the version-pinned API evidence.

```rust
    /// Resolve one canonical export from a statically known plugin interface.
    ///
    /// The old homogeneous `.call*` conveniences are intentionally absent:
    /// each source method name is an interface export, and its complete
    /// parameter/result contract is checked here before TIR sees the call.
    pub(crate) fn check_plugin_method(
        &mut self,
        method: &str,
        interface: Option<&PluginInterface>,
        args: &mut [crate::AST::CallArg],
        span: Span,
    ) -> Option<Option<Type>> {
        self.record_effect(Effect::Exec.name(), span);

        if matches!(method, "call" | "call_int" | "call_bool" | "call_text") {
            self.diags.push(Diagnostic::error(
                "E1257",
                format!("`Plugin.{method}` is retired"),
                "plugin handles expose the frozen named exports of their registered Component interface"
                    .to_string(),
                "write the plugin's exported method directly, for example `plugin.index(rows)`"
                    .to_string(),
                Some(span),
            ));
            self.infer_plugin_args(args);
            return Some(Some(result_ty(Type::String, Type::String)));
        }

        let Some(interface) = interface else {
            self.plugin_method_diagnostic(method, None, span);
            self.infer_plugin_args(args);
            return Some(Some(result_ty(Type::String, Type::String)));
        };
        let Some(export) = interface.exports.get(method) else {
            self.plugin_method_diagnostic(method, Some(interface), span);
            self.infer_plugin_args(args);
            return Some(Some(result_ty(Type::String, Type::String)));
        };

        let result = self.check_plugin_export(export, args, span);
        let result = result.map(|ty| self.resolve_type(ty)).unwrap_or_else(|| {
            Type::Named(crate::Syntax::INTERNAL_UNIT_TYPE.to_string())
        });
        Some(Some(result_ty(result, Type::String)))
    }
```

```rust
//!
//! Resolution is intentionally local and offline. Inline dependencies use a
//! committed or explicitly materialized local source tree, not an implicit
//! registry network request:
//!
//!   1. `<script_dir>/.jet/inline-deps/<name>/<version>/` — a committed (or
//!      previously `jet fetch --lock`-populated) local copy. `.jet/` is the existing
//!      managed-folder convention (`.jet/lock`, `.jet/inline-deps`).
//!   2. `JET_INLINE_DEPS_FIXTURES=<dir>` — an offline test/dev override with
//!      the same `<name>/<version>/` shape, checked only when the env var is
//!      set (mirrors Jetpack's own `JETPACK_FIXTURES` test convention).
//!
//! Anything else is E1253 — an honest unresolved dependency, never a fake
//! success (I2/I3).
```
