# C++23 / GCC 14.2 and Rust 1.85.0 scripting context

## Capture metadata

- Retrieval date: 2026-09-11.
- Scope: official, version-pinned documentation and source inventory for command-line entry, process invocation, native/shared-library boundaries, typed JSON, and package/toolchain surfaces.
- Capture state: documentary evidence only. No compiler, linker, Cargo, process, JSON, or shared-library execution was performed.
- Exact-version rule: an unavailable exact-version statement is recorded as a gap. No later-version documentation is substituted.

## C++23 working-draft surface and GCC 14.2

### C++23 source identity and command-line entry

Primary source: WG21 N4950, *Working Draft, Standard for Programming Language C++*, Document Number N4950, dated 2023-05-10:
<https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2023/n4950.pdf>

Locator: §6.9.3.1 `[basic.start.main]` (PDF text). The draft states that a program contains exactly one function named `main` in the global scope, and that executing a program starts a main thread in which `main` is invoked. The accepted function forms include a function taking `int` and a pointer to pointer to `char` and returning `int` (the draft's wording is “function of (int, pointer to pointer to char) returning int”).

Locator: §6.6 `[basic.link]`. The draft states that a name with external linkage can be referred to by names from other translation units. Its linkage example includes `extern "C" void h();` and identifies this as C language linkage. This is the captured C/C++ ABI boundary evidence; no native extension ABI policy is inferred from it.

Capture limit: N4950 identifies itself as a working draft and is explicitly an early/incomplete draft, not a final ISO publication. The capture does not establish a final C++23 publication's wording.

### GCC 14.2 compiler and native shared-object surface

Release identity: GCC's official GCC 14 release page records GCC 14.2 released on 2024-08-01 and links the versioned manuals at `14.2.0`:
<https://gcc.gnu.org/gcc-14/>

Versioned manual index:
<https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-14.2.0/gcc/>

Locator: *Invoking G++*, §3.3 “Compiling C++ Programs”:
<https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-14.2.0/gcc/Invoking-G_002b_002b.html>

- The manual identifies `.C`, `.cc`, `.cpp`, `.CPP`, `.c++`, `.cp`, and `.cxx` as C++ source suffixes.
- `g++` calls GCC and automatically specifies linking with the C++ library; `gcc` does not automatically add the C++ library.

Locator: *Link Options*, §3.15 “Options for Linking”:
<https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-14.2.0/gcc/Link-Options.html>

- `-shared` produces a shared object that can subsequently be linked with other objects to form an executable. The manual notes that the option is not supported on every system and that code should be compiled with the same `-fpic`/`-fPIC` model (or target-specific equivalent) used for the shared object.
- `-l library` searches for a library; on supported targets shared libraries usually use the `lib*.so` naming form.
- `-rdynamic` passes `-export-dynamic` to an ELF linker and can be needed for some `dlopen` uses and backtraces.

Locator: *Code Generation Options*, entries `-fpic` and `-fPIC`:
<https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-14.2.0/gcc/Code-Gen-Options.html>

- `-fpic` generates position-independent code suitable for a shared library when the target supports it.
- `-fPIC` emits position-independent code suitable for dynamic linking and avoids a global-offset-table size limit on targets where the distinction matters.

### GCC dialect capture limit

Locator: *C Dialect Options*, §2.2 “C++ Language”:
<https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-14.2.0/gcc/Standards.html>

The retrieved GCC 14.2 manual describes C++ language standards through C++20 and records the default without a dialect option as `-std=gnu++17`; it does not contain a C++23 or `-std=c++23` statement. This packet therefore records GCC 14.2 compiler/linker documentation and does **not** claim an exact GCC 14.2 C++23 mode from that manual. No later GCC manual was substituted.

### C++ process invocation capture limit

The N4950 capture above establishes program entry but did not yield the final C++23 `<cstdlib>` `system` wording. The current generated C++ draft synopsis at <https://eel.is/c++draft/cstdlib.syn> declares `int system(const char* string);`, but that page is an unversioned current draft (generated 2026-08-23), not exact C++23 evidence. It is not used as a C++23 claim. Exact-version C++23 process-invocation behavior remains an evidence gap.

## Rust 1.85.0 surface

### Version identity

Primary release source: Rust Release Team, “Announcing Rust 1.85.0 and Rust 2024,” 2025-02-20:
<https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/20/Rust-1.85.0/>

The release page identifies Rust 1.85.0 and Rust 2024 as stabilized and links the versioned release notes:
<https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/releases.html#version-1850-2025-02-20>

All Reference and standard-library URLs below use the exact `1.85.0` path.

### Command-line entry and arguments

Reference locator: `[main functions]`:
<https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.85.0/reference/crates-and-source-files.html#main-functions>

- A crate containing `main` can be compiled to an executable.
- If present, `main` takes no arguments; its return type must implement `Termination`.
- The page examples include `fn main() {}` and returning `std::process::ExitCode`.

Standard-library locator: `std::env::args`:
<https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.85.0/std/env/fn.args.html>

`pub fn args() -> Args` returns the arguments with which the program was started, normally from the command line. The first item is traditionally the executable path but may be arbitrary or absent. The documentation records Unix shell glob expansion, Windows differences, and the Unicode panic behavior; `args_os` is the documented alternative when non-Unicode arguments must be retained.

### Child-process invocation

Standard-library locator: `std::process::Command`:
<https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.85.0/std/process/struct.Command.html>

`Command` is documented as a process builder for fine-grained control of a spawned process. `Command::new(program)` sets the executable path; `.arg` and `.args` add arguments; `.spawn`, `.status`, and `.output` launch or wait for the child. The documented defaults inherit environment, current directory, and standard streams for `spawn`/`status`, while `output` pipes output. Arguments are passed as arguments rather than being interpreted by a shell; the page separately documents platform-specific Windows `cmd.exe`/batch-file caveats and untrusted-argument concerns.

### Native ABI and dynamic-library boundary

Reference locator: external blocks, `ABI` and `#[link]` sections:
<https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.85.0/reference/items/external-blocks.html#abi>

- External blocks declare foreign functions and statics for Rust FFI; calls to foreign functions are unsafe.
- The default external-block ABI is the platform's standard C ABI. The page lists cross-platform ABI strings including `unsafe extern "C"` and `unsafe extern "system"`; Rust 2024 requires `unsafe extern` blocks.
- `#[link]` supports native-library kinds including dynamic `dylib` (the default), `static`, `framework`, and Windows `raw-dylib`.

Reference locator: crate types and linkage:
<https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.85.0/reference/linkage.html>

- `--crate-type=bin` produces a runnable executable and requires `main`.
- `--crate-type=dylib` produces a dynamic Rust library (`.so`, `.dylib`, or `.dll` by platform).
- `--crate-type=staticlib` produces a static system library for linking Rust into an existing non-Rust application.
- `--crate-type=cdylib` produces a dynamic system library intended to be loaded from another language (`.so`, `.dylib`, or `.dll` by platform).

These are reference/toolchain declarations only; no Rust library or ABI was built or loaded for this capture.

### Cargo run and lockfile surface

Versioned command reference: `cargo run`:
<https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.85.0/cargo/commands/cargo-run.html>

The synopsis is `cargo run [options] [-- args]`. The command runs a binary or example of the local package; arguments after `--` are passed to that binary, and the binary's current directory is the current directory. The `--locked` option requires the existing `Cargo.lock` and errors if dependency resolution would change it; the page also records `--offline` and `--frozen` modes.

Versioned Cargo guide: `Cargo.toml vs Cargo.lock`:
<https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.85.0/cargo/guide/cargo-toml-vs-cargo-lock.html>

- `Cargo.toml` declares dependency requirements and is written by the package author.
- `Cargo.lock` records exact dependency information, is maintained by Cargo, and is not manually edited.
- The guide documents the lock file's reproducibility role, including exact commit SHAs for git dependencies, and states that `cargo update` recalculates dependencies and updates the lock.

## Go 1.24.1

### `go run`

- Source: `https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.24.1/src/cmd/go/internal/run/run.go`
- Ref: `golang/go` branch/tag `go1.24.1`; retrieved `2026-09-11`.
- Locator: package comment and `CmdRun` command definition (`UsageLine`, `Short`, `Long`).
- Capture: complete requested source file; no commit SHA exposed by the GitHub reader; no command invocation.

The exact command definition documents:

> `go run [build flags] [-exec xprog] package [arguments...]`

> Run compiles and runs the named main Go package.
>
> Typically the package is specified as a list of .go source files from a single directory, but it may also be an import path, file system path, or pattern matching a single known package, as in 'go run .' or 'go run my/cmd'.

The same `CmdRun` text documents these boundaries:

- A package version suffix such as `@latest` or `@v1.0.0` uses module-aware mode while ignoring a `go.mod` in the current directory or a parent directory.
- Without a version suffix, module-aware or GOPATH mode depends on `GO111MODULE` and `go.mod` presence; module-aware execution is in the context of the main module.
- By default the compiled binary is run directly; `-exec xprog` runs it through `xprog`.
- The `go run` command's exit status is not the exit status of the compiled binary.
- By default the binary is compiled without debugger information; the source says to use `go build` to include it. This is recorded as source text, not as a recommendation from this packet.

### `os/exec`

- Source: `https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.24.1/src/os/exec/exec.go`
- Ref: `golang/go` branch/tag `go1.24.1`; retrieved `2026-09-11`.
- Locators: package comment; `Command`; `CommandContext`; `Cmd` fields (`Path`, `Args`, `Env`, `Dir`, standard streams, `WaitDelay`); `Cmd.Run`, `Cmd.Start`, `Cmd.Wait`.
- Capture: complete requested source file; no runtime process launch.

The package comment states:

> Package exec runs external commands. It wraps os.StartProcess to make it easier to remap stdin and stdout, connect I/O with pipes, and do other adjustments.

> Unlike the "system" library call from C and other languages, the os/exec package intentionally does not invoke the system shell and does not expand any glob patterns or handle other expansions, pipelines, or redirections typically done by shells.

The same source documents:

- `Command(name, arg...)` sets `Path` and `Args`; if `name` has no path separator, it uses `LookPath` to resolve the name where possible. `Args[0]` is the command name, not a resolved path.
- `CommandContext` is like `Command` with a context. If the context finishes before the command, the documented default cancellation calls `Kill` on the process; the caller may modify cancellation behavior before starting it.
- `Env == nil` uses the current environment; an empty `Dir` uses the caller's current directory; `Dir` otherwise controls the child working directory. Standard streams can be connected through the documented `Stdin`, `Stdout`, and `Stderr` fields.
- `Run` starts and waits, returning nil only when the command completes with zero exit status and stream copying has no problem; a started non-successful command returns an `*ExitError`.
- `Start` starts without waiting, sets `Process` on success, and requires a later `Wait` to release associated resources. `Wait` waits for process exit and stream-copy completion and releases resources.
- `Command` and `LookPath` return an error satisfying `errors.Is(err, ErrDot)` when resolution would rely on an implicit or explicit path entry relative to the current directory under the documented Go 1.19-and-later behavior. The source documents an explicit `./prog` path as the way to request a current-directory program; this packet does not evaluate that behavior.

### `encoding/json`

- Sources: `https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.24.1/src/encoding/json/encode.go` and `https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.24.1/src/encoding/json/decode.go`
- Ref: `golang/go` branch/tag `go1.24.1`; retrieved `2026-09-11`.
- Locators: package comment; `Marshal` in `encode.go`; `Unmarshal` in `decode.go`.
- Capture: both requested source files complete; no serialization/deserialization run.

The package source says it implements JSON as defined in RFC 7159 and describes the mapping between JSON and Go values through `Marshal` and `Unmarshal`.

`Marshal` documentation records:

- It returns the JSON encoding of a value and traverses that value recursively.
- A non-nil value implementing `Marshaler` supplies `MarshalJSON`; otherwise `encoding.TextMarshaler` may supply text for a JSON string.
- Arrays and slices encode as JSON arrays, with `[]byte` as a base64 string and a nil slice as `null`.
- Struct values encode as objects; exported fields become members unless omitted, and `json` struct tags customize field encoding. Maps encode as objects when keys are strings, integer types, or `encoding.TextMarshaler` implementations.
- Channel, complex, and function values cannot be encoded and produce `UnsupportedTypeError`; cyclic data is not handled and produces an error.

`Unmarshal` documentation records:

- It parses JSON into the value pointed to by `v`; nil or non-pointer `v` returns `InvalidUnmarshalError`.
- It uses the inverse of the `Marshal` encodings, allocating maps, slices, and pointers as necessary.
- For structs it matches incoming keys to field names or tags, preferring exact matches while accepting case-insensitive matches. Unknown object keys are ignored by default; `Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields` is documented as the alternative.
- Syntax errors return `SyntaxError`. Inappropriate values or numbers that overflow a target type are skipped as far as possible, with an `UnmarshalTypeError` for the earliest such error when no more serious error occurs.
- Invalid UTF-8 and invalid UTF-16 surrogate pairs in quoted strings are replaced by U+FFFD rather than treated as an error.

- Sources: `https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/v1.9.1/README.md` and `https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/spf13/cobra@v1.9.1`
- Ref: `spf13/cobra` tag `v1.9.1`; retrieved `2026-09-11`.

The tagged README defines Cobra as a Go library with a structure of commands, arguments, and flags. Its documented surface includes:

- Commands can have child commands and an optional action.
- Subcommand-based interfaces and nested subcommands are supported.
- Flags include POSIX short and long forms, and may be global, local, or cascading to child commands.
- Help generation, help-flag recognition (`-h`, `--help`, and similar), shell autocomplete generation (bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell), man-page generation, command aliases, and custom help/usage definitions are listed.

The README is a project overview and example document; the bullets above are source inventory only and do not assert behavior observed at runtime.

## Java 21

### Single-source `java` launcher

- Source: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/man/java.html`
- Source identity: Oracle Java SE/JDK `21` documentation (`release: 21`); retrieved `2026-09-11`.
- Locators: `#synopsis`, `#description`, and `#using-source-file-mode-to-launch-single-file-source-code-programs`.
- Capture: requested launcher sections captured from the Java 21 page; no Java launch or compilation.

The synopsis documents:

> `java` [*options*] *mainclass* [*args* ...]
>
> `java` [*options*] `-jar` *jarfile* [*args* ...]
>
> `java` [*options*] `-m` *module*[`/`*mainclass*] [*args* ...]
>
> `java` [*options*] *source-file* [*args* ...]

The page states that source-file mode is selected when the class argument identifies an existing `.java` file or `--source` is specified; the source file is compiled and run. In this mode:

- The effect is documented as compiling the source into memory.
- The first top-level class found is executed, and it must contain `public static void main(String[])`.
- No other source files are found or compiled, as if the source path were empty.
- The source is compiled in an unnamed module, and annotation processing is disabled as if `-proc:none`.
- `--source N` selects the accepted source/API version.
- Source errors are written to standard error and the launcher exits non-zero.
- Arguments after the source file are passed to the main class.

### `ProcessBuilder`

- Source: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/ProcessBuilder.html`
- Source identity: Java SE/JDK `21` API documentation; retrieved `2026-09-11`.
- Locators: class description; `start()`; `startPipeline(java.util.List)`; process-attribute list; `redirectErrorStream(boolean)`.
- Capture: targeted sections from the 865-line page; not a complete-page transcript; no process start.

The API page documents that each `ProcessBuilder` manages process attributes and that `start()` creates a `Process`; `start()` may be invoked repeatedly on one builder to create subprocesses with identical or related attributes. The documented attributes are:

- a system-dependent command list containing the external program and arguments;
- an environment mapping initially copied from the current process environment;
- a working directory defaulting to the current directory;
- standard input, which by default is a pipe read by the subprocess;
- standard output and standard error, which by default are pipes written by the subprocess and can be redirected;
- `redirectErrorStream`, initially false, which can merge standard error into standard output when true.

The page also documents `startPipeline` for creating processes whose output is sent directly to the next process. Most error checking is performed by `start()`, and an empty command list may not fail until `start()`. The class is not synchronized; concurrent structural modification requires external synchronization. The page includes a warning that using this type with untrusted data is a security risk.

### JNI

- Sources: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/jni/index.html`, `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/jni/intro.html`, and `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/jni/design.html`
- Source identity: Oracle Java SE/JDK `21` JNI specification; retrieved `2026-09-11`.
- Locators: JNI specification contents; `intro.html` introduction and native-method/Invocation API list; `design.html` JNI interface functions and pointers, native-library loading, and `RegisterNatives` discussion.
- Capture: contents page and targeted introduction/design sections captured; no native compilation, linking, loading, or VM invocation.

The introduction states:

> The JNI is a native programming interface. It allows Java code that runs inside a Java Virtual Machine (VM) to interoperate with applications and libraries written in other programming languages, such as C, C++, and assembly.

The same specification lists native-method capabilities to create, inspect, and update Java objects (including arrays and strings), call Java methods, catch and throw exceptions, load classes and obtain class information, and perform runtime type checking. It also documents use of the Invocation API by an arbitrary native application to embed the Java VM.

The design section documents that native code accesses VM features through JNI functions and an interface pointer valid only on the current thread. Native methods are loaded with `System.loadLibrary`; the page gives platform filename mappings such as Linux `libp_q_r_A.so` and Windows `p_q_r_A.dll`. The contents page lists reference management, object/string/array access, method and field calls, exception handling, native registration, Java VM interface, and Invocation API operations including create, attach, detach, and destroy VM. The source warns that `RegisterNatives` can change documented JVM behavior; this is recorded as a documented warning, not as an evaluated scenario.

### Jackson Databind 2.18.3

- Source: `https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-databind/blob/jackson-databind-2.18.3/README.md`
- Ref: `FasterXML/jackson-databind` tag `jackson-databind-2.18.3`; retrieved `2026-09-11`.
- Locators: README project description, `## Maven`, `## Compatibility`, `## Tutorial`, tree-model, and streaming sections.
- Capture: complete requested README; no Maven resolution, Java execution, JSON processing, or runtime compatibility probe. GitHub wrapper did not expose a commit SHA.

The tagged README states that the project contains general-purpose data-binding and a tree model, builds on the Jackson Streaming API, and uses Jackson Annotations for configuration. It documents:

- `ObjectMapper` construction and reuse, `readValue` from a file, URL, or JSON string, and `writeValue` to a file, byte array, or string.
- `readTree` returning a `JsonNode` tree.
- A streaming model based on incremental processing, exposed through `JsonParser` and `JsonGenerator`.
- Functionality in Java package `com.fasterxml.jackson.databind`, with dependencies on `jackson-core` and `jackson-annotations` when using a build tool.
- Compatibility text stating that versions `2.13` and above require JDK 8, and that Jackson `2.10` and above include `module-info.class` definitions for JPMS.

Version limit: although the file is from the `jackson-databind-2.18.3` tag, its Maven tutorial sample sets `<jackson.version>` to `2.17.1`. That sample is preserved as README content but is not evidence of a `2.18.3` Maven declaration.

It lists SDK `9.0.201` and `9.0.104` as SDKs included in `9.0.3` runtimes, states that the .NET SDK includes a matching updated .NET Runtime, and gives sample `dotnet --version` output `9.0.201`. The release note also lists runtime binaries and checksums for Windows, macOS, and Linux. Those availability statements are release-note evidence only; no artifact was downloaded or checked.

### `dotnet run`

- Source: `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-run`
- Source identity: Microsoft Learn current/live CLI article retrieved `2026-09-11`; article metadata says it applies to `.NET 6 SDK and later` and was updated `2026-09-08`.
- Locators: command synopsis/description, project context, arguments, restore/build, and launch-profile sections.
- Capture: first 300 of 417 rendered lines with target sections; current/live docs are not patch-pinned to `.NET 9.0.3`; no command run.

The article documents:

- `dotnet run` runs source code without an explicit compile or launch command and is used in the context of projects, not built assemblies.
- It depends on `dotnet build`; build requirements apply to `dotnet run`.
- Dependencies outside the shared runtime are resolved from the NuGet cache, and implicit restore runs unless `--no-restore` is supplied.
- Options include `--project`, `--framework`, `--runtime`, `--no-build`, `--no-restore`, and `--self-contained`.
- Arguments not recognized by `dotnet run` are passed to the application; a literal `--` separates application arguments.
- `Properties/launchSettings.json` profiles can use `Project` (build project and start the command) or `Executable` (start the command at `executablePath`).

### `ProcessStartInfo` and `ArgumentList`

- Sources: `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.processstartinfo?view=net-9.0` and `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.processstartinfo.argumentlist?view=net-9.0`
- Source identity: Microsoft Learn ranged/current API pages with a `net-9.0` view; retrieved `2026-09-11`. Page metadata can default to newer monikers, so these are not patch-pinned to `9.0.3`.
- Locators: `ProcessStartInfo` class description and property list; `ArgumentList` property description.
- Capture: targeted class/property sections; no process start.

The API docs state that `ProcessStartInfo` is used with the `Process` component and that `FileName` must be set at minimum. They document properties for command arguments, environment, working directory, standard-stream redirection, and shell execution. `UseShellExecute` controls whether the operating-system shell starts the process; when false, the new process inherits standard streams unless redirection properties are set true. The class page also warns that using the type with untrusted data is a security risk.

The `ArgumentList` page states:

> Gets a collection of command-line arguments to use when starting the application. Strings added to the list don't need to be previously escaped.

The same page documents that `ArgumentList` and `Arguments` are independent and only one can be used at a time, and that `ArgumentList` escapes provided arguments while internally building the single string passed to the operating system. It repeats the untrusted-data security warning.

- Sources: `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.text.json.jsonserializer?view=net-9.0` and `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.text.json.jsonserializer.serialize?view=net-9.0`
- Source identity: Microsoft Learn ranged/current API pages with `net-9.0` views; retrieved `2026-09-11`. Current package/page metadata is newer than the requested patch in places, so no `System.Text.Json` package version `9.0.3` is asserted.
- Locators: `JsonSerializer` class description and `Serialize` method table/overloads.
- Capture: targeted class and method sections; no serialization run.

The class documentation states:

> Provides functionality to serialize objects or value types to JSON and to deserialize JSON into objects or value types.

The method table documents `Serialize` overloads that convert an object/value to a JSON string, write UTF-8 JSON to a `Stream`, or accept a specified type and `JsonSerializerOptions`; generic overloads and asynchronous stream overloads are also listed.

### `System.Runtime.InteropServices.NativeLibrary`

- Source: `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.interopservices.nativelibrary?view=net-9.0`
- Source identity: Microsoft Learn ranged/current API page with a `net-9.0` view; retrieved `2026-09-11`. Page metadata defaults to a newer moniker in places and does not patch-pin `9.0.3`.
- Locators: `NativeLibrary` class description and method table.
- Capture: targeted class/method sections; no native library load or symbol lookup.

The class documentation states:

> Provides APIs for managing native libraries.

The method table lists:

- `Load(String)`, a simple API for loading a native library that wraps the operating-system loader and uses default flags;
- `TryLoad(...)`, which loads a library and returns success status;
- `GetExport(IntPtr, String)`, which gets the address of an exported symbol;
- `TryGetExport(...)`, which gets an export and returns success status;
- `Free(IntPtr)`, which frees a loaded library using its operating-system handle; and
- `SetDllImportResolver(Assembly, DllImportResolver)`, which sets a callback for resolving native-library imports.

## Serde 1.0.219

- Source identity: docs.rs Serde API index.
- Version: `1.0.219`.
- Canonical URL: https://docs.rs/serde/1.0.219/serde/
- Exact body excerpt: `Serde is a framework for serializing and deserializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.` The page says data structures and data formats interact through Serde.
- Exact design excerpt: Serde is based on Rust's trait system; `Serialize` and `Deserialize` are the central traits; derive attributes generate implementations at compile time; Serde does not use runtime reflection or type information and its machinery is often optimized away.
- Exact module/trait index: modules `de`, `ser`; traits `Deserialize`, `Deserializer`, `Serialize`, `Serializer`.
- Exact format list caveat: the page gives a partial community list including JSON, Postcard, CBOR, YAML, MessagePack, TOML, Pickle, RON, BSON, Avro, JSON5, URL query, Starlark, Envy, Envy Store, S-expressions, D-Bus, FlexBuffers, Bencode, token streams, DynamoDB Items, Hjson, and CSV, and explicitly labels it a partial list.
- Exact constraints: derive is compile-time; no runtime reflection/type info. The docs index does not provide a complete export/default/error/ownership/allocation/async/platform inventory for every module item.

# Value-law inventory: plugin, reload, failure, lifecycle, and budgets

## Capture metadata

- Retrieval date: `2026-09-11`.
- This packet was written from bounded local reads at UTC `2026-09-11T22:03:21Z`.
- Local source identity: dirty working-tree source inspected on `2026-09-11`; the shared baseline recorded by the scripting campaign is `f119f2041adfd25b2810e813d21a71050cf94bb6`; it is not a clean-tree identity.
- Scope: exact existing ratified decision/card references and local public/spec/source anchors for five requested value-closure categories. The read set was limited to `docs/spec/spec.md`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md`, `docs/spec/architecture.md`, `docs/spec/reference/canvas-protocol.md`, scripting/runtime/compiler source, and the existing scripting campaign records.

  - **Ratified** = the cited decision text states a ratified/shipped decision and its card/date when the entry supplies one.

  - **Not located** = the item was not found in the bounded read set; this is not a repository-wide absence claim.

## 1. Host source preparation and load/call APIs

### Ratified entries

- `D-PLUGIN1 / D-DEP-WASM1` is the application-plugin substrate. The decision text records `target: plugin` as a sandboxed WASM Component Model module with typed `.wit`, safe-by-default operation, homogeneous `Int`/`Float`/`Bool`/`Text` exports, deny-by-default effects, `.wit` emission, `wasm-tools` lifting, host loading through `core.plugin`, version compatibility checks, and Jet diagnostics `E1257`–`E1260` (`docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:3042-3050`). The captured entry does not state a card number. The entry distinguishes application plugins from compiler extensions and PATH helpers.
- `D-ONCE-SANDBOX1=A` is in the say-it-once slate, ratified `2026-08-07`, card `#1656`; it states that the isolated package kind is `target: sandbox` and `target: plugin` retires as a rename (`docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:6688-6697`).
- `D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1 (=A, shipped c81)` states that top-level entry-file `pub fn` items form the exported surface; each v1 export uses one homogeneous `Int`, `Float`, `Bool`, or `Text` shape; the manifest `export:` field names the surface and defaults to the package name; `Sema::ApiFreeze` freezes the public-metadata snapshot; `.wit` is generated from those signatures; there is no source keyword (`docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:3482-3489`).
- `D-PLUGIN-VERSION1 (=A, shipped c81)` states structural load-time compatibility through the `ApiFreeze` snapshot keyed as `plugin__<export>` in `.jet/cache/api/`; unchanged interfaces load, while an incompatible change is `E1257` naming the interface delta (`docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:3490-3495`).
- The package/reference walkthrough records source preparation: `jet build main.jet --target=sandbox` emits `.wit` and wasm32 guest Rust, invokes `rustc --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --crate-type cdylib`, then `wasm-tools component embed` and `component new`, producing a `.wasm` Component (`docs/spec/spec.md:4494-4499`).
- The same walkthrough records host loading and call examples and the historical typed instance spellings (`Plugin.load`, `.call`, `.call_int`, `.call_bool`, `.call_text`) (`docs/spec/spec.md:4501-4518`). The current sema source below records retirement of those homogeneous convenience methods.
- `D-DX5-HOOK1=A`, ratified `2026-07-14`, card `#549`, is a distinct compiler-extension boundary with a compiler-specific `compiler-extension-v1` world, not the application `core.plugin`/`target: sandbox` surface (`docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:3057-3077`).

### Present public/spec/source anchors

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.jet:77` registers `module core.plugin exports { load } depends_on [core.files, core.process]`; `:278` maps `core.plugin load` to the Prelude symbol `jet_plugin_load` and marks it without direct AOT/JIT lowering. These are the directly read public registry/dispatcher rows.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/HandlesRaylib.rs:37-46` defines `JetPlugin` as a thin `Clone, Copy` wrapper around a `u64` handle. The comments state that the live wasmtime `Store`/`Instance` stay in the FFI bridge's thread-local map and that receiver-type dispatch supplies plugin methods.
- Current sema checking is in `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib/plugin_checks.rs:120-164`. It resolves an export from a statically known `PluginInterface`, checks recursively closed Component Model types and arity, and returns a checked `T ! String` shape. It explicitly diagnoses `Plugin.call`, `call_int`, `call_bool`, and `call_text` as retired with `E1257` (`:134-145`), then resolves the method name as a registered named export (`:148-163`). Unsupported Component shapes are `E1260` (`:81-112`).
- Runtime-side source identity and constants are in `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Plugin.rs:1-27,44-89`. The file comments identify `D-DEP-WASM1=A`, a runtime-side wasmtime Component loader, canonical authority, no-follow `FS.Read` root, zero-grant behavior when no capability is declared, thread-local `u64` handles, and handle `0` as an error sentinel. Constants are fuel `10_000_000`, memory `16 MiB`, table elements `10_000`, wire bytes `16 MiB`, and call timeout `2,000 ms` (`:44-48`); `plugin_limits` applies a memory-size cap, table-element cap, and one-instance/one-memory/one-table limits (`:82-89`).
- Host-import preparation is present in current source: `plugin_host_import_call` checks the stored authority decision and dispatches `FS.Read`, `FS.Write`, `Net.Connect`, or `Exec` (`crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Plugin.rs:674-702`); `plugin_register_function` requires a declared authority need and an allowed decision (`:705-738`); recursive import registration walks Component functions/instances (`:741-830`).
- `jet_plugin_load_declared` parses the authority wire, requires an allowed `FS.Read` load decision, reads/compiles the Component, registers/preflights imports, creates a limited store, and instantiates (`crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Plugin.rs:866-931`). A successful instance is put in the thread-local map as a `PluginInstance` and returns `O:<handle>` (`:932-957`).
- `jet_plugin_call` checks the handle, reuses the load-time authority decision, rejects over-limit parameter wire, resolves the named export, decodes and checks argument count/types, resets fuel and epoch/timer limits, requires exactly one supported result, and calls the Component function (`crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Plugin.rs:974-1087`). It copies the result before `post_return`, runs `post_return` before another call, enforces the result wire cap, and returns `O:<wire>` or `E:<message>` (`:1088-1112`).
- `jet_plugin_close` is present as a runtime-side function that removes a handle from the thread-local map and returns `true` only when a live entry was removed (`crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Plugin.rs:968-972`). Its public `core.plugin` registry row is not present beside `load` in the directly read `Core.jet` rows.
- JIT/interpreter bridge anchors are in `crates/jet-jit/src/Plugin.rs:593-646,721-783,793-814`: the JIT path calls `runtime::jet_plugin_call`, decodes the result, and maps failure through `plugin_error`; the interpreter path calls the same runtime symbol and maps decode/call errors to interpreter diagnostics. The host function declarations name `jet_plugin_load` and `jet_plugin_call` with checked handle/name/value-list/component-descriptor signatures (`:793-814`).
- Specification text records a zero-import application-plugin statement: the host “registers zero host imports” and filesystem/network/clock access fails at load (`docs/spec/spec.md:4519-4527`); the current local runtime source contains the typed host-import registration and authority checks cited above. No reconciliatory decision text was located in the bounded read.
- The specification also distinguishes native and sandbox host boundaries: one top-level `pub fn` export list is shared, native `jet build --lib` has no WASM runtime and is trusted, while `target=sandbox` uses the Component runtime and sandbox (`docs/spec/spec.md:4544-4564`).

### Not located in the bounded read

- A current ratified decision/card for a public application-`Plugin` call spelling that reconciles the historical `.call*` prose with current sema rejection was not located. The ratified export/version decisions above are present; the source/example mismatch is recorded separately by campaign claim `SCRIPT-C63`.
- A public `Plugin` close operation or plugin-specific public lifecycle decision was not located. The runtime-side close function is present, but the directly read public module registry exposes `load` only.

## 2. Hot reload, last-good state, and development replay

### Ratified entries

- `D-MEM-VIEWRET1=B`, ratified `2026-07-15`, card `#643`, allows named `View<T>`/`ViewMut<T>` across return/field boundaries only when sema proves the owner outlives the view and at most one mutable view is live (`docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2327-2336`).

## 1. CLI entry, typed options, and completion

### LAW

- `S12` defines `fn run()` as the entry point, with no required `pub`; it is fallible by default. `D-CLIFLAG1` is marked implemented (`c7cliflag`): `fn run(args: ServeArgs)` opts into typed CLI parsing. Struct fields derive `--flag` names/defaults/help from `#CLI` and field-level `#Doc("...")` markers, using bracket form matching `#Codable`. Jet has no `main` entry and no variadic entry signature. Raw argv remains explicit through `core.process.argv`. The existing `core.args` `ArgsSpec` builder is the non-entry parsing floor; typed entry generation lowers onto it rather than adding a second parser. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 216-229.)
- Bare top-level statements in a direct entry file are the body of one implicit fallible `fn run()`; declaration scope/order and the same entry law apply to `jet run`, `jet dev`, and `jet test`. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 231-239.)
- `D-COREARGS1=A` names `ArgsSpec` as the one CLI parsing model. Typed `fn run(args: T)` derives an `ArgsSpec`; library/tooling code may build the same spec dynamically for subcommands, environment fallbacks, completions, and tests. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3730-3732.)
- `D-JPK-DISCOVER1` names `jet search`/`jet info` plus LSP completion and hover for package names and typed option fields from a local offline index. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 5643-5657.)
- The marker registry exposes `CLI(pack: Ident{none})` on types and field-level `Flag`, `Short`, `Env`, and `Doc` markers. `Rename` has an `args` spelling among its format-specific names. (`LAW`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet#29DD`, lines 102, 126, 134-140.)

### SOURCE

- `Args.rs` identifies `D-ARGS1` as declarative CLI parsing. The builder accumulates a spec; `jet_args_parse` runs it against argv and returns parsed arguments or an error string; `jet_args_parse_or_exit` adds the conventional CLI boundary while keeping parsing pure. Builder methods consume the spec by value and return a new spec. (`SOURCE`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Args.rs#A44F`, lines 1-12.)
- The source parser's entry kinds are `Flag(name, short, help)`, `Option(name, short, help, meta, default, env, required, repeat, value)`, `Positional`, and nested `Subcommand(name, help, spec)`. Value kinds are `String`, `Int`, `Float`, and `Choice(Vec<String>)`. Parsed output stores flags, options, positionals, selected subcommand, and explicit-presence sets for flags/options. (`SOURCE`, `Args.rs#A44F`, lines 14-76.)
- Generated help renders `Usage: <prog> [positionals] [options]`; positional arguments precede options; option notes include required/repeatable/default/env/choices; `--help` is listed automatically and `--version` is listed when a version is specified. (`SOURCE`, `Args.rs#A44F`, lines 83-180.)
- `--help` is recognized by the parser but is not removed from argv by this layer; callers test `parsed.flag("help")`. Help text is available from `spec.help()` and `spec.help_auto()`. (`SOURCE`, `Args.rs#A44F`, lines 1-12.)
- `ArgsProjection.rs` projects one `JetArgsSpec` parse into a typed decoder and merges only explicitly present flags/options into settings; parse/shape failures are represented as `FieldError`. (`SOURCE`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/ArgsProjection.rs#3E5A`, lines 1-83; `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/ArgsProjectionCore.rs#3EF3`, lines 1-163, previously captured.)

This is a capture gap, not a runtime absence claim. The law only states that the shared `ArgsSpec` may be used for completions and that package/typed-option completion is supplied through the local offline-index LSP surface cited above.

## 2. Streaming and codecs

### LAW

- `D-ENCBIN1=A` selects CBOR (RFC 8949) as the canonical binary interchange format. Whole-value verbs are `parse`, `decode<T>`, `to_bytes`, and `to_bytes_canonical`; CBOR has no `to_string`. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/encoding-decisions.md#B16D`, lines 10-26.)
- `D-ENCSTREAM1=A` selects one adapter identity per codec, with whole-value and bounded reader/writer modes. The formats are exactly JSON, JSONL, CSV, XML, and CBOR. Reader/writer access is a mode of the same codec, not a second library. (`LAW`, `encoding-decisions.md#B16D`, lines 28-51.)
- `D-ENCSTREAM-SURFACE1=A` fixes codec-native synchronous pull handles. Shared `EncodingLimits`, `EncodingError`, `EncodingCause`, `EncodingFormat`, `EncodingErrorKind`, `DataEvent`, and `DataTree` live in `core.encoding`; format handles/options/events live in `core.encoding.json`, `.jsonl`, `.csv`, `.xml`, and `.cbor`; `FileReader`/`FileWriter` remain `core.files` types. JSON/JSONL/CSV/CBOR reader/writer types are opaque and non-`Codable`, non-`Copy`, non-`Clone`. Readers expose `next(&self)`, writers expose `write(&self)`, `flush(&self)`, and required idempotent `finish(&self)`. (`LAW`, `encoding-decisions.md#B16D`, lines 53-61; `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3836-3859.)
- The item algebra is format-specific but closed: JSON and CBOR use `DataEvent`; JSONL uses `DataTree`; CSV readers use `CSVRow`; CSV writers use `[String]`; XML uses the exact tagged `DataTree` algebra selected by `D-ENCXML1`. Calls are blocking and provide backpressure; no hidden task, queue, callback, partial-success state, or `WouldBlock` exists. Clean EOF follows structural/trailing-input validation; the first terminal error is retained. `finish` validates/flushes output and is required for success; successful finish is idempotent and writes after finish are `State` errors. (`LAW`, `encoding-decisions.md#B16D`, lines 59-72; `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3841-3857.)
- `EncodingLimits` fields are `buffer_bytes`, `max_depth`, `max_item_bytes`, `max_total_bytes: ?Int`, `max_expansion_depth`, and `max_expansion_bytes`; `safe()` values are `65536`, `256`, `16777216`, `None`, `32`, and `8388608`. The documented valid ranges are buffer `4096..16777216`, depth `1..4096`, item `1..1073741824`, total `None` or `0..Int.max`, expansion depth `0..256`, and expansion bytes `0..1073741824`. Constructors reject the first invalid field before IO with `Limit` and zero byte offset. (`LAW`, `encoding-decisions.md#B16D`, lines 59-65.)
- `D-ROWS1=A` keeps one CSV engine for whole-value and streaming records. `core.encoding.csv.rows(text, delimiter: ",", header: false, skip_blank: false) -> [CSVRow] !String` exposes delimiter/header/blank options; a delimiter is one character other than quote or a line ending; `header` skips the first logical record; `skip_blank` skips records with no field content; `CSVRow.line` is the one-based physical opening line, including multiline quoted records and records after CRLF. `csv.parse` and `csv.reader` share the same options and engine; `csv.reader.next()` returns `CSVRow`. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3861-3870.)
- `D-ENCXML1=A` selects lossless, namespace-aware ordinary-`DataTree` XML rather than an `XmlDocument`/`XMLEvent` type. It preserves ordered document/namespace/attribute data and lexical evidence; safe parsing never opens external identifiers or executes files, URLs, catalogs, external entities, parameter entities, or replacement markup. Exact XML/expansion limits reject rather than truncate. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3872-3891.)
- `D-JSONCANON1=A` defines strict RFC 8785 JCS in edition 2027: UTF-8 without BOM/LF/whitespace, array-order preservation, unsigned UTF-16 key ordering, rejection of duplicate keys/Bytes/non-finite numbers, and exact-representability requirements for `Int`. Whole `json.canonical` and `json.writer(canonical: true)` output/errors/bounds are byte-identical. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3893-3902.)
- `D-ENCBIN1=A / D-ENC-CBOR-SURFACE1=A` selects RFC 8949 CBOR. Untyped `DataTree` rejects byte strings, tags, bignums, non-text/duplicate map keys, and unsupported values rather than coercing; typed Codable `[U8]` uses native byte strings. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3904-3911.)

### SOURCE

- The current stream helper advances one item per pull, returns no further items after clean EOF, and makes errors terminal. `jet_encoding_fail` stores the first `EncodingError` and returns an equal snapshot on later calls. (`SOURCE`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/EncodingStream.rs#3535`, lines 1-44.)
- The source validates buffer/depth/item/total/expansion limits before constructing a reader/writer and calculates a codec heap ceiling from those bounds. The shown validation emits `EncodingErrorKind::Limit`, byte offset `0`, line/column `1`, empty path, and a field/range reason. (`SOURCE`, `EncodingStream.rs#3535`, lines 302-342.)
- The JSON reader constructor validates limits and stores owned input, limits, offsets, line/column, parser frames, root/EOF/terminal state, typed-number mode, allocation budget, and output-heap accounting. The JSON writer constructor validates limits and stores output, frames, root/finished/terminal state, byte totals, canonical mode, canonical frames, and retained canonical bytes. (`SOURCE`, `EncodingStream.rs#3535`, lines 519-563.)
- The current source therefore directly evidences the bounded pull/terminal-error/limit-validation/JSON reader-writer state machinery. The packet does not claim that every law surface is shipped on every execution tier; no runtime execution was performed.

## 3. Native distribution and artifact identity

### LAW

- Architecture R8 states that the root native build calls `rustc` directly with explicit profile flags, strips symbols, and uses thin LTO for optimized AOT. It honors explicit `RUSTC_LINKER`/`CC`, selects mold/lld through the C driver before the system linker, links content-addressed reachable runtime/Core rlibs, and emits one self-contained native binary. `jet build --small` is the size-minimal profile. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/architecture.md#E735`, lines 646-666.)
- Architecture R9 states that `jet run foo.jet` compiles/runs one complete file without a manifest, project folder, or config. `run`, `dev`, `check`, `build`, and `test` share the resolver; generated `.rs` remains standalone; user code does not create or require a Cargo project. (`LAW`, `architecture.md#E735`, lines 667-678.)
- Architecture R10 says imported Core namespaces are free until called; sema records called helpers and codegen emits only reachable helper templates. (`LAW`, `architecture.md#E735`, lines 679-693.)

### SOURCE: platform bundle plan

- `Bundler.rs` owns deterministic desktop/game package bundle plans and typed layouts. It explicitly does not invoke platform packers, signers, launchers, or update services; callers supply an explicit target and executable bytes, and a later platform adapter may materialize the layout. (`SOURCE`, `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Bundler.rs#4D99`, lines 1-9.)
- Bundle targets are explicit and not inferred from the host: `LinuxAppImage`, `MacOSApp`, and `WindowsMsix`; accepted parse aliases include `linux`, `appimage`, `macos`, `mac`, `app`, `windows`, and `msix`; artifact suffixes are `.AppImage`, `.app`, and `.msix`. Bundle intent is `Desktop` or `Game`. (`SOURCE`, `Bundler.rs#4D99`, lines 22-78.)
- `BundleExecutable` records the in-layout name, source path for receipt provenance, and exact executable bytes; its digest is SHA-256 over those bytes. (`SOURCE`, `Bundler.rs#4D99`, lines 81-108.)

### SOURCE: `.jetlib` native library boundary

- A `.jetlib` must pass compiler identity and declared-effect-grant checks before mapping. Compiler mismatch is a checked refusal (`E1338`); requesting effects beyond the host grant is refused (`E1339`). Identity is checked before claimed effects are trusted; the complete header, target, and exact export table are checked before writing/mapping payload. (`SOURCE`, `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/JetLib.rs#5C21`, lines 1-25.)
- The current `.jetlib` ABI constants are `ABI_VERSION: u32 = 2` and `ABI_IDENTITY = "jet.library.abi.v2;call=extern-c;scalar=homogeneous;access=read-write-move;text=jet-text-v1;ptr-len=checked-utf8"`. Native scalar values are `Int`, `Float`, `Bool`, `Text`; access conventions are `Read`, `Write`, `Move`. (`SOURCE`, `JetLib.rs#5C21`, lines 31-103.)
- Each export records name, emitted symbol, scalar, parameter count, and explicit ownership conventions. The stamp records compiler version/build, library name, optional entry, target/triple, linker identity, ABI identity/version, export table, declared effects, and payload digest; the artifact is the checked stamp followed by opaque native payload bytes. (`SOURCE`, `JetLib.rs#5C21`, lines 106-172.)

### SOURCE: bridge, lock, and CAS identity

- Foreign bridge identity schemas are `jet-ffi-bridge-identity-v1`, `jet-ffi-bridge-provenance-v1`, and `jet-ffi-boundary-v1`. An `ArchiveInput` with `bytes == None` records an absent/unreadable candidate and does not authorize fallback to a different host tool or guessed library. Identity records use ordered length-delimited fields and lowercase SHA-256. (`SOURCE`, `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/ForeignBridge.rs#8A08`, lines 1-18, 30-73.)
- `ForeignBoundaryIdentity` separately records source, overlay, generator, implementation, toolchain, and target; its derivation identity and digest include those fields. (`SOURCE`, `ForeignBridge.rs#8A08`, lines 75-140.)
- `LockedPackage` records name/version/source, exact locked revision when applicable, plan fingerprint, optional installed-tree `content_hash`, dependencies, runtime/effect provenance, envelope, receipt, and dependency provenance. (`SOURCE`, `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Lock.rs#B8AC`, lines 25-79.)
- `NixClosureRecord` is portable and content-addressed: it records channel/revision/system, signed index manifest, derivation/output/NAR hashes, size/compression, references, upstream proof, cache key, and project CAS bundle. Validation rejects missing/path-bearing/control-byte values and enforces the listed channel, system, digest, and compression forms. (`SOURCE`, `Lock.rs#B8AC`, lines 81-186.)

## 4. Tool installs, script dependencies, and package realization

### LAW: Jetpack/package tools

- `D-DEP-PY1 (=A)` permits CPython as a runtime-side dependency (libpython for embed plus interpreter for broker), not in `Source/`; it is hash-pinned and acquired only by projects using `py.*`. `D-JPK-EXTPROV1 (=A)` makes npm/PyPI/SwiftPM first-class Jetpack providers resolved by `<lib>: <lang>@"ref"`, fetched into the hangar, vendored and hash-pinned, offline-obeying, provenance-bound, and hash-verified on arrival. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3474-3481.)
- `D-JPK-TOOLCHAIN1` places a top-level `jet:` toolchain pin in `package.jet`; `.jet/lock` records the exact version. A differing Jet realizes the pinned toolchain into the hangar and executes it; the law states prebuilt-object/cache substitution, offline thereafter, no Nix requirement, and no daemon/root. `jet self toolchain` shows the pin and `jet update jet` moves it deliberately. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 4809-4819.)
- The Jetpack engine is a separate `jetpack` binary owning the user model, refs, lock, and shells; its named surface includes `env/use/add/remove` and `hangar list`/`hangar clean`. Nix is one provider behind the Core-first resolver; no alternate evaluator ships in Jetpack. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 5004-5010.)
- `D-JPK-BUILDTOOL1 (=A)` requires bridge crates to build with a pinned, realized Rust toolchain, using a hash-pinned hangar object or nixpkgs on Nix machines and an honest error otherwise; host cargo/rustc is not used. Same source plus same pinned toolchain yields the same output hash, and the toolchain ID enters provenance. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 5105-5110.)
- `D-JPK-BUILDRECIPE1 (=A)` limits executable adapters to `Recipe.build(steps: […])` with `.fetch(url:, sha256:)`, `.exec(tool:, args:)`, `.install(src:, dest:)`, and `.install_tree(src:, dest:)`. The parser lowers these into the existing `BuildStep` action graph; unknown/missing fields, unlocked fetches, invalid paths, cycles, and partial outputs remain errors; no ambient authority or second build mechanism is added. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 5240-5251.)
- `D-JPK-STORECLI1=D` assigns physical store verbs to `jetpack hangar`: verify, repair, copy, import, export, dump/restore, and sign. `jet explain`/`jet inspect dossier` own causal questions; `jetpack hangar clean` is the GC/optimization intent. Mutations use plan-before-apply and stable JSON; imports are verified and quarantined before registration. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 5979-5984.)
- `D-JPK-RESOLVEMODE1=D` limits resolver modes to `conservative`, `latest`, `lowest`, and `lowest-direct`; `jet update <pkg>` defaults to conservative and records rationale, while realize verbs never resolve. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 6026-6031.)

### SOURCE: manifest-less Jet script dependency path

- A `.jet` script may use `use pkg#version;`. `jet run` resolves/locks by file-content hash; `jet fetch --lock` writes `<script>.lock`; `jet init` lifts inline refs into a generated `package.jet`. Resolution is intentionally local/offline: `<script_dir>/.jet/inline-deps/<name>/<version>/` is checked first, then optional `JET_INLINE_DEPS_FIXTURES`; otherwise the result is unresolved `E1253`, never a fake success. (`SOURCE`, `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/ScriptDeps.rs#E248`, lines 1-20.)
- Exact three-part selectors such as `1.4.2` are considered pinned; looser selectors such as `1.4`, `1`, `latest`, and `*` are not reproducible without `jet fetch --lock`. Resolved records carry the selected directory and a content hash. (`SOURCE`, `ScriptDeps.rs#E248`, lines 60-80.)
- Resolution is a pure local directory lookup followed by source-tree hashing; it performs no network request and no code execution, and does not silently substitute a registry dependency for a local cache entry. (`SOURCE`, `ScriptDeps.rs#E248`, lines 93-129.)

## 5. Non-HTTP protocol APIs

### LAW

- `D-NETSOCKET1=A` defines `core.net` typed blocking-looking TCP/UDP/Unix/DNS/TLS APIs over task-compatible handles. Deadlines, cancellation, readiness, and high-concurrency serving share one socket model. String entrypoints are the beginner path; `IPAddr` and `SocketAddr` are the expert path. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3952-3956.)
- `D-NETDNS2=A` delegates ordinary IP resolution to the host resolver, preserving hosts files, search domains, VPNs, and enterprise policy. `DNSResolver.at` is the expert wire-resolver escape hatch; it uses unpredictable transaction IDs, validates sender/header/question and packet bounds, bounds compression/CNAME chains, retries truncated UDP over bounded TCP, and never invents a public resolver. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3957-3962.)
- `D-NETIO1=D` makes TCP, Unix, and TLS streams byte-canonical and conformant with file/codec stream operations; checked UTF-8 helpers project over bytes. UDP is packet-oriented and reports source, original length, and truncation. Half-close is explicit, close is idempotent, and later misuse returns `.Closed`. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3963-3967.)
- `D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A / D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B` establishes one nominal `core.io.Reader`/`core.io.Writer` byte-stream contract. Reads require a positive limit, return at most that many bytes, and reserve empty success for clean EOF. Writes may report a positive prefix; zero for nonempty input is an error; `write_all` loops. Close is inherent/idempotent, not a trait member. File/TCP/Unix/TLS/explicit codec adapters map native failures to the closed `IOError` tree. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3968-3977.)
- `D-IOERROR-TREE1=A` closes `IOError` to `InvalidInput`, `NotFound`, `PermissionDenied`, `TimedOut`, `Cancelled`, `Closed`, `Protocol`, and `Other`, each carrying `IOContext`. `IOContext` has `operation`, `resource`, `os_code`, and `cause`; `IOOperation` is exactly `Read`, `Write`, `Flush`, `Connect`, `Accept`, `Close`, `Resolve`, or `Codec`. Clean EOF is empty successful read; zero limits are `InvalidInput(.Read)`; no compatibility constructor or flat-string adapter remains. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3978-3989.)
- `D-NETERROR1=A` makes every fallible network operation return structured `NetError` with stable invalid-input, permission, address/connection-state, closed, timeout, cancellation, unsupported, DNS, TLS, protocol, and other-OS-failure variants; operation/address/name are stable data and OS code is optional audit data. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3990-3994.)
- `D-NETTASK1=A` requires blocking-looking calls on the one socket-handle family to observe current `#Context`, yield through the shared runtime where available, and obey the earliest context, persistent-socket, or explicit per-call deadline. Readiness is on the same handles; cancellation and expiry remain distinct `.Cancelled` and `.Timeout`. The law text then records implementation status for TCP reads/writes and shared AOT readiness. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3995-4001; capture ends at line 4001 for that subsection.)
- The same current decision index separately names typed URL and MIME modules (`core.url`, `core.mime`) and an email mechanism (`core.email`) with SMTP surface/config/DKIM decisions; this packet only captures the SMTP tail and does not claim source implementation for those modules. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3772-3807 and 3808-3835, previously read.)

### SOURCE

- The current prelude networking module states that networking uses `std::net` only, with the `wasm32-wasip2` `std::net` implementation as the shared `wasi:sockets` adapter. TLS uses the shared native callback bridge; AOT/JIT hosts marshal into these Prelude operations rather than implementing a second TLS policy. (`SOURCE`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/NetHTTP.rs#4483`, lines 1-6.)
- `JetTCPStream` carries closed/read-shutdown/write-shutdown state and optional read/write timeouts. The generic `JetIOReader` requires a positive read limit and returns `IOError`; `JetIOWriter` exposes `write` and `write_all`. (`SOURCE`, `NetHTTP.rs#4483`, lines 8-41.)
- Network errors are translated to `IOContext` and the shared IOError tree. The shown mapping includes invalid input, permission denied, timeout, cancellation, closed/not-connected, protocol, and other; operation/resource/OS-code/cause are populated from the network error detail. (`SOURCE`, `NetHTTP.rs#4483`, lines 43-75.)
- TCP, Unix, and TLS reader implementations reject non-positive limits with `InvalidInput`; their byte operations map to the shared IO error path. TCP/Unix/TLS writers expose `write` and `write_all`. (`SOURCE`, `NetHTTP.rs#4483`, lines 77-147.)
- The source `JetNetError` family includes invalid input, permission, address-in-use/unavailable, connection refused/reset/not-connected, closed, timeout, cancellation, unsupported, DNS, TLS, protocol, and other; DNS has `NotFound` and `Failure`. It also defines explicit `Read`, `Write`, `Both` shutdown and `Read`, `Write`, `ReadWrite` readiness interests, plus `JetIpAddr`, `JetSocketAddr`, `JetUDPSocket`, and `JetUDPPacket`. (`SOURCE`, `NetHTTP.rs#4483`, lines 149-226.)

# Narrow addendum: URL/MIME/email, FTP lookup, and tool-install index

## 7. Exact URL, MIME, and email decisions

- `D-URL1=A` is the ratified typed URL/MIME split. `core.url` owns `Url` parse/build/join/normalize, typed repeated query pairs, component percent-encoding, IDNA host handling, and `file:`/`data:` URLs. `core.mime` owns extension mapping and `type/subtype; param=value` parsing. `core.http` and `core.web` consume these typed values rather than re-solving string escaping. (`LAW`, `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3772-3776.)
- `D-EMAIL1=A` makes `core.email` the one provider-neutral email mechanism. The named surface is `Address`, `Message`, `Attachment`, `Envelope`, `Mailer`, `SMTPConfig`, `SMTPSecurity`, `SMTPAuth`, `DkimConfig`, `SendReport`, `RecipientReport`, and `EmailError`. `smtp_from_env` supplies verified STARTTLS beginner defaults; `smtp(config)` exposes the same `Mailer` with expert policy. Port 587 requires verified STARTTLS; port 465 TLS is explicit; STARTTLS never downgrades and password AUTH never crosses plaintext. MIME uses CRLF, bounded safe folding, Unicode encodings, content-derived collision-resistant boundaries, bounded attachments, and envelope-only Bcc. `RequireAll` rejects before `DATA` if any recipient is rejected; `DeliverAccepted` is explicit; `SendReport` means relay acceptance, not inbox delivery. `EmailError` distinguishes configuration, DNS, connect, TLS, auth, protocol, rejection, transient, timeout, cancellation, and `DeliveryUnknown`. No hidden retry, thread-per-send, raw transport error, credential disclosure, external dependency, or duplicate async API exists; DKIM signs final bytes and SPF/DMARC remain DNS policy. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3777-3792.)
- `D-EMAIL-SMTP-SURFACE1=A` fixes closed SMTP records/enums and one `Mailer.send(message)` mechanism. `Envelope` contains `from:Address` and `recipients:[Address]`; `email.envelope` validates it; `message.with_envelope` changes SMTP routing only, leaving MIME headers unchanged. `SMTPConfig` carries host, port, `.StartTls`/`.TLS`, `.None`/`.Password`, `.RequireAll`/`.DeliverAccepted`, verified system/system-plus-CA trust, and bounded `Limits`. `SendReport` records server, accepted/rejected recipient reports, final response, and acceptance time. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3793-3807.)
- `D-EMAIL-SMTP-CONFIG1=A` uses move-only redacted `Secret` for SMTP passwords. `Limits.safe()` is `512, 100, 100, 100, 33554432, 4096` for reply-line bytes, reply lines, capabilities, recipients, message bytes, and auth-challenge bytes; the source gives the corresponding checked ranges. `.SystemPlusCa(pem:[U8])` extends system roots while retaining DNS-name verification; empty/malformed/certificate-free PEM is rejected before credentials can be sent; no trust-all mode exists. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3808-3819.)
- `D-EMAIL-DKIM-CONFIG1=A` adds optional `dkim:?DkimConfig` to `SMTPConfig`. `DkimConfig` has exactly `domain:String`, `selector:String`, `private_key:Secret`, and `signed_headers:[String]`; signing is fixed to `ed25519-sha256` with relaxed/relaxed canonicalization over final MIME bytes. Invalid identity/header/key conditions fail as `EmailError.Configuration` before connecting; signing failure never falls back to unsigned delivery. `smtp_from_env` accepts DKIM only when all three required environment values are present, with optional signed-header override. (`LAW`, `syntax-decisions.md#0DB1`, lines 3820-3835.)
- The bounded implementation reads for this addendum did not include `core.url`, `core.mime`, or `core.email` implementation modules. The bullets above are law-source captures only; no implementation/runtime status is inferred.
